Nia Okundaye assesses houses for a living. She works for the county's hoarding and neglect program, which means her week is a list of addresses and a set of tools: a moisture meter, a tablet, a box of shoe covers, a paint fan she uses to name colors in notes in case anyone asks her, later, to testify. Each house pays a flat fee. The route is set by dispatch. She has thirty-five minutes per property and a supervisor who flags her if she runs long.

Her skill isn't reading people. It's reading rooms. She has stood in something like nine thousand houses and she can date a room to about the week it stopped being lived in. The last clean sliver of countertop. The mail fanned on the floor, escalating from coupons to shutoff notices to nothing. The chair pulled to a window and pulled back. She is not sentimental about any of it, which is why she's good at it.

She isn't a detective and can't be one. Her reports are confidential, they travel between two departments, and after a write-up two years ago she was told plainly that anything she observes goes in the file and nowhere else. She carries a phone older than her car and she keeps the notes app empty.

The reason she's in this story: the coroner's office releases a name, and Nia has been inside that house before. Twenty-two months ago. She filed the assessment herself, and the report in the system is not the report she wrote.

Imagine a very large apartment building. So large that nobody who lives in it has ever seen all of it, and nobody knows everyone. You live in one room. You want to ask a question of someone in another room, far away.

You can't walk there. The building is too big, and the halls twist. So you write your question on a piece of paper. You fold it, and on the outside you write where it should go. Then you slip it under your door into the hallway.

In the hallway there are people whose entire job is carrying paper. That's all they do, all day. One of them picks up your note. This carrier doesn't know the whole building either. He only knows a little: which way to go to reach the next hallway. He carries your note a short distance and hands it to another carrier, who knows a little more about that part of the building. That one hands it to another. The note gets passed along, room to room, hall to hall, until it reaches the person you named.

Here's the part that matters. If one hallway is blocked — a door stuck, a flood, a carrier who's sick — the note doesn't stop. The carriers just find another way around. There's always another path, because the building is woven together with hallways the way a cloth is woven with threads. No single hallway is the only way.

Sometimes your question is too big to fit on one piece of paper. So you tear it into many pieces, number them, and send each piece its own way. They may travel by completely different routes and arrive at different times. The person at the other end collects all the pieces and puts them back in order. If one piece is lost, she writes back and asks you to send just that piece again.

And some rooms aren't homes. They're storehouses — rooms full of shelves, where a note sits waiting. If you ask for something that's kept in a storehouse, the storehouse itself answers you, the same way a person would, by writing back. You don't know or care whether a person or a storehouse answered. All you know is a note came back.

So: the internet is that. Millions of rooms, no one in charge, no one who sees the whole thing. Just notes, addresses on the outside, and an enormous number of carriers who each know only their own small stretch of hallway — and who keep passing things along anyway, finding another way when one way is blocked.

The reason it keeps working is that no one has to know everything. Each carrier only has to know the next step.

Think of the internet as a library where nobody is allowed to walk to the shelves.

You sit at a desk by the door. You write what you want on a slip of paper, and you hand the slip to a runner. You never see the shelves. You have no idea which room your book is in, or which building, or which town. You just get a slip back, or a book.

Here is the part that surprises people. Nothing you ask for travels as one piece. Your request gets torn into small numbered pages, and each page goes out by a different runner, down whichever hallway happens to be moving that minute. Some go through the big downtown hall, some slip through back corridors, some go the long way around. Each page has the address of where it is headed written on it, and each runner only has to know the next doorway, not the whole journey. At the far end, a clerk collects whatever pages have arrived, puts them back in order, and if one is missing, sends a note asking for just that one page again.

Two things follow from this.

First, no single person anywhere understands the whole library. Not the clerks, not the runners, not the people who built the halls. Everyone knows their own doorway and the name of the next one. That is all it takes, multiplied a great many times.

Second, the library has no front door to close. There is no center to knock out. If a hallway collapses, the pages simply go a different way, maybe slower, and the desk at the far end waits a little longer. This is why it was built this way in the first place.

The desk you are sitting at is your computer. The card with your name and address that the clerk uses to send things back to you is what people call your connection. You do not own a piece of the library. You have a seat in it, and the seat has an address.

Who is the person you are explaining this to — someone elderly, someone from a village with no electricity, an office colleague?

Think of the internet as a postal system for a town that has no street names, only house numbers.

When you want a page, your device writes a letter that says, in effect, "send me the page at number 93.184.216.34," and drops it in the box at the end of your road. Your provider's sorting office takes it from there. Every town of letters is linked to other towns, and each sorting office keeps a list of which road leads toward which number. Nobody holds the whole map. Each office only knows its next stop.

The letter does not travel whole. It is cut into small envelopes, each with the sender, the destination and its place in the order. The envelopes can take different roads. One may pass through a busy hub, another through a quiet lane, and if a road is blocked, the office reroutes them. At the far end, the destination puts the envelopes back in order and reads the page.

The reply goes back the same way, cut into envelopes and rebuilt on arrival.

The part people find strangest is the naming. Numbers are hard to remember, so a directory, the domain name system, turns a name like "bakery.example" into its number, the way a phone book once turned a shop's name into a phone number. You type the name, the directory answers with the number, and the letters start moving.

So nothing ever goes straight from you to the page. It is a chain of small hand-offs, each one knowing only the next address, and the page arrives because every office along the way did its small job.

Think of the internet as a postal service that runs on a town's streets, with houses for every address.

Every time you ask for a page, your device writes a request on a slip of paper: "Please send me the page at this address." It puts that slip in an envelope and hands it to the nearest post box on your street. That box belongs to your home network, usually the box mounted on the wall of your house or flat, connected to the phone line or cable running into it.

The post box does not know where the letter needs to go. It hands the envelope to the sorting office at the end of your road, and that office hands it to the next one, and the next, until it reaches a central depot covering the whole city. Each office only needs to know which office is next. Nobody holds a full map of the town, and that is why the system keeps working when one road is closed: the envelope takes another route.

When the request reaches the building that holds the page, a worker there checks the address on the envelope, takes out the page, and folds it into several envelopes, because a whole page is too big for one. Each small envelope is numbered so that its order is clear. These go back out through the same network of offices, not necessarily by the same roads, and your device opens them, lays them in order, and shows you the page.

Think of the internet as a postal service that runs on a town's streets, with houses for every address.

Every time you ask for a page, your device writes a request on a slip of paper: "Please send me the page at this address." It puts that slip in an envelope and hands it to the nearest post box on your street. That box belongs to your home network, usually the box mounted on the wall of your house or flat, connected to the phone line or cable running into it.

The post box does not know where the letter needs to go. It hands the envelope to the sorting office at the end of your road, and that office hands it to the next one, and the next, until it reaches a central depot covering the whole city. Each office only needs to know which office is next. Nobody holds a full map of the town, and that is why the system keeps working when one road is closed: the envelope takes another route.

When the request reaches the building that holds the page, a worker there checks the address on the envelope, takes out the page, and folds it into several envelopes, because a whole page is too big for one. Each small envelope is numbered so that its order is clear. These go back out through the same network of offices, not necessarily by the same roads, and your device opens them, lays them in order, and shows you the page.

Think of the internet as a postal service that runs on a town's roads, with one difference: the letters are cut into pieces before they go out.

Say you want the recipe your aunt wrote on the back of a card. You ask her to mail it. The card is too big for one envelope, so she tears it into numbered strips, puts each strip in its own envelope, and writes the address on each. Each envelope takes whatever road is open at that moment. Some go through the market, some by the river bridge, and one may sit in a depot for a while if the bridge is shut. Nobody at any junction reads the whole card. Each post office only looks at the address and passes the envelope on.

At your end, the strips arrive in a jumble. Your own postbox collects them, puts them in number order, and once the last strip is in, the card is whole again. If one strip is missing, the box writes to your aunt and asks her to send that number again.

The address on each envelope is the only thing that matters to the roads. Your aunt's house has a number, the post office knows which way it lies, and that is the whole job. Each junction only needs to know the next stop.

The web is the part where you ask for things. Typing a web address is like giving the postbox the name of a shop. The postbox looks up the shop's address in a directory, sends your request out in strips, and the shop sends back the page in strips, which your box reassembles. Some shops are small houses with one clerk, and some are huge warehouses that answer from many copies of themselves at once, but to you it all looks like one place.

Marisol kept the sock. Not out of sentiment—she'd have said so, she says everything—but because when Petrov took his boots off after a shift, he balled one sock inside the other and left it standing on the deck like a small grey animal. She'd told him a hundred times. He'd done it a hundred times. It was the only thing on the whole station that ever moved without being asked.

She does the EVA alone now. The checklist still says TWO CREW, and she reads it out loud anyway, both parts, doing Petrov's voice bad on purpose, because he did her voice bad on purpose and she never got to win that argument.

The station smells like hot metal and the lemon packets from the ration boxes. She leaves one sock balled on the deck by the airlock. It's not a shrine. It's just that if she stops doing it, then the last thing he did on this station is the last thing he did, and there's nobody left to complain to about it.

Sometimes, in the sleep shift, she hears the fan in the number-two scrubber start its rattle—the one he swore was a bearing and she swore was a screw—and she lies there in the dark with her eyes open, furious and glad, waiting for him to be right.

The tomato plant was the only thing aboard that did not need her to be cheerful.

Mara had brought the seeds in a sandwich bag taped inside her locker, the way you'd smuggle something you weren't supposed to want. Nine weeks out, the first flower opened yellow and absurd in the grow-light, and she stood in front of it longer than she should have, until Teo knocked on the hatch to ask if she was alive.

"It's flowering," she said.

"Good for it," Teo said, and meant it, and went back to the galley where the four of them ate at a table built for six.

They were kind to her. That was the difficulty. Priya cut her hair in the mess on Thursdays and asked about her sister's wedding with real interest. Dov sent her the playlists he made for the long watches. Sam, who never said much, had quietly reassigned himself to her cleaning rotation twice without telling her. Mara loved them, and at night, in the narrow bunk, she could feel how much of her day went to being seen, correctly, by people who were never more than six feet away.

She was the only thing aboard that had been to Mars, and the only thing returning, and her job for the last four hundred days had been to keep the water moving. The toilet is not a toilet. It is a machine that runs vacuum through its lines and takes what you give it, and it hums while it works, and the hum has a pitch like a person on the other side of a wall, trying not to cry.

On Earth she had run a bike repair shop for nine years. She was good at her job in every one of them. She kept the water on the station and the water kept her, and the only other thing on the station with her was a mouse in a box in the docking module.

You would think it would be the light that got you. At first you do. You flip the panels and watch the dawn come up thirty times for nothing; you stand at the window and put your hand up against the cold and feel it as a wall of glass. You stop doing the camera, which is fine, it has long since stopped sending. Then you stop noticing the window at all, which is the smaller death. The stations are not dim, the corridors are not gray. They are the color of a carpet in a van. You live in a van. You have been living in a van for a year and you cannot remember to want to get out. You cannot remember to want to get out.

The mouse knew. She was not supposed to care about the mouse. She was supposed to keep it alive, and there was a difference; she kept the thing alive and did not name it, and did that mean they were calling the mouse by nothing, and that was worse. She did not name it.

But the mouse was company. She could say it. The mouse was company. The mouse was a single living thing, and its hunger was its own, and the flecks of water on the wall were shed by its body and not by the machine and this was the closest thing to a person she had.

The mission voice was a person. The voice came in the fourth second, and the fourth second was the wall between them, and the fourth second was the entire point of the mission. They said, "Copy that," and, "We can see the tank," and, "Y'all are doing real good," and she could hear the third of the fourth second in the room, and the room was the air between them, and the room was also a person, and the room couldn't move.

Then the mouse was dead. The box was designed to make it not die, so she was the one who made it die. She took the box and the mouse and she put it in the airlock and cycled the airlock, and it did not die. It died in the air, the way the air was not the air, and then the box was in the air and her hand was still in the air a second later, and she had killed the mouse and she was still here. She had a fever, and the fever was a fever, and it was not a strange thing. She was the only person in the world.

She did not lie to the room, not exactly. She said "the specimen was euthanized," which was a way to say she used her hands and her own judgment. She heard the room say copy. She heard the room say the room. She went to the toilet. She moved the water. The tank was low and the tank was the only thing she had to save. She stood there and called the tank a name, a small sound, the way she used to call the mouse. It was the name of the mouse. She put it in the tank and it came back to her in the drinking.

She read the manual that said a normal person in an isolated space would be fine. She held the manual and it was the weight of a life and the weight of a life was the same as a life. She knew they had been engineering this, the fever and the water and the small sound, and she went with the lines and the lines were good and the lines were the human beings of the world.

She could not go back. She could go back. She was at month four hundred and she could go back and she did the training and she had the world in the window, and the window was the world, and the world and the window were not the same, and the world was the woman who was a stranger and the world was the woman who couldn't do nothing. The world was the woman who was her and the world was the woman who did this. She had made this and the world was the world and she was a good person and the world was a good person and the world was the world and she was not.

The moon was the color of the moon. The moon was the moon. The human being was the mouse was the moon was the tank and the tank was the line. In the afternoons the water moved and the line moved. The water was a body and the line was a human being and she was a line and the line was the human being and the water was the human being and the human being was the line.

A tank is a line. A tank is a line. The line is the water and the water is the human being and the human being is the human being and the human being is the moon.

The moon was the color of the moon.

The desk still had a nameplate, though someone had tried to take it off. A rectangle of cleaner wood sat under the screws, brighter than the rest of the surface, the way skin looks under a bandage.

"Ah, that's yours now," said Marisol, who was showing me around and had already told me she had been here eleven years. She didn't look at the desk when she said it. "IT will bring a new one."

The monitor had a sticky note on it in handwriting I didn't know yet: *Do NOT delete the 2am backup. Ask Marisol.* I read it twice, then peeled it off and put it in the drawer with the pens and the single wooden chopstick and the cough drop, unwrapped and fossilized.

Nobody said his name all morning. I learned the shape of him anyway. He'd liked his chair a little lower than I did. The drawer on the left was stiff because he'd yanked it too hard maybe a thousand times. The keyboard's W key was worn down to a pale shine, which meant he typed "we" a lot, or "what", or "why". I found a coffee ring on the desk that had soaked into the wood and would not come out, the way some proof does not come out.

"Everything's on the drive," Marisol said, when I asked where the files were. "Should be."

The first email I opened was from a client named Dovetail asking, for the third time, about something called the Marchetti report. I didn't know what the Marchetti report was. I searched the drive. There were forty-one files with that word in the name, and none of them opened, and one of them opened and was blank, and one of them was a photograph of a parking lot.

I sat in his chair and turned it down a click.

Around two the printer started, on its own, and spat out a single page. It was a schedule for next week, and at the top, in the header, the old name. Nobody had updated the template. The page came out warm. I held it for a second before I put it in the recycling, and then took it back out and put it in the drawer with the chopstick. Not sentimental. I just didn't want to be the one who threw it away.

Marisol walked past and stopped.

"You found the Marchetti thing yet?" she said.

"No."

"Yeah," she said. "He never gave it to us either. We told the client we'd look." She drank her tea. "You want lunch? The place on the corner is bad but fast."

At four I finally got my password to work. My name populated the corner of the screen, small and clean, mine. I wrote an email to Dovetail that said I was new and would find out and get back to them by Thursday, and sent it before I could decide not to.

Then I turned the chair back up one click, because it wasn't my chair yet, and went to find the bad place on the corner.

The glove came back to Dana Ferrier's bench in a padded envelope with a note clipped to the cuff. *Left thumb, seam split at the second joint. Patched with the grey tape, not the white, sorry, we were out of white. Hope the grip holds. —Ops, Suit Lab 3.*

Dana turned it over under the lamp. The stitching was a little uneven, the way a person stitches when they are thinking about something else. She knew, because she had done it herself for eleven years. She ran her thumb along the tape and felt the place where the seam had been.

Somewhere above the Pacific, a woman she had never met was living inside a suit Dana had checked. That was the arrangement. Dana sealed the joints, pressure-tested the rings, sent back the gloves with a note, and in return got a blank orbit's worth of silence. The suits went up and the suits came down. Nobody on the crew had ever asked her name.

She wrote back on the form that goes in the outgoing box. *Patch accepted. Grip should hold. Thumb is the first thing to fail on a long EVA, so keep an eye on it.* Then, because the form had no room for the thing she meant, she wrote on the back: *The grey tape is fine. I like it better.*

The next week there was a note on the returned hood. *Noted. Grey is fine. Tell whoever you share the bench with that the left thumb held for six hours. Also the coffee in this station tastes like a warm penny. —E.*

Dana laughed, alone at the bench at two in the morning, and was startled by the sound.

After that the notes grew. A joke about the cold. A list of what the crew was eating, which was always too much rehydrated chicken. A question about whether the ground ever really got dark on Tuesdays. Dana answered each one on the back of the form, folded the form into the envelope, and sealed it herself. She stopped using the printed labels on the envelopes.

She never saw the woman's face. She saw the woman's hands, in the sense that she saw every glove the woman had ever worn, and she knew where they wore thin, which fingers pressed hardest, which seam tore first. She knew the woman talked to herself while suiting up. She had learned this from a note that said only: *Gloves are fine. I told the thumb to hold and it listened.*

In March the notes stopped for nineteen days. Dana kept checking the box. On the twentieth day a new suit arrived with a glove still warm from the transit case, and tucked beneath the wrist ring was a folded sheet.

*Long shift. Mission extended. I've been sitting by the window a lot. The planet looks smaller from here than it ought to, and I keep wanting to tell someone about it. You're the only one I can tell who knows what the thumb is supposed to feel like.*

Dana read it twice. Then she pulled the grey tape from the spool, cut a strip, and began to mend the thumb before she had even looked at it, the way you start a conversation with someone you are already sure is listening.

The inventory log on Station Hadley-3 was the only document that never asked how she was doing, so Ilse Varga kept it honest.

Pantry, aft bay. Freeze-dried chili, forty-one pouches. Chili is the one item the crew rotated on purpose, because Pell hated it and she liked it, and for two years the cabinet was a small treaty with an empty chair at dinner. Pell had been gone eleven weeks. The chili stayed.

She counted it on Tuesdays. Thirty-nine on the second Tuesday after the transfer, forty on the next, because she had miscounted and then remembered that Odell had swapped one for a bag of pretzels as a joke nobody laughed at. She wrote down forty and did not correct it. Corrections were how you told yourself a thing was getting better.

The air handlers hummed in the frequency they hummed in, a note she no longer heard unless she tried. Out the port the planet filled a third of the frame, its night side pricked with the lights of cities she could name by shape. Somewhere in one of them a woman named Mirela had a standing video call with her mother every Thursday, and Ilse had once overheard the whole thing through a bad link, the two of them arguing over a cake recipe that neither had ever actually made.

The ration schedule was printed on the galley wall in a font chosen by someone who believed in order. Breakfast at 0700, not 0701. The water tab was due at 1400. Under the tab, in the fine print, a line she had never noticed until the quiet got loud: *Consume crew meals together where possible.* Where possible. She laughed out loud, one bark, and the sound went flat against the bulkhead.

Mission control pinged at 1100 to ask about the coolant loop. She answered in full sentences. Yes, pressure nominal. No, nothing unusual. The controller, a man whose voice she recognized and whose name she had never asked, said, "Copy, Hadley. Good work," with the faintly bored warmth of someone reading from a card. Then, after a pause that was longer than protocol: "You doing okay up there?"

She looked at the chili.

"Forty pouches," she said. "Pantry's squared away."

A long hiss on the line, like someone breathing out through a straw. "Copy, forty," he said, and she understood that he had written it down too, somewhere in a log of his own, and that he would not know what it meant either.

After the call she opened a pouch, added water from the warmer, and sat at the table with the schedule above her. She ate slowly. At 1400 she took the water tab, as required. Then she typed one more line into the log, under the count:

*Pantry: 40 chili. Dinner: 1. Still cooking for two.*

She left it in. Nobody would be checking that field. Outside, the night side of the world turned under the station, and the lights of the cities kept coming on in an order that had nothing to do with her.

The inventory log on Station Hadley-3 was the only document that never asked how she was doing, so Ilse Varga kept it honest.

Pantry, aft bay. Freeze-dried chili, forty-one pouches. Chili is the one item the crew rotated on purpose, because Pell hated it and she liked it, and for two years the cabinet was a small treaty with an empty chair at dinner. Pell had been gone eleven weeks. The chili stayed.

She counted it on Tuesdays. Thirty-nine on the second Tuesday after the transfer, forty on the next, because she had miscounted and then remembered that Odell had swapped one for a bag of pretzels as a joke nobody laughed at. She wrote down forty and did not correct it. Corrections were how you told yourself a thing was getting better.

The air handlers hummed in the frequency they hummed in, a note she no longer heard unless she tried. Out the port the planet filled a third of the frame, its night side pricked with the lights of cities she could name by shape. Somewhere in one of them a woman named Mirela had a standing video call with her mother every Thursday, and Ilse had once overheard the whole thing through a bad link, the two of them arguing over a cake recipe that neither had ever actually made.

The ration schedule was printed on the galley wall in a font chosen by someone who believed in order. Breakfast at 0700, not 0701. The water tab was due at 1400. Under the tab, in the fine print, a line she had never noticed until the quiet got loud: *Consume crew meals together where possible.* Where possible. She laughed out loud, one bark, and the sound went flat against the bulkhead.

Mission control pinged at 1100 to ask about the coolant loop. She answered in full sentences. Yes, pressure nominal. No, nothing unusual. The controller, a man whose voice she recognized and whose name she had never asked, said, "Copy, Hadley. Good work," with the faintly bored warmth of someone reading from a card. Then, after a pause that was longer than protocol: "You doing okay up there?"

She looked at the chili.

"Forty pouches," she said. "Pantry's squared away."

A long hiss on the line, like someone breathing out through a straw. "Copy, forty," he said, and she understood that he had written it down too, somewhere in a log of his own, and that he would not know what it meant either.

After the call she opened a pouch, added water from the warmer, and sat at the table with the schedule above her. She ate slowly. At 1400 she took the water tab, as required. Then she typed one more line into the log, under the count:

*Pantry: 40 chili. Dinner: 1. Still cooking for two.*

She left it in. Nobody would be checking that field. Outside, the night side of the world turned under the station, and the lights of the cities kept coming on in an order that had nothing to do with her.
</final>

Vosk sleeps from 0400 to 1200. I sleep from 1600 to 2400. There is a four-hour overlap, which is the only time the station has two people in it, and she spends most of it in the centrifuge bay, which has no camera, doing stretches that the medical officer on the ground calls non-compliant.

I know this because I read her logs. She knows I read her logs. That is the arrangement: eight people, four sleep shifts, a rotating roster that the scheduler reshuffles every eleven days so nobody's circadian rhythm settles. It's for the bones. It's for the psychology, the flight surgeon says, and I've decided not to ask which of us the psychology is for.

We leave each other things. Not notes — we tried notes. The station's messaging system time-stamps everything and the ground reads it, so a note becomes a document, and a document becomes a concern. Instead: she leaves the good bulb of the water reclaimer installed when it's my shift. I leave the torch where she'll find it. Once I found a single sock of hers wedged behind the exercise rack, and I knew it wasn't an accident, and I put it in the laundry anyway, because the ground reads the laundry manifest too.

The four-hour overlap is the worst part. Not the absence — the nearness. She's two bulkheads away, awake, moving through the same recycled air. I've stood in the node with the hatch open and heard her breathing. I didn't say anything. Neither did she. There's an etiquette to it, and the etiquette is: don't make the other one choose.

The flight surgeon asked last week if I felt isolated. I said no. I said the station is well-lit and the food is fine and I speak to the ground twice a day. All true. The lie was in the word isolated, which means *alone*, which I am not. I have never once been alone up here.

I'm something else. There isn't a word for it in the checklists. Eight people, and the station is a long hallway where you can hear someone's whole life happening through the wall and never knock.

Vosk's shift starts at 0400. I go off at 1600. For four hours we're both up there, breathing the same air, and then she goes to the centrifuge bay and I go to my bunk and the air moves on without either of us.

Tomorrow the roster reshuffles. Eleven days from now it reshuffles again. The bones will be fine.

Marisol got to the office at seven because she wanted to be the kind of person who got to the office at seven. The lights were off. She stood in the corridor with her bag against her legs and listened to the building hum, and at seven-forty a woman came down the hall carrying two coffees and a ring of keys, and said, "You're early," in a way that meant she was not.

"I'm Paul," she said. "Short for Paula. Nobody's called me Paula since 1994."

She unlocked the door and put one coffee on the desk by the window. The other she kept. She showed Marisol where the coats went, where the good stapler was hidden, which drawer stuck. "Don't use the microwave at noon," she said. "Terry from Claims heats fish."

There were four desks. One held a dying fern. Paul's had a photograph of a dog and a stack of paper an inch and a half thick with a binder clip on top.

The work was reconciling invoices against a system that had been built in 2006 and had opinions. Paul sat beside her for the first hour and did not touch the mouse. When Marisol made an error she said, "Okay. So why did that happen," and made her find it, and when she found it, Paul wrote something in a small notebook, which Marisol pretended not to see.

At lunch Paul took her to the sandwich place, and over the second half of a turkey club she said, "They're having me write it down. The whole thing. Every exception, every workaround, so that it's—" she turned her hand over. "So it's not just in my head."

"Because you're retiring?"

"Because they're going to move it to a team in Hyderabad and the team in Hyderabad has never met an invoice like the Hensley account." She said it lightly. She was sixty-one and had been doing this for nineteen years and had a knee that hurt in the rain, and she told Marisol all of it before the check came.

Back at the desk, she pulled the binder-clipped stack across and set it between them. "This is you," she said. "Every time you hit something that isn't in the system, you write it here. In a year you'll have your own."

Marisol said, "In a year you'll—" and stopped.

"I'll be in Portugal," Paul said. "There's a man there. Long story."

At four-fifteen Paul went to a meeting, and Marisol was alone with the invoices and the stuck drawer and the good stapler. She hit an exception at four-forty. A vendor had been paid twice, in 2019, and someone had noted it in the margin in pencil in handwriting that wasn't Paul's. She looked at the desk by the window, at the fern that had clearly been somebody's, and understood that the chair she was sitting in had a history, and that she was the fourth person to sit in it since the fern's owner left, or maybe the fifth.

She wrote the exception in the notebook in her own hand, dated it, and drew a box around it because she liked boxes.

At five Paul came back with her coat already on. She looked at the notebook, at the box, and laughed once through her nose. "Good," she said. "That's the first one. Keep the pen."

She left. Marisol stayed another ten minutes doing nothing, then turned off the light over the desk by the window and went out through the corridor, which was dark again, and hummed, badly, the whole way to the elevator.

The badge printer was cold when Marcus got to it. He held his thumb on the pad, and the machine considered him, and the plastic came out with his name and a small color photograph taken four years ago, when he still had the beard.

He had come in early to clear the drawer.

The desk was the third one back from the window, and it had already been emptied by someone else. Facilities did it Friday, he guessed, because the framed photograph of his daughter was face-down in a cardboard box with the tape still soft. The drawer had been wiped. There was a smell of lemon cleaner and, underneath, the smell of the building itself, which was carpet and coffee and the cheap plywood of the shelves.

At eight-twelve the elevator opened and a woman came down the hall with a lanyard already around her neck, badge facing out, and stood at the desk and looked at the empty chair.

"Hi," she said. "I think this is me."

"That's you," Marcus said.

He showed her the drawer. He showed her the coffee machine and the fact that the middle button made tea water and nothing else, and the fact that the left-hand cabinet was where the good mugs were, and the fact that someone named Denise took the good mugs and never brought them back. He showed her how to log in, which required a password change every ninety days, and how to log in again, which was the real lesson, and he did not tell her that his own login had been deactivated at ten-forty the night before, because she would learn that soon enough.

She asked good questions. That was the thing. She asked what the Thursday meeting was actually for, which was a question nobody there had answered in nine years.

He told her what he knew: that the Thursday meeting was for a decision that had been made on Tuesday, and that the woman at the far end would start with the weather and end with a number, and that the number would not change.

She wrote it down. He thought about the notebook in his own drawer, which was in the box now, and how he had written the same note down once, in blue ink, and how the notebook had been useless and important anyway.

At nine-thirty the department manager came by and shook her hand and said, *We'll get you set up,* and shook Marcus's hand too and said, *Good luck out there,* in the voice of a man who believed it.

At noon she went to the deli on the corner with someone from the other team, and Marcus took his lunch out of a plastic bag on the bench by the loading dock and ate half a sandwich and put the other half away. He had sixty emails forwarded to his personal account and he read eleven of them and did not answer any.

At two o'clock there was a fire drill. Eight minutes standing in the parking lot with everyone else, the sun in their eyes, the alarm still ringing in the stairwell behind them. She found him near the bike rack and stood there and said, "Is it always like this?"

"Once a month," he said. "They never tell you which month."

She laughed. He had not meant it as a joke.

At four-forty he carried the box out through the loading dock, because the front door would have meant the lobby and the lobby would have meant someone stopping him. The box was not heavy. He put it in the trunk and sat in the driver's seat and looked at the building, which had no window on the third floor where he could see anything he recognized.

At five-ten he started the car.

Somewhere behind him, on the third floor, the woman at the third desk from the window was trying the middle button on the coffee machine.

**Soundings**

The lead goes down on its own line
and comes up greased with the bottom:
gray ooze, a smear of shell.
The leadsman calls what the line tells—
by the mark, and a quarter less—
and the sea is given a number
it does not argue with.

Six fathoms here. Thirty there.
The line runs out and the hand stops
and what the hand cannot reach
is not the deep. It is the length
of the rope.

At night the bottom is the same
bottom, dark on dark,
and the line still finds it,
tallow cold against the mud,
carrying up a little of the floor
to say: this much, and no more.

The tide goes out and the number
changes under the same water.
The sea was never asked to hold still.
It only lets the line down
into whatever it is now.

A week inland, you find it still on you.
The cuff of your coat has kept its own small weather.
Salt sits in the seam the way a thought sits
in the back of a mouth before it's said.

A tide came up the floorboards overnight.
You tell yourself it didn't. There is a ring
on the table leg the height of the table leg.
You count it anyway, the way you'd count

the ribs of something that had hauled itself
onto the beach and not gone back.
Somewhere the landlord of all this
is sweeping the same water from the same porch.

You are dry now. Dry as a nail.
And still, at the back of the throat,
that low, habitual dragging, like a drawer
opened in another room, and shut.

**Weather from Below**

There is no surface here, so no sky to report.
What falls is not weather exactly:
a steady drift of shell, of glass-winged plankton,
of the small hard ears of squid, coming down
for weeks, for months, the way snow would
if snow were made of everyone who finished.

A whale passes and is a blizzard in reverse.
It takes a rib cage a decade to reach us.
We are patient. We are the floor.
We keep what the light was done with.

Above, a man in a boat calls this a calm day.
Below, it is always settling.
The bone arrives. The bone lies down.
Nothing is asked to come back up.

Below, it is always settling.

The card reader beeped red at the lobby turnstile, and the security guard, a man named Desmond with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair, looked at the screen and then at Priya with the patience of someone who had done this before.

"New?"

"Today," she said. "Priya Anand. Accounts payable."

He typed. The screen said nothing she could read from where she stood. "Your badge is in the system," he said. "It just hasn't been told yet. Give it till nine."

She waited by the potted fig. At nine-oh-four the reader blinked green and she walked through, feeling absurdly like she had passed an exam.

Her floor was the fourth. The door to it was another card reader, and it also said no. She tried twice more, then stood there holding the badge like a stranger's passport until a woman in a cardigan came out of the stairwell, swiped her own card, and held the door with her hip.

"Left the rest of us out in the cold too, the first week," the woman said. "I'm Bev. You'll be in the cubicles at the back, next to the printer. It sounds like a dying animal but it's harmless."

The printer did sound like a dying animal. Priya's desk had a mug already on it, a plant with three leaves, and a sticky note that said WELCOME in someone's careful handwriting. Her manager, a tall man named Okafor, came by at ten to say hello and to ask whether she had found the coffee. She had not. He showed her the machine behind the copier, the one that took cups, and told her the trick was to hit it twice.

At eleven she was given an invoice to check and a login that worked on the first try. She found a mismatch in the second column, a vendor billed twice, and sat looking at it for a long time before she walked it over to Bev's desk.

"Oh," Bev said, reading. "Oh, that's the old contractor. Nobody caught that. Good." She didn't make a fuss. She just initialed the page and handed it back.

At lunch Priya ate a sandwich on the bench by the fig and watched people come through the lobby, swiping and nodding at each other, none of them looking at the reader at all. She thought about Desmond, and the card that had been told at nine, and how long it had taken for the building to decide she belonged.

When she went back up, the fourth-floor door opened for her on the first swipe.

The sea keeps the accounts.
Each evening it walks the beach
and collects what the day dropped:
a shoe, a child's red spade,
the blue cap of a bottle,
a name written in wet sand.

Every morning it comes back
with the receipts.
Here is the shoe. Here is the spade.
Here is the name, a little softer,
pressed flat and returned
without a word of apology.

I have stopped asking why it does this.
I bring my own things down the steps
and set them on the tideline,
and wait for the water to read them,
and turn them over, and send them back.

My grandmother never saw the sea
and still kept it in the kitchen.
Every Sunday she boiled the water down
until the pot gave up its white,
and the grains sat in the bottom of the pan
like something that had been left behind.

She said it had to be stirred clockwise,
or the fish would forget the way home.
I stirred it wrong once, when I was nine.
She didn't scold. She just tapped the spoon
against the rim and said, "Well, they'll manage."

Now I cook the same way, badly,
tasting my own tears in the broth
and calling it a family recipe.
The jar on the windowsill still holds
a little of what she kept.

The shell says ocean
when you hold it to your ear,
but it is only the blood in you
going round, as it always does,
making a sea out of the quiet.

whether anyone is listening.

a small hollow that borrows the tide
and gives it back to me
in the one place I can hear it.

The desk had been cleared, but not quite. Someone had left a pencil in the drawer, sharpened down to a stub, and a strip of masking tape on the underside of the blotter that said *Don't trust the 3rd floor printer*, in a hand that pressed hard on the T.

Ines found it at 8:40, twenty minutes before anyone else arrived, because she had not been able to sleep and had decided that arriving early was a kind of competence. The building smelled of toner and somebody's microwaved fish. Her badge opened the door on the first try, which felt like a small, rare mercy.

Her title was Records Coordinator. Nobody had been able to tell her, in the interview, exactly what that meant, only that the last person had "kept things straight."

At nine, Dev from accounts came by with a coffee he did not offer her and a clipboard he did. "You're taking over the Hollis binders," he said, and then, seeing her face, "Don't worry. They're just the ones with the coloured tabs. The rest is mostly ghosts."

The binders lived on a steel cart by the window. Forty-one of them, each labelled with a year and a region and, in the margins of the older ones, notes in that same hard-pressing hand. *Call before the 14th. Mrs. Adair takes her tea without the cream, don't ask why.* *Bring the good stapler, not the stapler.* In 2016, a single line: *If you're reading this, you're doing fine.*

She read the note twice and laughed out loud, and a woman two desks away looked up and smiled as if she had been waiting for that.

"Mariam," the woman said, holding out a hand. "I sat next to Teodor. The one who wrote all over everything." She nodded at the margins. "He retired last spring. Said he'd leave the place better than he found it, and then he left it exactly as messy, just more organised about it."

By eleven Ines had matched four binders to four phone calls, found the printer on the third floor that did not, in fact, print, and learned which elevator could be coaxed. Mariam showed her the kitchen, the fridge with the shelf that was the unofficial lunch pool, and the window in the stairwell where the light came through green in the afternoons.

At half past three there was a request in her inbox from a client wanting a file from 2011. Her stomach dropped. She opened the cart, found the year, ran her finger down the spines, and there it was, tagged in yellow, with a note in the margin: *Under the other binder. It's always under the other binder.*

It was. She sent the file with two minutes to spare, and the reply came back in four words: *Perfect. Thank you, Ines.*

She stayed until six, longer than she needed to, writing her own first note on a sticky tab and pressing it inside the cover of the binder she had used most: *Mrs. Adair takes the tea with cream now. Don't ask why. Good luck.*

Then she went home, and the next morning she came in at 8:40, and the pencil in the drawer was still there, and she left it where it was.

**THE SPATULA**

It does one thing.

It will not dice. It will not spiralize. It has no app, no twelve attachments, no opinion about your health.

It turns things over so they don't burn on one side. That's the whole job. It has been the whole job for a hundred years, and nobody has improved on it, because there is nothing to improve.

The blade is thin enough to get under an egg and stiff enough to lift a burger. The handle is one piece, so there's no seam for grease to live in. It has a small bend near the neck. That bend is the only clever thing about it, and it took someone decades to think of it.

It will outlive the pan. It will outlive the stove. Give it to someone when you die, and they'll use it, and they won't think about you every time — they'll think about you maybe twice a year, standing at the stove, and that's the correct amount.

Sold at the hardware store, probably, for four dollars.

One thing. Done well. Every day. For as long as you need it.

The badge arrived on Tuesday, two days before Maren was supposed to start, in a padded envelope with a note that said only *Welcome aboard, don't lose this*. It had her photo on it. She looked like someone who had been caught doing something.

On Monday she walked the four miles to the Greyhook Light Authority depot because the bus schedule had lied to her. The gate guard, a man named Oyelaran with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair, checked her name against a clipboard and said, "You're the new keeper."

"I'm the new maintenance tech."

"Same thing out here." He handed her a key on a red lanyard. "Desk's in the back. Don't touch the radio until Benedikt shows you the switch. It's temperamental, like the last one."

The last one had been Hal Pruitt, who had kept the Dunmore Point light for thirty-one years before his heart gave out in a parking lot. Maren had read about him in the job posting, which had praised his dedication, and in the paper, which had printed a photo of him in a fisherman's sweater, squinting. She had not expected to inherit his desk. She had not expected the desk to be full.

It was full of paper. Logbooks, stacked and rubber-banded, spines labeled in careful capitals: *TIDES. LAMP HOURS. FOG. SHIPS SIGHTED. WEATHER, 1988–1991.* Someone had written a small note on the top one in pencil: *Start here. —H.*

Benedikt, when he came in, was a broad man with paint on his knuckles who looked at the stack and laughed. "He never let anyone clear that desk. Said there was nothing in there but the job."

"Is that true?"

"It's true that he thought it was." He pulled out a chair. "Read the top one. Then tell me what's wrong with the lamp at Dunmore."

She opened the book. The entries were brief and exact. *0410. Wind NNE, 12 kn. Lamp steady. Gull on the rail, will not move.* *0415. Gull moved.* On a page in late October: *Ferry late, probably the fog. Waited. Ferry came. Good.* Nothing else. Thirty-one years of mornings, each one a line or two.

She read until the window went from gray to white. Benedikt came back twice with tea and didn't speak. By noon she had worked out three things about the lamp: its bearing was off by a degree, its oil was consumed faster in the cold, and Hal had written the same fix on four separate dates, as though he had needed to remind himself.

She found the fifth date. It was nine years old and said: *Didn't fix it. Told myself next week. Still meant to.*

Maren sat with that for a while. Then she took a pen from the cup and wrote under it, in her own small hand: *Fixed it, 2:15 p.m. Still working.*

Benedikt looked over her shoulder when he came back. He read it, grunted, and set down a fresh mug beside her elbow. "Good," he said. "Now the radio."

She has been in the drawer eleven years. She started pale and square-shouldered, the color of new pine.

You use her for the sauce, because the metal one burns the sauce and she does not. You use her for the eggs. You use her to fish the olive out of the jar when company is coming and you are pretending everything is fine.

Nobody has to tell her any of this. A wooden spoon knows by the handle.

Here is what eleven years does to a spoon: the bowl thins on one side because you stir counterclockwise. The edge softens where it meets the pot, which means it has learned your pot. The handle has a shine in one spot, worn by your hand and no one else's, and the shine is slightly off-center. Not where a hand would go. Where *your* hand goes.

You could buy a new one. They cost about a dollar. It would be straight and pale and it would hate the pan and it would sit in the drawer and it would still be new in 2035.

This one has about four hundred more sauces in her. Then you will break her against the rim of a pot, badly, at the worst moment, because they always go in the middle of something.

She won't mind. She was never saving anything up.

They're in the drawer at the hardware store. Bottom aisle. Loose, in a bin, no packaging, no labels, a dollar each. Pick the one that already feels like yours. It won't yet.

Nobody has to tell her any of this. A wooden spoon knows by the handle.

Here is what eleven years does to a spoon: the bowl thins on one side because you stir counterclockwise. The edge softens where it meets the pot, which means it has learned your pot. The handle has a shine in one spot, worn by your hand and no one else's, and the shine is slightly off-center. Not where a hand would go. Where *your* hand goes.

You could buy a new one. They cost about a dollar. It would be straight and pale and it would hate the pan and it would sit in the drawer and it would still be new in 2035.

This one has about four hundred more sauces in her. Then you will break her against the rim of a pot, badly, at the worst moment, because they always go in the middle of something.

She won't mind. She was never saving anything up.

They're in the drawer at the hardware store. Bottom aisle. Loose, in a bin, no packaging, no labels, a dollar each. Pick the one that already feels like yours. It won't yet.
</final>

*A light switch. The most-used object in your house and the only one you've never looked at.*

Think about the last ten minutes before you left this morning. Keys, coffee, phone, the thing you forgot. Somewhere in there your hand did the same thing it has done every day for years, and you didn't look down once.

Nobody gathers around a light switch. No one puts it on a wedding registry. It just stands there in the plaster, doing the only job it has, at the exact moment every day bends. On: the house is awake, the kids' shoes are wherever the kids left them, someone is reading in the next room. Off: you're gone, or you're home, or it's over.

Your hand knows the plate before your eyes do — that first second of fumbling, the small click, the dark going copper as the streetlight comes up through the blinds. It is the piece of this place you touch more than your own front door.

There is nothing to sell you. Pick the plate that matches the wall, or the one that doesn't. One of ours is a thousand flips old already, and it doesn't know it.

**Sale ends when you leave the room.**

Every spell is a loan taken out against the dead: you name an ancestor, you draw their remaining years, and the debt comes due not in your lifetime but in your children's, in their luck, their health, their firstborn — whatever the ledger's terms happen to specify. A bureaucratic procedural with a debt to Hell at the bottom of it, about the difference between owing someone and belonging to them.

<final>
**Vera Klimt, "the Nose"**

Vera Klimt authenticates antiques for the big auction houses, which means she is paid to be certain, and she is certain with her face six inches from the object, inhaling.

She can date a Gustavsberg vase by the mineral tang of the clay slip. She can tell a genuine Shaker chair from a fake because the real one has absorbed two hundred years of woodsmoke and hand sweat; the fake smells like a hardware store. A woman once brought her a "family heirloom" locket that smelled faintly of gun oil. Vera told the auction house to call someone else.

What she cannot do is smell a lie coming. She is wrong about people constantly. Her third husband was a forger; she found out when she pressed her nose to his collar and smelled the fixative he used on the phony signatures, and even then she told herself it was cologne for eleven days.

She works out of a rented back room in a Copenhagen auction house, and she solves the crimes that find her the way she solves everything—by knowing what a thing is supposed to smell like and noticing when it doesn't. A drowned man's coat smelled of fresh tobacco, not the harbor. A stolen Vermeer smelled wrong in a way she couldn't name and spent two years naming. She keeps a mental catalogue of ten thousand smells and no friends.

Her nose is failing. She's known for a year. Some days everything smells like wet cardboard, and on those days she can't work, can't eat—the food all tastes of nothing—and can't trust the one thing that has ever made her useful. She has told no one, because the moment she does, she is a woman with a hobby and no name.

She is trying to solve her last case before her sense goes, and she is scared the whole time that she is already too late to smell the answer, and that the murderer knows it too.

# The Adjuster

Mira Okonkwo has spent nineteen years being lied to for a living, and she has never once minded. She works claims for a mid-sized insurer out of a strip-mall office, the kind of job nobody writes about, and she is very good at it in a way that has nothing to do with spreadsheets. When someone describes a fire, she listens to the verbs. When someone describes a fall, she watches their hands. People rehearsing a lie use tidy sentences; people telling the truth wander, correct themselves, remember the dog was barking. She has a file of the tells she has collected, handwritten, going back to her first year, and she has never shown it to anyone.

Her territory is a two-hundred-mile loop of small towns where the adjuster is the only stranger who comes to the door with a reason. Nobody is suspicious of her. She carries a clipboard. She asks to see the room. She is expected to ask about money, and so she asks about everything else while she is there.

She is not fearless, and she is not a hero. She is cautious to the point of cowardice about her own life — she has never learned to swim, she will not drive after dark, she has lived in the same apartment for eleven years and still keeps the lease in her sister's name — and this is precisely why she notices when someone else is afraid. Fear has a texture. She has walked into houses where the air was wrong before a word was spoken.

The case that gets her is a drowning. A man went into a lake in February, and the coroner called it an accident, and the payout is small enough that no one at the company cares. Mira cares because the widow used the past tense before the body was found. Not once. Four times, in a phone call Mira was supposed to be taking notes on for a different reason entirely. Four times is not a slip. Four times is a woman who has already moved her husband into memory and is now waiting to be believed.

Mira has no authority to investigate anything. She has a clipboard, a mileage cap, and a manager who has told her twice to stop flagging claims as suspicious because it costs the company money to look. So she does it the way she does everything: she reopens the file, she schedules a routine follow-up visit, she brings a tape measure. She stands in the widow's kitchen measuring a hallway that does not need measuring, and she asks about the lake, and she asks about the boat, and she asks what the man's hands were like, because grief will answer a question about hands even when it has been coached not to answer anything else.

What she finds is not what she expected. The widow did not kill him. The widow helped him disappear, and the reason is smaller and sadder and more ordinary than murder — a debt, a diagnosis, a favor asked by someone who is now dead and cannot be asked why. Mira can prove it. Proving it will end a woman's life as she knows it and will not bring anyone back, and the company will not thank her, and her manager will write her up for the hours.

She does it anyway, slowly, badly, without any of the satisfaction she expected, and she goes home and adds one more line to the file. Not a tell. A note to herself, in the same handwriting she has used for nineteen years: *the tidy ones are lying about something, but not always about the thing you came for.*

She is fifty-three. She is afraid of the dark. She is the only person in four counties who will drive two hours to look at a wet floor and ask the right question.

**Wren Adebayo-Lisk, 58, court stenographer**

Wren has transcribed eleven thousand trials and has never once been asked what she thinks of them. She sits below the witness box, fingers on the keys, and her job is to disappear. She is very good at it. Her colleagues call her "the wall" because nothing gets past her and nothing she hears ever leaves the room.

Her gift is not memory for words. It is the pause before them. Wren can hear a lie by the length of the gap before it, the way a speaker's breath catches when they reach for a sentence they rehearsed. She has never told anyone this, because a stenographer who claims to detect deception is a stenographer who gets removed from cases. So she keeps it to herself and types what is said, exactly, while her private ledger fills with what is not.

She lives alone above a dry cleaner's, in a flat that smells faintly of pressed wool, and she keeps a notebook of every case where her ledger disagreed with the verdict. There are forty-one entries. Thirty-nine ended with the wrong person in prison, according to the nagging certainty in her chest. The other two she has never been able to prove either way.

The mystery opens when a defendant she transcribed years ago sends her a short letter: "You heard me. Tell them." Wren has to decide whether to act on a feeling no court would accept, and in doing so become the one person in the building who speaks.

Flaw: she is more loyal to the record than to the people in it. Want: to be heard by someone who is not a machine. Fear: that the pauses she trusts are only the sound of her own loneliness.

**Wren Adebayo-Lisk, 58, court stenographer**

Wren has transcribed eleven thousand trials and has never once been asked what she thinks of them. She sits below the witness box, fingers on the keys, and her job is to disappear. She is very good at it. Her colleagues call her "the wall" because nothing gets past her and nothing she hears ever leaves the room.

Her gift is not memory for words. It is the pause before them. Wren can hear a lie by the length of the gap before it, the way a speaker's breath catches when they reach for a sentence they rehearsed. She has never told anyone this, because a stenographer who claims to detect deception is a stenographer who gets removed from cases. So she keeps it to herself and types what is said, exactly, while her private ledger fills with what is not.

She lives alone above a dry cleaner's, in a flat that smells faintly of pressed wool, and she keeps a notebook of every case where her ledger disagreed with the verdict. There are forty-one entries. Thirty-nine ended with the wrong person in prison, according to the nagging certainty in her chest. The other two she has never been able to prove either way.

The mystery opens when a defendant she transcribed years ago sends her a short letter: "You heard me. Tell them." Wren has to decide whether to act on a feeling no court would accept, and in doing so become the one person in the building who speaks.

Flaw: she is more loyal to the record than to the people in it. Want: to be heard by someone who is not a machine. Fear: that the pauses she trusts are only the sound of her own loneliness.
</final>

Ilsa Brann does the wash for the whole valley, which means she is the only person who knows that Widow Prideaux bleeds on Mondays, that the schoolmaster's shirts come home with someone else's hair, and that the Hollis boy wears two pairs of underwear every day of November. Nobody thinks about the laundress. Secrets walk into her yard in pillowcases.

She was a nurse once, before her hands started shaking, so she knows how to read a body from cloth: arterial spray leaves a fan, venous leaves a pool, and the shirt from the night Annika died had neither. It was dunked. Somebody panicked and dunked it, and the water was cold, because the stain went brown at the edge and stayed blue at the heart.

The problem is she can't say any of this. Not to the constable, who was Annika's cousin. Not at the inquest, where she is a witness only of laundry. She tried once, years ago, about a different thing, and the town has since decided she is a woman with opinions.

So she works the way she always has, one bundle at a time, and waits to be underestimated. In the village's mind she is equipment — a basin, a line, a smell of soap she has to carry home in her skin. She has learned to lean on it. People undress their conversations around her the way they undress their bodies. She stands at the gate with the week's clean linen folded over both arms, and they talk past her about money, about alibis, about who was where.

She is not clever. She is exact. She keeps a ledger of every item, in pencil, in case anyone ever asks.

Nobody asks.

Think of a village where people send each other notes, but there is no post office and no postman.

Instead, every house keeps a small wooden box by the door. If you want to send a note to someone, you fold it, write on the outside who it's meant for, and drop it in your box. Then the boxes do the rest: each one is connected by a thin string to a few other boxes nearby, and by longer strings to boxes far away. When your note goes into your box, it gets passed along, box to box, until it reaches the person whose name is on it.

Nobody owns the strings. Nobody owns the boxes. That's the strangest part. The whole village just agreed, over years, on a few simple rules: how to fold a note so it doesn't fall apart, how to write a name on the outside that everyone will read the same way, and what to do if a string breaks. As long as everyone follows the same rules, it doesn't matter who made their box or where they live — the note still arrives.

Now, the boxes aren't smart. They can't read. They only know how to hand a note to the next box in the right direction, like a person pointing down a road without knowing what's at the end. So messages travel in small pieces, sometimes by different routes, and get put back together at the far end. If one string is cut, the note usually finds another way around.

The "internet" is just this village, grown enormous — every house on Earth joined by the same kind of strings and the same few agreements about folding and addressing. Your computer, the thing on your desk, is only one box by one door. It doesn't hold the village. It just knows the rules well enough to pass a note along.

When you "go online," you're really just dropping a note in your box and waiting to see who writes back.

Marguerite Oyelaran-Pike has taken down every word spoken in Courtroom 4B for nineteen years, and she has never once been wrong about what someone said. This is less a gift than a condition. She hears a sentence and it stays put, flat and exact, with its commas. People who lie to her are, in a sense, lying to a notebook.

She is forty-eight. She keeps a tin of cloves in her purse, chews them through lunch, and types with her left hand on a machine she bought secondhand from a closed-down insurance firm. Her ex-husband still calls her "the Transcript," which she tolerates because he has never once asked her a question he did not already know the answer to.

Her method is simple and a little rude. When a witness says something, she waits, then asks them to say it again. Not the same question. The same sentence. Most people change a word without noticing: "I went home" becomes "I got home," and the difference between going and arriving is where a thirty-year-old alibi begins to fall apart. She keeps a second ledger, separate from the court record, in which she writes down every variant. She calls it her ghost copy.

She does not chase killers. She is not interested in motives or the warm glow of a confession. She wants the record to be true, and when it is not, she considers it her duty to find out where it bends. The city's detectives have learned to bring her the statements they cannot make add up, and to not ask how she knows what she knows, because she will tell them the exact words and the exact second the story changed.

The case that opens the book is a fire in a rented flat on Vellum Street. The man who died was an accountant whose witness statement, given to police the morning after, contains one sentence she cannot stop hearing: "The light was still on when I left." Two days later, he says, "The light was on when I left." The difference is small, and the difference is enough to keep her awake, her cloves tasting of something she cannot name.

She begins, as she always does, by asking someone to repeat themselves.

Think of a letter.

You write one. You put it in an envelope, write a name and a street and a town on the front, and drop it in a box. Days later it arrives. You never met the mail carrier. You never saw the road it took. You don't need to.

The internet works like that, with three differences.

The first difference is speed. A letter takes days. A message sent this way arrives in less time than it takes to blink — faster than you could finish reading this sentence. Not because it's carried fast, but because the distance stops mattering. The message isn't a thing moving down a road. It's a copy being made, over and over, closer and closer to the person you're writing to, until the last copy is the one they hold.

The second difference is that the letter gets cut into pieces. Not one envelope — hundreds, sometimes thousands, each piece small enough to fit through the narrowest doorway. They leave in any order, by any route that happens to be open. If one road is blocked, a piece goes another way. At the other end the pieces are counted and stacked and put back in order, and the person reads one whole letter. They never see the cutting. Neither do you. This is the part people find hardest to believe: nothing travels as itself. Everything travels as scraps and arrives whole.

The third difference is where the address points. You write a street and a town, and there is a house there, with a door, that someone built. On the internet, an address points to a machine that might sit in a basement in another country, or in a building with no windows, or in a stack of machines in a desert where the electricity is cheap. It doesn't matter where. What matters is that the machine is awake and knows how to answer. There's no house, no street, no neighborhood. Just a name that machines agree on.

So when you sit down and send something, here is what actually happens. You write it. It is cut apart. The scraps scatter across the world by every open road at once. They meet again somewhere, in order, and become the thing you wrote. And somewhere far away, a machine that has never seen you hands it to the person you meant.

The mail carrier never existed. There is no road. But the letter arrives.

That's the whole trick, and it's the only thing you need to know to start. You will learn the rest by using it — the way you learned mail.

**Imogen Tarrant, 41, forensic document examiner**

Imogen cannot recognize a face. Ten years ago a fever left her with prosopagnosia, and she has spent the decade building a working life around the parts of people she can still hold: their voices, their gait, and above all their handwriting. She is the only examiner in the county who will sign a report that begins, "I have never seen this person, and I know exactly who wrote this."

She works from a converted sunroom in a house that smells of ink and cold tea. Her desk is lit by a single lamp angled so the pen strokes cast shadows. She keeps a ledger of every hand she has ever studied, indexed not by name but by the way a person crosses a seven or loops a lowercase g. Clients think of her as eccentric. Police think of her as useful and a little uncanny. She prefers to think of herself as precise.

**Why she is unusual as a detective**

- She never investigates a scene. She investigates paper: notes, cheques, wills, the margin of a library book. Every crime, to her, is first a question of who held the pen.
- She cannot identify a suspect across a room. In interviews she asks everyone to write a line of their own choosing, and she reads the result before she looks at them. The moment she finally meets someone, she is often wrong about their face and right about their hand.
- Her disability is not a gimmick the plot resolves. It shapes her method, her blind spots and her relationships. Her closest ally is her nephew, who describes faces to her in careful, slightly bored detail, and who has learned never to say "you'll know him when you see him."
- She distrusts anything she has not written down. Her weakness is that she believes handwriting cannot lie, and a skilled forger knows exactly how to make it.

**The hook**

A retired schoolteacher brings Imogen a short, neatly written note left under a dead man's door. The loops are a perfect match for the dead man's own hand. Imogen is certain the man did not write it, and certain the person who did learned to write the way he wrote, a lesson taught to them by someone who loved him.

The note is a letter of apology, and it is addressed to Imogen herself.

Imagine a city where nobody has a street address, only a name, and every letter you send is cut into dozens of small envelopes. Each envelope is numbered, and each one can take a different route to the same house. Some pass through a post office in one neighborhood, some through another, and a few get stuck at a busy junction and wait their turn. When the last envelope arrives, the receiver stacks them in number order and reads the letter as if it had come in one piece.

No single post office knows the whole route. Each one only knows which neighbor to hand the envelope to next, and that is enough. If a road is blocked, the envelopes simply go around it. The city does not need a central boss to keep the mail moving.

When you open a web page, you are asking for a letter from a faraway house. Its name is looked up in a city-wide directory, so the request knows where to go. The reply comes back as envelopes, which your device reassembles into the page you see. The address is the name, the envelopes are the data, and the post offices are the cables, phone lines and radio towers that carry them.

Imagine a village where nobody has a post office, and no one has ever needed one.

You want to send your cousin, three villages away, a message that's too long for one scrap of paper. So you don't send it whole. You tear it into small pieces, number each one, and write "for my cousin, in the village past the river" on every single piece. You hand the pile to your neighbor.

Your neighbor doesn't know your cousin. She doesn't need to. She knows the villages on her road, and she looks at each piece and hands it to whoever is heading the right direction — someone going toward the river, or someone who knows someone who is. The pieces split up. One travels with a fish cart, another with a boy on foot, another waits a day in a stranger's kitchen. They arrive by three different roads, out of order, and your cousin lays them by their numbers until the whole message is there.

Now the part that makes it work: any piece that gets lost is simply sent again, because you still have the pile. And if one road floods, the pieces just go around. That's why the village never falls apart when a bridge washes out.

The internet is that village, with two differences. The pieces are called packets, and the people handing them along are computers. Every computer has a sort of address, like a house with a name on it, so the pieces know where "my cousin" lives. And the villages are every village at once — which is why a message can cross the world by a route nobody chose in advance, and still arrive, piece by piece, in the right order.

There's no central office. There's no one in charge of the roads. There's just a great many people, each willing to pass the next thing along.

You want to send your cousin, three villages away, a message that's too long for one scrap of paper. So you don't send it whole. You tear it into small pieces, number each one, and write "for my cousin, in the village past the river" on every single piece. You hand the pile to your neighbor.

Your neighbor doesn't know your cousin. She doesn't need to. She knows the villages on her road, and she looks at each piece and hands it to whoever is heading the right direction — someone going toward the river, or someone who knows someone who is. The pieces split up. One travels with a fish cart, another with a boy on foot, another waits a day in a stranger's kitchen. They arrive by three different roads, out of order, and your cousin lays them by their numbers until the whole message is there.

Now the part that makes it work: any piece that gets lost is simply sent again, because you still have the pile. And if one road floods, the pieces just go around. That's why the village never falls apart when a bridge washes out.

The internet is that village, with two differences. The pieces are called packets, and the people handing them along are computers. Every computer has a sort of address, like a house with a name on it, so the pieces know where "my cousin" lives. And the villages are every village at once — which is why a message can cross the world by a route nobody chose in advance, and still arrive, piece by piece, in the right order.

There's no central office. There's no one in charge of the roads. There's just a great many people, each willing to pass the next thing along.
</final>

Think of the internet as a postal system for a town that never sleeps.

Every house has an address, a number that tells the mail carriers where to bring things. When you want a page, a photo, or a message, you write a request and drop it in the box. The request does not travel in one piece. It is cut into small envelopes, each stamped with the sender's return address, the recipient's address, and its place in the order, so that if the envelopes take different roads, the far end can still lay them out in sequence and read the whole letter.

The roads are shared. Carriers pass the envelopes from one post office to the next, and each one looks at the address and decides which road is fastest right now, the way a driver reroutes around a jam. If one road is closed, the envelope takes another. Nobody needs to know the whole map, only the next stop.

At the far end sits a library. Its books are the websites and videos you want, and its catalogue tells the carriers where each one lives. When the envelopes arrive, the library's staff put them back in order, and the book is handed back down the same network, to your door.

So when you open a page, you are not summoning something from a single place. You are asking a distant library to mail you a book, and a thousand strangers' post offices quietly carry it across the town for you.
