Imagine a city where nobody owns a single road, but everyone can still send a letter to anyone else. That is roughly how the internet works.

When you ask for a web page, your request is written on a small card and handed to a clerk at your local post office. The clerk does not know the whole city, only a few neighbors. So the card is passed along from office to office, each one deciding only which neighbor is closest to the address on the card. Nobody plans the route ahead of time. Each office just points the card in a sensible direction and trusts the next one to know more.

The address on the card is not a street name but a number that stands for a building, like a long string of digits that some directory office keeps track of. When the card finally reaches the building that holds the page you want, a worker there photocopies the page, cuts the copy into many small pages numbered in order, and sends each piece off on its own journey through the same offices. The pieces may take different paths. Some arrive early, some late, one may be lost and quietly requested again.

At your house, a tidy clerk gathers every piece as it arrives, puts them back in numerical order, checks that none are missing or smudged, and lays the finished page on your table. That is when you see it.

The strange part is that no single office holds the whole city's map, and no office knows the full story of your letter. It works because everyone follows the same simple rules for addresses, cards and numbering, so a card sent from anywhere can be understood anywhere.

The house closes Friday, so they started with the big things and worked down. Priya had a list. Dev had the car, which decided more than the list did.

"Range," he said. "It fits."

"It's a rental range, Dev."

"It's a range."

She let him have it. The fridge went to her, not because she wanted it but because he'd said "fits" twice and she could hear their mother in it, the way she said *it fits, it fits* about a coat she'd never wear.

They were quick through the cupboards. Bowls, lids, the good knife that went to Dev because he cooked and she didn't and they both knew it. She kept the cutting board with the burn ring on it. He didn't ask why. That was the whole negotiation, mostly — someone reaching, someone not asking.

Then the drawer by the stove, the one with the tongs and the whisk and a corkscrew shaped like a bird.

"I'll take the tongs," Dev said.

"You don't use tongs."

"I'll use tongs."

She looked at him. He was holding them like something he'd found, not chosen, thumb on the scalloped edge, and she understood he was taking them because their mother had used them every night for forty years and he had never once been the one standing at that stove, and the tongs were the closest he was going to get.

"Take them," she said.

He put them in his coat pocket. They finished the drawer.

The colander is hers, Marcus says, and then, because it's the wrong thing to say, he says it again.

Dana holds the whisk the way you'd hold a stranger's dog. "You can have the cast iron."

"I don't cook."

"You make eggs."

"I make eggs out of spite."

They have a system: a roll of blue painter's tape and two columns on the counter. Her side, his side. The tape keeps lifting at the corners, so every item gets a little pressure from the thumb, like pressing a stamp down.

The spatula with the split handle goes to Marcus without discussion. Neither of them mentions the twelve-year-old rubber band wound around the drawer pull, or the note in the junk drawer, *ask Gerald about the gutter*, in a handwriting neither of them can make themselves read twice.

At the bottom of the cabinet: a Tupperware lid with no container. They look at it together.

"Keep it," Dana says. "It's for something."

"It's for nothing," Marcus says, and puts it in her column.

The fridge hums with nothing in it. Someone unplugged it earlier and forgot, or nobody wanted to be the one to do the last thing, so it runs empty and cold.

By four they have only the table left, pressed against the window, and two chairs that don't match. Neither of them wants the table. Neither will say so.

"I'll take the chairs," Marcus says.

"You'll take the table."

"Then we're both taking something we don't want."

The room behind the lost-and-found counter had no clock and no windows, which Marisol had come to think of as its only mercy. She'd worked the counter eleven years. The room she'd worked three.

People came to the airport to leave or to meet. Almost nobody came for her window. The ones who did had the face of someone who'd already failed at something: the man whose mother's urn was routed to Tampa without him, the teenager whose guitar went to the wrong belt, the woman in the good coat who stood there with the claim ticket shaking in her hand and said *please* like it was the only word left in her.

The shelves held what nobody returned for. Marisol kept them in rows. Strollers. A single ski. Fourteen phone chargers, all the same black braid, from fourteen people who would swear theirs was different. A wedding dress in a garment bag, unclaimed for six years, the tag still reading the bride's name in looped pink marker. A child's stuffed rabbit with one ear gone soft from being held, which had been on the shelf so long she'd stopped putting it at the front.

She'd written to the rabbit's owner twice. Neither letter came back, and neither letter got an answer, which she'd decided meant the family had moved and the mail had died the way mail does, not that they'd stopped wanting it. You can tell yourself a thing for six years if you're patient.

The trick was that the airport never stopped. Above her, the boards flipped and flipped. Flights to places she'd never go spun their letters over and pulled people up the jet bridges by the hundred, and Marisol sat under all of it with the rabbit and the dress and the ski, the keeper of everything the sky refused.

Once, a boy came in with his father. The boy was maybe seven. He looked at the shelves the way children look at shelves — for the thing that was his, not for the things that weren't. *Is that mine,* he said, pointing at the rabbit, and his father said no, buddy, that's somebody else's, come on, we're gonna miss it, and the boy kept looking back over his shoulder as they went, as if he knew something the adults had agreed to forget: that on the other side of that counter was where the airport actually kept its people.

Marisol didn't say what she thought. She never did. She slid the man's form across the counter for a signature and stapled the ticket and said *it'll be on the next one, I promise,* because that was her job and because it was usually true.

Tonight the last flight thinned out. The boards went quiet one row at a time. Marisol locked the counter at eleven and went into the room to do the thing she did some nights, which was not quite inventory and not quite prayer.

She stood in front of the shelves and put her hand flat on the rabbit's head, one slow pass, the way you'd do it to a child you weren't waking. Somewhere past the far windows a plane got smaller and smaller without ever seeming to arrive anywhere, and the room kept everything it had been given, and that, she'd decided, was the whole of it. Not arrivals. Not departures. Just this: the bags come down the belt, the belt keeps turning, and somebody down the line is paid to remember.

Marcus put the cast iron in his yes pile before we'd finished the top cabinets. He said he'd learned to cook in it. He'd learned to cook the year Mom got sick, four months, three recipes.

I didn't argue. I know what the skillet is. I also know it has never once been seasoned right, because Mom only used it for cornbread and she liked it pale.

We went by shelves. He took the good knives. I took the chipped bowl with the rooster, because he looked past it and I have watched Mom's hands in it for thirty years, cracking eggs.

"You want the stand mixer," he said.

"I don't want the stand mixer."

"It's worth something."

"So is the freezer."

He went quiet. The freezer is where she kept the meat she never cooked, a brisket from 2019, freezer-burned gray, and the two casseroles from church that she labeled in my handwriting.

"Take the mixer," I said. "I'll take the freezer."

He carried it out to his truck and didn't help me with the brisket. I wrapped it in three bags and set it in my trunk, next to the rooster bowl, and drove the long way home, past the church, past the road that used to be a field.

Dana taped the box shut before Ray could argue. "The colander."

"You take the colander. I'll take the Pyrex."

"You don't want the Pyrex. You never cooked with it."

"I wasn't cooking with anything. I was on the phone." He said it before he could stop himself.

She didn't answer. She opened the drawer by the stove, the one that stuck, and lifted out the wooden spoons, each one grey at the handle where Mum's thumb had worn them down. She held one up to the window.

"She made you a list, you know. Of who gets what."

"I know."

"It's in the cupboard with the foil. It's from three years ago. Half of it's crossed out."

"Then we don't need the list."

Dana set the spoon on the counter, between them, like a coin she was waiting to see him pick up. He didn't. He looked at the calendar still on the fridge, March, with her handwriting on it: *Ray Sunday.* Every Sunday for two years, in pen, a little hopeful.

"The knives are yours," Dana said.

"They're yours. You're the one who sharpened them."

"I sharpened them because you never came round to do it."

Neither of them moved. The kettle ticked as it cooled. Outside, a car door shut, and someone laughed on the pavement and then didn't.

Ray picked up the spoon. He turned it over slowly, his thumb finding the same worn place.

"Keep the spoons," he said. "Keep the list too, if you want it. I'll take the Pyrex."

"You hate the Pyrex."

"I know," he said, and put it in his box anyway.

The good knife went to Dana without discussion, because Dana had cooked for their mother for eleven years and Ruth had sent a card at Christmas. That was settled before the boxes came out.

The drawer by the stove was harder.

"Twist ties," Ruth said. She lifted out a fistful, pale green and wire-stiff, then a rubber band gone brittle at the edges, then another. There were forty, maybe more, looped around each other like something that had been growing in the dark.

"She saved them from bread," Dana said. "Every loaf. You remember."

"I remember her doing it. I didn't know she kept them."

"She kept everything that might be useful someday."

Ruth turned one over in her fingers. "That someday never came, did it."

Dana almost laughed. Then she didn't. She took the drawer out entirely and set it on the counter, where its contents slid and clicked. In the back, under the paper, was a receipt from a bakery that had closed in 1998, folded small and flattened by years of being pressed under things.

"Do you want the drawer?" Ruth asked.

"Do you?"

"No."

"Then we're both saying no to the same thing," Dana said, and she pushed the drawer, bands and all, across the counter until it was between them, neither one anybody's.

They stood there a while. The radio on the windowsill was still tuned to the station she liked, low, a man reading the weather for a town neither of them had visited.

"I'll take the bands," Ruth said finally. "If you take the ties."

"That's not fair. The ties are better."

"The bands are older."

Dana picked up the receipt and read it, then put it in her coat pocket without saying why. Ruth watched her do it and didn't ask.

The night shift starts when the last Starbucks gate pulls down its grille and the terminal becomes a building again instead of a current. Odell takes Level C first, because Level C is where the flights to Manila leave, and the families on those flights eat like they're provisioning a voyage. He finds the usual: orange peels, a sock, a boarding pass torn in half and taped back together.

The sock goes in the trash. The boarding pass he smooths and leaves on the seat, in case.

He has rules. He doesn't read the screens — the screens are for people who still have somewhere to be. He reads the floor. A scatter of pistachio shells means a nervous flyer who bought snacks at the last kiosk and ate them too fast. A single high heel under a row of seats means a woman who took it off during a delay and then ran when they finally called her, and somewhere over the Pacific she is going to notice. Wet napkins, a lot of them, balled tight, means crying, and Odell sweeps around those seats the way you'd walk around a grave.

Tonight there's a man asleep across four seats at C12, shoes on, jacket folded under his head like a pillow he was taught to make. No luggage. He has the look of someone who is either very early or not going anywhere, and Odell has learned not to ask which. He vacuums the next row over, loud enough to be a kindness if the man wants to wake up and loud enough to ignore if he doesn't. The man doesn't.

At the far gate, a girl of maybe nine is drawing on the window with her finger, tracing the runway lights like she's connecting constellations. Her mother is on the phone, walking a tight circle, saying *I told him the flight number, I told him twice.* The girl doesn't turn around. She's drawn a plane, and then below it a smaller shape, a house, and then a line between them, very long.

Odell empties the bins. In one of them: a corsage, still in its plastic box, wilted. Somebody came to the airport to say goodbye to someone they loved, and then stood at the curb afterward and dropped the flowers in the first can they passed. He looks at it a while. Then he ties the bag and moves on, because there are nine more levels, and by four in the morning, the whole terminal has to be clean enough to look like no one has ever left it.

Nadia does the bins at Terminal 2 on the overnight, 11 p.m. to 7. She knows the flight schedule better than the board does, because the board tells you what's coming and the bins tell you what came. International arrivals drop duty-free bags, receipts, the plastic sleeves from neck pillows. Domestic red-eyes drop coffee cups with the lids bitten. When the Orlando flight lands, the bins fill with mouse ears, sometimes still on the headband, and once a child's tooth in a ziplock with a note: For the Tooth Fairy, we are flying, please hurry.

She does not judge. She has a route and a cart and a grabber, and she moves like the floor is hers, which between 2 and 4 a.m. it nearly is. Gate B12 sleeps. The Cinnabon closes its grate. A man in a suit charges his phone at the wall outlet and cries quietly, and she passes with her cart and does not look, and does not not-look, and that is a skill she has.

At 3:40 she finds a boarding pass in the bin by Security, torn in half and taped back together with masking tape, then torn again, then kept. She has seen this one before. People do it in stages. They throw the trip away, change their mind, throw it away again, and the second throw is slower.

She puts it in her vest pocket the way she puts some things, not all things. Some nights she goes home with a boarding pass, a keychain, a paperback with a stranger's margin notes. Her apartment has a shelf. She does not call it anything. Her daughter does.

At 5 the sky turns gray at the window line, and the first bank of departures wakes up and starts to want things. Nadia wheels the cart to the compactor. In the vest pocket, the pass says DENVER and a name she won't remember by Tuesday and a seat, 14C, which is a middle, which is the worst one, which means whoever it was got the last seat on the plane and then stood at the machine and paid again to keep it.

She clocks out at seven. She takes the employee shuttle with the other night people, and nobody talks, and the sun comes up over the rental car lots, and it is a Tuesday, it is just a Tuesday, and a plane goes over, low, gear up, gone.

# Two Plates

Every evening, Judith set the table for two.

One plate for herself. One across from her, with the good fork, the one that didn't wobble. She never said why, and her mother never asked.

Tonight the stew was thin. It had been thin for a long time, though Judith couldn't have told you how long. She carried the pot to the table and ladled out two bowls. The second bowl went cold, the way it always did.

"You're late," she said, to the empty chair.

The masking tape had been on the mixer since before either of them could read. MOM in blue Sharpie, and under it, in smaller letters, DO NOT.

"You take it," Ruth said. "You bake."

"I don't bake. I own a baking dish." Daniel turned the mixer's paddle with one finger. "She labeled the Tupperware. Did you see? Every lid. Lids that don't even go to anything."

They worked the way they had as kids, when the last slice of cake was on the line: one picks, the other vetoes. Ruth picked the cast iron. Daniel vetoed nothing, which was new. He picked the radio, the one with the dial that only got AM, and she said fine, and he put it by the door like it was already gone.

The tape was the trouble. On the freezer bags, in her hand: SOUP — 2019, DO NOT. On the junk drawer: BATTERIES, TAPE, DANIEL'S. On the cabinet above the stove, where the good glasses lived, she had written FOR COMPANY and then, later, in a different pen, not company anymore.

Ruth peeled that one off and stuck it to her own wrist. Daniel watched her do it and didn't say anything, and they kept going, cabinet by cabinet, until the kitchen was two piles on the floor and neither pile had a mother in it.

My cousin Lena moved into the old Rourke house in October, and for three nights she slept fine.

On the fourth night she heard someone crying in the hallway.

She sat up. The crying stopped. She lay down. It started again — small, hiccupy, like a little kid trying not to be heard.

"It's okay," Lena said, because that's what you say.

The crying stopped for a long time. Then, very quiet, from the other side of her door: "You can see me?"

Lena turned on her lamp. There was nobody there. Just the hallway, and the wallpaper with the little faded birds.

"I can't see you," she said. "But I can hear you."

"Oh," said the voice. It sounded relieved. "Good."

That was the strange part. Relieved.

Every night after that, they talked. The voice wouldn't say its name. It asked questions instead — what year is it, is the mill still standing, does anyone still slide down the banister. Lena told it everything. It liked hearing about the school bus. It had never been on one.

One night Lena asked, "Why are you scared of me seeing you?"

The voice went quiet. Then: "Because the last people who saw me ran out of the house and never came back. And it gets so lonely, being a thing that makes people run."

Lena thought about that for a while.

"Then don't be a thing that makes people run," she said. "Be a thing that talks."

The next morning there was a drawing on her windowsill. Chalk, or something like it. A stick figure, and beside it a smaller stick figure, holding hands. Neither one had a face.

Lena kept it. She still has it. She's thirty-one now, and sometimes, late, when the house is settling, she says, "Still here?"

And from the hallway, quiet, like someone trying not to be heard:

"Still here."

At 4:10 a.m. Terminal C belongs to Marisol and the buffer machine.

She knows its moods. The polisher hums a flat B until the floor is wet, then rises. She works the seam between gate 22 and gate 23, where the carpet tiles meet and the grime collects. Nobody flies at this hour except the stranded, and the stranded do not look at the floor.

A man sits by the window with a paper cup going cold. His shoes are unlaced. A blue lanyard hangs from his neck with a badge he has turned face-down against his shirt. She has seen him three nights now. He does not sleep. He watches the planes being pushed back with their lights blinking, one at a time, as if he is counting them out.

On the fourth night she stops the machine beside his chair.

"They'll call your row soon," she says. "They always do the aisles first."

He looks up, startled, as if she had spoken from inside the window. Then he almost smiles. "You know the boarding order."

"I know which chairs people wait in."

He lifts the cup, sees it is empty, sets it down. "My daughter is in Lisbon. Her flight got in at two. I was supposed to be on the one before that."

Marisol nods. She does not ask why he missed it. Her own father once spent a whole Christmas on the wrong side of a border, and she learned that most reasons are heavier than the people carrying them.

"Lisbon's warm this time of year," she says.

"It was raining when I left." He gives a short laugh. "She'll be annoyed I didn't come."

The polisher groans behind her, low and patient. Marisol bends to fix the cord. When she straightens, he has unfolded the lanyard badge and is holding it up to the light, reading it as if it might say something new.

"Thank you," he says. He does not say for what.

She pushes the machine onward, leaving a clean wet stripe across the seam. At gate 23 the first dawn light lies pale on the glass, and somewhere far off a voice begins to call the aisles.

The lost-and-found at Terminal C is a closet behind the Cinnabon, and Dolores has run it for nineteen years.

People leave the strangest things. Reading glasses on top of heads. Prosthetic legs, twice. A wedding ring in a packet of gum. Once, a live tortoise in a shoebox, which she kept in the break room until a man from Ohio came in with a face like a bruise and said yes, that was his, he'd been carrying it since his mother died and had forgotten.

Most things nobody claims. The rule is ninety days, then donation. Dolores keeps a ledger, a green spiral book, where she writes each item in pencil: *navy scarf, one child's mitten, phone, cracked, passcode unknown*. The phones bother her most. They keep lighting up in the bin with messages from people who are still waiting for someone to answer.

On Tuesdays a young man comes in about a jacket. Dark green, corduroy, a pocket that bulges with something square. He describes it the same way every week. He never says what he's lost it for or who gave it to him.

"Not yet," Dolores says, and he nods and goes back out to the gates, where the boards are flipping over to *DELAYED* in a soft clatter like a rain of small cards.

In the spiral book there is a page with no entries on it. She turned it to make sure, last spring. Blank paper, faint ruled lines, nothing she could donate. Sometimes she runs her thumb along the edge of it while the public address system says her name is not the name of anyone it is looking for.

At the end of her shift she sweeps the closet floor. A single earring, a button, the paper wrapper from a cough drop. She puts them all back into their labeled bags, one by one, as if somebody might still come asking for them tomorrow, and turns off the light.

The girl in the window had been there three nights.

Not at the glass — *behind* it, in the attic window, which had been painted shut since before Grandpa was born. She didn't wave. She just stood there with her hands folded, like someone waiting for a bus.

On the fourth night, Marcus opened the window from the inside.

It took both hands and a butter knife. The paint cracked like sugar. Cold came in, and then the girl came in, and she wasn't cold at all. She was warm, actually. That was the worst part.

"You're the one who used to live here," Marcus said.

"I'm the one who *does* live here," she said. "You're the ones who keep leaving the light on."

Marcus looked at his lamp. He'd left it on every night because of her.

She sat down on the floor by the dollhouse — his sister's dollhouse, the one they'd found in the wall when they moved in. She picked up the tiny mother and put her back in the tiny kitchen.

"I only wanted the window open," she said. "It gets close in there."

"So go outside."

"I can't. Someone has to invite me out." She looked up. "Not in. Out."

Marcus's hand was on the latch. All he had to do was say *come on, then.*

He thought about the light he'd leave on for the rest of his life. He thought about her standing at that window every night, hands folded, waiting for a bus that stopped here once, a long time ago, for somebody who never came down the stairs.

He closed the window instead.

She didn't get angry. She just nodded, like she'd expected it, and went back up through the ceiling the way water goes down a drain — quietly, all at once.

The lamp's still on. He checks the window every night now, out of habit.

Sometimes it's open. Just a crack. He never remembers doing it.

The gate at Concourse C had a man who ate oranges and left the peel in the shape of a fish. Dimitra found it at 2:10 a.m., folded in the seat pocket of row 14, still a little damp.

She had cleaned Gate 31 for six years and knew the leavings of strangers the way other people knew handwriting. The businessman who wrapped his gum in receipts. The girl who lined up her shoes on the carpet before she slept. The grandmother who left one peppermint, unwrapped, on the armrest, as if for whoever came after.

The fish-peel man came back. Not that night. Three weeks later, a Tuesday, same row, same seat. He had a cardboard box on his knees with a hole cut in one side, and something inside it made soft scratching sounds.

"Is that allowed," Dimitra said, pushing the cart past him.

"It's a cat. It has a ticket." He held up a boarding pass. Destination: Lisbon. Name: Pim. "I'm taking her to my sister's. My sister says it's time I stopped carrying things around."

Dimitra looked at the peel shaped like a fish on the seat beside him, then at the box, then at the clock above the boarding door, which said 2:14.

"Did you leave something last time?" she asked. "I found an orange peel."

"I didn't leave it." He smiled a little, the way people smile at a thing they can't explain. "I was practicing how to make something that wouldn't rot if I forgot about it."

The boarding call came, soft and polite. He stood, lifted the box, and the cat made a sound like a question. Dimitra bent for the peel, meaning to throw it away, then stopped and tucked it into the pocket of her apron instead.

At the jet bridge he turned around, one hand on the box.

"You can keep it," he said. "It was never really mine to leave."

She watched him disappear down the ramp. Then she went back to row 14 and wiped the seat with the grey cloth, slow, the way she did everything at this hour, and felt the peel in her pocket go a little lighter, and then, somehow, a little warmer.

The Lost Property Box

Every Tuesday, Mira left something behind at school. A glove. A sock. Once, her whole lunchbox.

On Tuesday, she left her red hairclip on the bench by the old oak tree. She didn't notice until she was almost home, and by then the sky was going dark, the blue kind of dark that makes streetlights flicker on.

She ran back.

The hairclip was still on the bench. Next to it sat a small wooden box with a brass lock, and the lock was open.

Mira lifted the lid.

Inside were mittens. Dozens of them, folded neatly. A yellow ruler. A pencil with teeth marks. A tiny rubber dinosaur with one leg missing. All of them were things children had lost, and each one had a little paper tag tied to it with a name written in careful handwriting.

"Oh," said a voice behind her. It was soft, like wind through paper. "You found my box."

Mira turned around slowly.

A pale shape was sitting on the bench. It looked a bit like a girl wrapped in a grey blanket, and it was holding a mitten that didn't match its other hand.

"I'm the Keeper," said the shape. "I collect the things children drop. I keep them safe until someone comes looking. Nobody ever comes looking."

"I'm looking now," said Mira. "Can I take my hairclip?"

The Keeper seemed surprised. "You want it back? Most children just forget."

"I like my hairclip," said Mira. "And I think the mitten's name is Pip. It says so on the tag."

The Keeper looked down at the mitten in its hand. Then, very slowly, it began to glow, a warm silver, like a lamp being lit.

"Pip," it whispered. "I've been wondering who you belonged to."

Mira laughed. "Come tomorrow. I'll bring Pip's friend, the other mitten, from my cupboard. Then you'll have a pair again."

The Keeper glowed brighter. "You'll come back?"

"Every Tuesday," said Mira. "Even if I don't lose anything."

And that is how Mira got a friend who never gives things away, and why, to this day, the old oak tree bench is the only place in town where nothing is ever really lost.

The Spoon in the Night

Every night, at ten o'clock, Mira heard it.

Tink. Tink. Tink.

It was the sound of a spoon going round and round inside a teacup.

Mira's grandmother had kept a blue teacup on the kitchen shelf for as long as anyone could remember. It had a chip on the rim, shaped like a tiny moon. Nobody drank from it. Nobody moved it.

"Why does the cup stay there?" Mira asked, one night, while Gran wiped the sink.

Gran dried her hands slowly. "Because someone once left in a hurry," she said, "and never came back to finish their tea."

Mira lay in bed that night and listened.

Tink. Tink. Tink.

It came up through the floorboards, soft and patient. It sounded like someone who had all the time in the world and wanted only to stir the sugar in.

So Mira crept downstairs in her socks.

The kitchen was dark. The moon sat in the window. And there on the shelf, the blue teacup was full to the brim with something that shimmered like milk in the moonlight.

The spoon lifted. Stopped. Hovered in the air, as if it were waiting.

Mira's heart went thump, thump, thump.

"Are you lonely?" she whispered.

The spoon went very still.

Then, slowly, it sank back into the cup, and the shimmer settled, and a voice like the rustle of an old letter said, "Yes."

Mira thought about this. Then she took the sugar bowl from the table, and she spooned one careful lump into the cup.

"There," she said. "Now it's sweet."

The spoon gave one last happy tink.

And from that night on, Mira never heard the sound again.

But every morning, Gran noticed something strange. The blue teacup was always a little fuller, and always a little sweeter.

It hung behind the register where it had hung since the store sold its first key, and every hook had a number, and every number had a name in the spiral notebook under the counter, though the names had stopped matching anything: the man who cut a spare for his mother's house in 1974 and then inherited the house and then died in it; the woman who wanted four copies because her daughters kept losing theirs, and the daughters had grown and scattered and mailed their copies back one at a time; a boy's first apartment key, cut too tight, recut free, the boy now fifty and somewhere in Oregon and never once asked to be refunded. When the liquidator came through with his clipboard he had walked the whole floor and touched everything, the bins of loose screws, the bolt ends, the shelf of paint the distributor would take back at thirty cents, and then he had stood in front of the board with his pen up and asked what the hell this was, and nobody in the family had been able to tell him, because it wasn't inventory and it wasn't trash and it wasn't theirs to sell, and it wasn't anybody else's either.

final:
The Night Light

Mira had a rule about her bedroom. The door stayed open a crack, and the hallway light stayed on, and nothing could come in from the dark.

So on the night the whispering started, she sat up and listened.

"Mira," said a small voice from the corner. "Please. Could you leave the light on?"

Mira pulled the blanket to her chin. "Who's there?"

"Nobody important. Just Oswin." The voice wobbled. "I used to live in this house, a long time ago. Before the new people, before the new paint. I've been here ever since."

"Why are you whispering?"

"Because I'm scared of the dark," said Oswin. "I always have been. When everyone else went to sleep, I had to stay awake in the black, all alone. It's the worst feeling in the world."

Mira thought about this. Her own rule, she realized, had been made for the same reason.

She got out of bed and looked into the corner. There was nothing there, only a faint silver shimmer, like moonlight on a spoon. It flickered and shook.

"Okay," said Mira. "I'll leave the light on. But you have to promise to stay in the corner."

"I promise," whispered Oswin. "Thank you. Thank you so much."

Mira switched on her bedside lamp, and the shimmer softened into a gentle glow.

"Oswin?"

"Yes?"

"Do you want to hear the rest of my bedtime story? I've got a book about a dragon who is scared of mice."

The glow brightened, almost happily. "Oh, yes please."

Mira read until her eyes grew heavy. When she finally drifted off, the lamp was still on, and so was the little silver light in the corner, humming softly, keeping watch over the girl who had not been afraid of him after all.

Her grandfather's bins ran the length of aisle nine, each one labeled in his square capitals (1/4 lag, 3/8 flat washer, hinge, butt, brass, 2 in.), and she had decided that the brass ones were worth more than the steel because they did not rust into the shape of their own boxes. final: My father cut keys for forty-one years, and by the last week of October the back wall of the shop held more of other people's houses than I had ever known to exist. Brass blanks in rows of small steel drawers, each one labeled in his square pencil capitals: MRS. OKAFOR, 1987. GREEN DUPLEX, NOT THE FRONT. CHURCH BASEMENT, ASK FOR DENISE. He never threw a key away. When the sale signs went up in the window, I started pulling the drawers and found locks that had been torn out, rooms that had been painted over, a whole street of doors that no longer opened onto anything at all. Nobody in town knew the shop kept such a record. We were, it turned out, the only place that remembered where the keys had once fit.

The officiant was the bride's uncle, Gerald, who had married her parents and her sister and, two summers ago, had begun to leave sentences unfinished. Everyone had noticed. No one had said so to the couple, who had noticed too.

He stood at the front in a jacket the color of wet stone. He had a card in his breast pocket, typed large, because Claire had printed it for him and told him it was for the light. He patted the pocket twice, the way you check for keys, and began.

"Dearly beloved," he said. Then he looked out over the rows and did not continue.

A plane crossed the sky above the field. The rented chairs were white, and the grass under them had been mown that morning by the groom's brother, who had not known how to tell anyone that the mower's blade was dull. There was a smell of cut grass and, faintly, of rain coming.

Gerald said, "We're here because—" and stopped. His mouth stayed slightly open, patient, like a man waiting for a bus he was sure would come.

In the third row, the bride's mother began to cry, quietly, the way she had cried for the last two years, which was not at all.

The groom, David, did not look at Gerald. He looked at Claire, and Claire was already looking at Gerald, and something passed between them that had nothing to do with each other. She gave a small nod, the kind you give a child at the top of a staircase.

David took Gerald's hand.

"We're here because they love each other," David said, "and because we want it said in front of all of you," and then he stopped, because he saw he was holding the whole thing now, this rope, and that Gerald was holding the other end.

Gerald's face cleared. He said, "Yes. Yes, that's right," and he finished it. He got through it. He put his hand on David's shoulder when he pronounced them, and David, twenty-nine years old, let him leave it there.

Later, under the tent, Gerald sat down beside the cake and stayed there for most of the reception, telling a story to a nine-year-old about a horse he'd owned in 1961. Nobody corrected him, because there had never been a horse, and because the nine-year-old had never heard anything better.

At the end, when the band packed up, the bride's father found Gerald standing alone by the folding chairs with his card in his hand, reading it. He didn't startle. He folded it back up and put it in his pocket and said, "It went well."

"It went well," her father said.

They stood for a while in the smell of grass and rain that never came, both of them agreeing, in the dark, to exactly what they'd agreed to all along.

- Fixed: short story, 400–600 words, one wedding, one thing going wrong. Reader wants a real turn, not just spilled wine.
- Default: something goes wrong at the altar — object dropped, secret revealed, groom bolts. Or: ex shows up.
- Directions: (1) *Material* — the wrongness is small and technical: the marriage license is invalid, a bureaucratic detail. (2) *Lens* — told by the youngest person there, a kid who only understands the wedding as a schedule of tasks. (3) *Premise reversed* — nothing dramatic goes wrong; the couple is fine, and the "wrong" is that the officiant is the groom's grandfather, mid-dementia, and the ceremony keeps slipping. (4) *Subtraction* — the wrong thing is never named; we only see the guests reacting.
- Pick: 3, but with lens 2 folded in? No — keep it clean. Pick a version where the thing going wrong is that the officiant, the bride's beloved uncle, keeps losing the thread, and the wedding is quietly rebuilt around him. Strong hook: everyone at the wedding knows something is wrong and decides, together, without saying it, to pretend otherwise. That's a retellable premise.
- Reason: a wedding is a ceremony where the script is supposed to hold; a wedding where the script fails but the thing the script was for still happens is truer than a wedding where nothing goes wrong.

<final>
The officiant was the bride's uncle, Gerald, who had married her parents and her sister and, two summers ago, had begun to leave sentences unfinished. Everyone had noticed. No one had said so to the couple, who had noticed too.

He stood at the front in a jacket the color of wet stone. He had a card in his breast pocket, typed large, because Claire had printed it for him and told him it was for the light. He patted the pocket twice, the way you check for keys, and began.

"Dearly beloved," he said. Then he looked out over the rows and did not continue.

A plane crossed the sky above the field. The rented chairs were white, and the grass under them had been mown that morning by the groom's brother, who had not known how to tell anyone that the mower's blade was dull. There was a smell of cut grass and, faintly, of rain coming.

Gerald said, "We're here because—" and stopped. His mouth stayed slightly open, patient, like a man waiting for a bus he was sure would come.

In the third row, the bride's mother began to cry, quietly, the way she had cried for the last two years, which was not at all.

The groom, David, did not look at Gerald. He looked at Claire, and Claire was already looking at Gerald, and something passed between them that had nothing to do with each other. She gave a small nod, the kind you give a child at the top of a staircase.

David took Gerald's hand.

"We're here because they love each other," David said, "and because we want it said in front of all of you," and then he stopped, because he saw he was holding the whole thing now, this rope, and that Gerald was holding the other end.

Gerald's face cleared. He said, "Yes. Yes, that's right," and he finished it. He got through it. He put his hand on David's shoulder when he pronounced them, and David, twenty-nine years old, let him leave it there.

Later, under the tent, Gerald sat down beside the cake and stayed there for most of the reception, telling a story to a nine-year-old about a horse he'd owned in 1961. Nobody corrected him, because there had never been a horse, and because the nine-year-old had never heard anything better.

At the end, when the band packed up, the bride's father found Gerald standing alone by the folding chairs with his card in his hand, reading it. He didn't startle. He folded it back up and put it in his pocket and said, "It went well."

"It went well," her father said.

They stood for a while in the smell of grass and rain that never came, both of them agreeing, in the dark, to exactly what they'd agreed to all along.
</final>

The arrangements were my job, so the mess was too. By nine the tables were bare except for the candle stubs and the place cards, which people had folded into tiny birds and left beside their glasses. I counted them the way I count stems. Forty-one birds. Thirty-six guests had stayed through the cake.

Lucia's father had asked for white peonies, but the peonies came in a box that smelled of wet cardboard, half of them already open to brown at the edges. I didn't say so. I rebuilt the centerpieces with the ranunculus and some eucalyptus stripped of its leaves on the lower stems, and by the time the first guests came up the lawn the tables looked like a choice.

The thing that went wrong was small, and I only saw it because I was crouched under table six, untangling a spool of ribbon. Two cousins from the groom's side had their heads close together. One was saying, "She told me in March," and the other said, "Then why didn't you?" It went on for maybe a minute. Then one of them laughed too loudly and the conversation folded back into weather and gas prices.

Nobody made a scene. That's what I keep returning to. The vows happened, the rings were passed, the music was the song they'd danced to at their first dinner, and the bride cried in the photographs the way brides are supposed to. But the wrongness was there the whole time, a second wedding happening on the edges, between people who had already decided how it would end.

At the head table the groom's mother held her wine glass with two hands and watched the bride's aunt, who was watching the bride. Nobody was looking at the couple. Everyone was looking at someone else who was looking at the couple, like a line of people all leaning toward the same door.

I left at eleven, after the band. The ribbon was in my bag, the birds were in the bin, and I stopped at the last table on the way out. Someone had left a single ranunculus in a water glass with the stem bent flat against the rim. I don't know who. It was still open, and the petals were holding their color better than anything else in the room.

I took it home. I'm not sure what I was keeping it for.

Mira had tuned her violin twice before the procession and once during it, out of habit, her thumb finding A as the bridesmaids came down the aisle in goose-colored dresses. The church smelled of floor polish and the pear candles Mrs. Aliyev had insisted on. Mira had played ninety-one weddings. She could do this one with her eyes on the north window.

The Aliyevs wanted the old custom: the bride's grandfather's violin, played at every family wedding since 1918, one verse of the dust-song before the vows. Mira had heard about the violin all spring. She had not been allowed to touch it until the night before, when it came out of a case shaped like a small coffin and Tahir, the elder brother, handed it over with both palms.

“It likes A,” he said. “It doesn't like E.”

It didn't like E. Mira found that out at the soundcheck in the empty church. The E string flat, then sharp, then a thin buzzing like a bee in a jar. She changed the string. Same buzz. She checked the bridge, the nut, the tailpiece. Fine, all fine. The instrument simply did not want what she was asking. As if it had been tuned for years to a key nobody used anymore and had made peace with it.

She didn't tell Tahir. There are things you don't say to a family on the morning of.

At the front of the church the priest opened his book. Mira lifted the bow and played the dust-song, and the violin sang the first bars true and low, warm as a kitchen. Then the phrase rose, the way the song always rises, and the E should have opened there like a door, and instead it caught. A small crack, a hesitation, like a voice breaking on a name. Mira felt the room feel it. A woman in the third row put her hand on her throat.

She kept playing. She went under the broken note and carried the tune the way you carry a tray with one bad glass on it, and the song came out somewhere darker and truer, and Ada the bride turned her head a quarter inch toward the sound, and it was not a mistake exactly. It was the song doing what the song had been doing in this family for a hundred years: arriving with something in it.

Afterward, in the sacristy, Tahir found her. He was holding his tie like a rope he'd been given.

“You heard it,” Mira said.

“I hear it every time.”

He'd been the one who tuned the violin since their father died. He'd kept it the way his father kept it, and his father before, and some uncle in 1961 whose ear, maybe, was a little off, and no one had ever corrected it because correcting it would mean saying the old man was wrong.

Ada came in, still in white, shoes off, holding a plate of the pear cake. She looked at her brother, and at the violin, and said, “Is that why it cries there?”

“It doesn't cry,” Tahir said.

“Play it at my kitchen someday,” Ada said. “I want to hear it wrong in a room with no one watching.”

Mira put the violin back in its coffin, closing the little brass clasps one by one, and it settled in like something that knew it would be forgiven.

My brother's wedding was above a shuttered carpet showroom, and the lease said forty people. There were ninety-one.

I was thirteen and had no job. I held the guest book for the first hour even though nobody signed it, because Aunt Delia brought her own pen and wanted everyone to use it. So I stood beside the rented arch with my mouth numb from the mints in a crystal dish I'd been told not to touch, and watched the room get smaller with people.

The floor along the south wall had been soft all week. Marco, who owned the building, stacked the potted ferns there to hide the dipped part where the boards went down an inch like a tongue. At four it was fine. At six the band set the speakers on it. At seven the aunts put the tables there because it had the good light for photographs, the long custard one with the pasteles and the one with the coffee urns, and the floor took all of it politely, the way a man takes a coat he can't carry.

I noticed first because I was sitting under the table hiding my shoes, which had heels, which I had never walked in, and I felt the boards breathing. Not a sound — a tilt, the sort a boat makes.

I got up to say something and the band hit the chorus of the song my mother had picked, and ninety-one people turned as one to watch my brother kiss his wife.

Then the coffee urn went over.

It did not fall. It sank, slow, a heavy thing riding down like a man in a tub, and the table with it, the custard, the pasteles, the ice bowl, everything sliding south and the floor going with it, opening a long lip of splintered pine, and after the creak came the noise, which was the whole crowd, no scream in it, just the animal sound people make when the ground lies.

Aunt Delia's cake was on the second table and it did not survive. Nobody cared, which surprised me most, even then. My mother was on her knees in the hole pulling coffee urns out like a woman digging clams. My brother had his wife by both wrists above the gap and was laughing, actually laughing, saying we're fine, we're fine, which was the first lie of the marriage and a week early.

They got everyone off in twenty minutes. The band's drummer carried out two burning candles and set them on the hood of a car. Marco stood in the ruin with a legal pad and did not write anything.

We ate outside, on the pavement, on the overturned tables, cake cut on the tailgate of my father's truck. Somebody had a speaker. My new sister-in-law took off her shoes and stood in the wet and gave out slices with her hands and said, to no one and everyone, this is better. People agreed. People kept saying it. And I stood at the edge because there was nothing left to hand anybody, and I watched the showroom glow under the streetlamp through the broken window, coffee slowly going into the floor, and I understood, at thirteen, that a thing can be ruined and still open, and that nobody would ever fix that floor.

**Plan (notes only — not part of the piece)**

1. **Fixed:** short story, 400–600 words, must contain a wedding and a thing going wrong. The "wrong" must be delivered clearly; anything else is open.
2. **Default:** the rings get lost / the groom jilts her / a drunk uncle toasts the ex / the cake falls. Something *interrupts the ceremony*; the couple endures it; there's a swell of feeling and a hug. Stock material: the sabotage is aimed at the couple or the union, which invites "love wins anyway."
3. **Directions:**
   - *Lens:* the groom's younger sister, the one person at the wedding with no role and no stake in the marriage, watches it come apart. Distinct from "someone sabotages the couple" — the wreck is aimed at the family, i.e. at the guests, not the love.
   - *Premise / material:* the wrong thing is a small, true odd fact from how weddings actually run — a sound-company contract that runs out, an ex, a collapsed floor — here, a collapsing floor under the reception tables.
   - *Form:* tell it in reverse, starting from the aftermath; risks being gimmick, and the swell of feeling gets harder to land.
4. **Pick:** Directions 1+2 merged: the something wrong is a floor; spectator is the groom's 13-year-old sister; the wreck is aimed at the family, not the couple, so the piece pays off differently from the standard sabotage story and earns real consequence.
5. **Reason:** the brief says only that *something* goes wrong — aiming the wreck at the guests, not the couple, and viewing it from a guest with no role, keeps it from being the wedding-vow cliché while still delivering the jolt the brief asks for.

The grandmother had asked for the toast to be short, so Marisol had cut it to four sentences the week before, and then the grandmother had sent back a voice memo of nearly ten minutes, in Tagalog, with a long laugh at the end that Marisol did not understand.

"Just translate what she says," Daniel's mother had told her at the rehearsal dinner. "Everyone will be drunk by then. Nobody will notice."

So Marisol stood beside the head table with a cordless mic and a glass of water she had not touched, and when the grandmother rose, small and certain, in a green dress somebody had ironed too hard, the room turned toward her like a field toward weather.

The first sentence was easy. Her grandmother had been married fifty-one years. Marisol said it, and the room laughed where the grandmother paused, because the grandmother had paused.

The second sentence was about the bride's hands. The grandmother said, in her quick, dry way, that the bride's hands were too cold for a girl who would be cooking for a husband, and then she looked straight at Daniel and said something that made the table of his cousins howl.

Marisol opened her mouth to say *cold hands, warm heart*, the phrase she had prepared, and the grandmother's word came out of her instead, the actual word, which was the one for *stubborn*.

The room was not sure what had happened. Marisol was not sure either.

She could feel the other choice sitting in her throat like a pill. The easy version was the one on the card. The true version was the grandmother's, and the grandmother was looking at her now, not smiling, waiting.

*Say what she said*, the grandmother's face told her. Or perhaps it said nothing at all, and Marisol was only tired.

The grandmother went on. Her voice rose and fell. She talked about a winter in a village Marisol had visited once as a child, about a man who had lied to her about a horse, about how you did not marry someone for their softness. Marisol translated it all, a half-second behind, and found that the half-second was where her own voice lived. In it she could choose a word that was gentler, or harder, or simply less exact, and each time she chose the exact one, because she had promised herself at fifteen that she would never again stand between her grandmother and the people she loved and make the grandmother smaller.

Halfway through the story about the horse, Daniel started crying, and the bride put her cold hand over his, and the cousins stopped howling and simply listened.

When the grandmother finished, she sat down without waiting for applause and reached for her water. Then she looked at Marisol and nodded, once, the way you might nod at someone who had carried something heavy without complaint.

"Good," the grandmother said in English, loudly, so the whole room heard. "You didn't make me sound nice."

Marisol laughed, startled, and the room laughed with her, and the first dance began a little late, because nobody wanted to move yet.

The rings came in a small velvet box that the florist had been carrying since six in the morning, because Rosa had insisted on the florist, and the florist had insisted on keeping the box in the cooler with the peonies so the metal would not sweat.

Tomas opened it in the back room of the chapel at ten to two. He held his up to the window. It was too big by a full size. He could tell by the way it slid over the knuckle of his finger and stopped on the bone, loose and turning.

"Oh no," Rosa said, from the doorway, in her dress already, holding her bouquet like a thing she might drop.

Her ring was too big as well. Hers spun. The inside of the band had a faint line of tarnish where it had rubbed against something that was not her.

They looked at each other and then at the box, which had a card tucked under the satin that said, in fountain pen, *For Tomas and Rosa, from Mr. Aldo Pell, Jeweller, Via Santa Chiara.* Aldo had been Tomas's father's oldest friend. He had made the wedding bands himself, last winter, when Tomas's father was already too tired to come to the shop. He had taken the measurements from Tomas's own hand while Tomas was distracted, talking about football. Tomas had remembered that and had not thought about it again until now.

"He sized them to Dad," Tomas said.

Rosa said nothing for a moment. Then she sat down on the upturned crate by the hymn books and laughed, a short wet sound that was almost crying. "He sized them to someone who wanted them to fit," she said. "He just got the wrong hand."

Outside, the organ began the processional early. Someone's aunt was calling for the bride's mother. The florist put her head round the door, saw the two of them, and quietly went away again.

Tomas turned the ring on his finger, slowly, the way his father used to turn his own wedding band when he was thinking about something he would not say out loud. It had been on his father's hand for thirty-one years. It had been on his hand for four weeks, in a drawer, before it had ever been taken out and measured.

"We can't walk out with these," Rosa said.

"No."

"We can't wear them on the wrong fingers."

"No."

He looked at the velvet box. Aldo had written the card himself. There was a second, smaller slip folded under it, which Tomas had not seen before, and when he unfolded it the handwriting was shakier, as if the writer had been sitting at the bench at night.

*Your father would have wanted the fit to be right. If it is not, the mistake is mine. Forgive an old man. — A.P.*

Tomas read it twice. Then he took his ring off, and then Rosa took hers off, and they put the bands back in their box side by side, and Rosa said, in a steady voice, "Can you get me a pair of pliers and some tissue?"

The organ started again, properly this time. The aunt was still calling. The florist came back in with a roll of white ribbon, which was not what anyone had asked for, and held it out without a word.

Nobody in Vela said the word at the funeral. They said *rendering*, and they said it in the flat voice people use for sewage and tax.

Sela worked the intake floor, which meant she was the one who weighed them. Forty-one kilos. Thirty-eight. The old man from the ninth floor came in at fifty-two and she logged him, and by evening he was moving through the membrane halls with the rest, giving up what he had left. A person is most of a person water. The city had learned that the hard way, in the year the aqueducts came down to mud and the reservoirs showed their cracked brown bottoms like cupped hands.

Now Vela drank its dead and called it a closed loop, and the engineers in the glass tower had a chart that climbed and climbed, and the mayor gave speeches about self-sufficiency, and Sela went home with her hands scrubbed red and drank her ration from a steel cup and tried not to think about the taste, which was faintly of nothing, which was the worst thing about it.

Her mother had signed the pledge at sixty. Sela had argued for a week. Her mother had said, *You weigh people all day. Weigh me. I'm done being a mouth.*

The trouble started with the numbers. Births were down four years running, and deaths were down too, because the clinics were good now, and the two curves were drifting toward each other like tired swimmers. The tower's chart had a second line on it that nobody in the mayor's office liked to show. Sela saw it because her department's quotas came down stamped with a projection: litres per capita, forecast to next spring.

She did the arithmetic on the back of an intake form, twice, because the first time she thought she'd misplaced a decimal. The closed loop was closing. Vela was drinking itself faster than it was dying.

That night she walked the membrane halls alone, past the tanks where the water sat settling, and she put her hand flat against the cold glass, and she thought about her mother, and she thought about the steel cup, and she thought: *we built a city that eats its own end.*

In the morning she filed a request to speak at the tower. She got a slot in eleven weeks.

She spent them learning the pipes. Every seam, every weeping joint, every place the old aqueduct still sweated a little into the dark under the streets, wasted and unmetered since the collapse. She mapped it. It came to almost nothing, a trickle against the city's thirst, and she sat with that trickle for a long while before she understood what it was worth.

Eleven weeks later she stood in the glass room and put two numbers on the board. The projection, and the trickle. The engineers went quiet. The mayor asked what she was proposing.

"Not a fix," Sela said. "A brake. If we patch the old lines and meter the seep, we buy four years. Four years to build the condensers the coast cities use, to get the rain-catchers up on the roofs, to stop pretending the loop is closed when it's a spiral."

"And if we don't?"

"Then in three years the intake floor won't have enough to weigh," she said, "and the tower will have to decide who goes first, and I don't think any of you want to be the ones who write that list."

They patched the pipes. It bought them what she said it would. The chart in the tower got a new line on it, and the line bent, and held, and every morning Sela went down to the intake floor and weighed what the city gave her and logged it, and drank her ration from the steel cup, and the taste was faintly of nothing.

On her desk, under the form, she kept the arithmetic in pencil. Four years. She crossed out the four and wrote three, because the pumps were old, and because the three was honest, and because in Vela a mouth was a mouth and a number was a number and the city had stopped being able to tell the difference.

The sign on the door said SUNRISE AQUIFER, which was a joke, and Verna had stopped correcting it. The aquifer was four rooms and a cold floor, and the aquifer came in through the front door in body bags.

You could tell a lot about a district by its clients. Eastside brought you grandmothers, ninety pounds, wrung out slow over ninety years, hardly worth the collection fee. Downtown brought the overdoses, the young men, dense and wet as fruit. Verna preferred the young men. She was not proud of this. She was a professional.

The machine did the work. You do not need to hear about the machine. What you need to know is that it gave back water, a lot of it, clean and clear and sold back at the pump at eleven dollars a liter, and the company kept two, and Verna kept eleven percent, and that was her whole life, that arithmetic.

Her daughter had drunk water from her body. Not hers, obviously. A man's, an overdose, downtown, thirty-one years old and full of it. Verna had signed the recovery slip like always and then she had taken the slip home and sat with it a while, and then she had gone back to work, because a mother does the math and a mother does it fast.

They asked her once, in the interview, do you believe the body is a vessel of the divine. She said I believe the body is a vessel. They liked that. She got the job.

The city still had its fountains. This was the cruel part. They kept them running, all over the districts, dry fountains, dry basins full of newspaper and dust, because the tourists came through twice a year and a fountain says water the way a flag says country. Verna walked past twelve of them on her way in. The pigeons landed on the rims and looked into the basins and then flew off again, and she thought every time: you see, they don't even remember what they're waiting for.

The last water in Veyra was not in the pipes. The pipes had been dry for eleven years, and Mira Kel kept them polished anyway, because that was the job and because a city that lets its pipes rust has already agreed to die.

She worked the Ninth District main, a pipe wide enough to crawl through, and twice a week she ran the soft cloth down its throat and looked for scale. There was no scale. There was nothing to scale. But the Council paid in coupons, and the coupons bought bread, and bread was the only thing left that everyone agreed on.

The water came from the cellars now. Not from rain—rain had stopped being a thing you could count on sometime before Mira was born—but from the old ice houses, the ones the city had built back when it was rich and stupid and froze lake water every winter to sell in summer. Eight hundred cellars, sealed and cold, and in them the last of it: blocks of lake ice gone cloudy with age, tasting of the wood they'd been stored against, of cedar and iron and something older that nobody had a word for.

You couldn't drink it straight. You bought it by the thimble, and you bought the *taste* of it, and the taste was the whole economy. There were men—they were almost all men, which Mira found telling—who called themselves watersmiths and could tell you which cellar a block came from by the smell alone. Cedar from the north shore. Iron from the foundry cellars, the ones that had been built over the old works. One old woman claimed she could taste the year, and people paid her to try.

Mira had never bought a thimble. She drank the ration, which was gray and flat and tasted of the pipes she kept clean, and she was fine. She was fine the way a person is fine when they have decided not to think about a thing.

Then the Council opened Cellar Forty-One.

It was the deep one, the one under the old market, and it had been sealed since before the drought, sealed by mistake or on purpose, nobody could say. The watersmiths gathered. There was a queue down the market steps and around the corner, and people stood in it for two days, and the price of a thimble went to a month's coupons, and then to two.

Mira went, because everyone went. She stood in the queue with her polishing cloth folded in her pocket and she listened to the men ahead of her argue about what it would taste like. Cedar, said one. No—ash, said another, the market burned in the bad year, it'll taste of ash. They were excited. They had something to be excited about.

She got to the front on the third day. The block sat on a chipped enamel tray, and it was not cloudy like the others. It was clear. It was the clearest thing Mira had seen in years, and it looked less like ice than like a window with nothing behind it.

The watersmith on duty chipped off a thimble and handed it to her, and she drank it.

It tasted of nothing.

Not nothing bad. Nothing at all. It was cold and it was wet and it went down her throat and there was no cedar, no iron, no year, no ash, no old woman's opinion, no argument, no queue, no price. It was water. It was just water, the way water must have been before anyone had to be clever about it.

She stood there with the empty thimble and she understood something she did not want to understand, which was that the whole city had been paying two months' coupons for *stories*. The taste was a story. The year was a story. The market had not burned before the cellars were sealed, she had checked, years ago, in the records, and no one had wanted to hear it. The water was water. It had always been water. It was only scarce, and scarcity is a kind of flavor.

Mira went back to the Ninth District main and crawled into the pipe with her cloth, and she polished, and she thought about Cellar Forty-One, and about the clear block sitting on the chipped tray, and about how the queue would get shorter in a week, and then longer again, because a thing that tastes of nothing is only worth what it costs, and the cost could always go up.

She finished the pipe and climbed out and stood in the street. It was a gray afternoon. The sky had the flat look it got before weather that never arrived. Somewhere behind her a watersmith was shouting a price, and someone was paying it.

Mira folded her cloth. There was still work in the Tenth District, and the pipes there had not been polished since spring, and she walked toward them with her coupons in her pocket and her mouth tasting faintly of iron, which was not a flavor. It was just the pipes. It had always been just the pipes.

The Ministry of Flow gave Teodor a tablet, a lanyard, and a route of four hundred and twelve addresses. Each morning he walked it, stopped at each door, and read the figure off the wall meter in the hallway. Then he entered the figure and the tablet made a small contented sound, as if something had been received.

The meters were old brass dials behind scratched plastic. The needles sat at the same place most days, a little above the red mark that the Ministry had painted on in the year the pipes went quiet. Teodor was supposed to record the position of the needle. He had been recording it for six years. In all that time he had never once seen the needle move.

"It's the pressure," his supervisor, Ilse, said when he asked. She ate almonds from a paper bag and did not look up from her screen. "The pressure's down. The needle reads pressure, not volume. You know that."

He did know that. Everyone knew it, the way everyone knew the tap at the bottom of the stairwell was for show, and that the wide blue cistern on the hill, the one with the chain-link fence and the sign reading NO ENTRY BY ORDER, held the city's water and always had. He had never been up there. Nobody he knew had been up there. It was understood that the cistern was full, the way it was understood that the sky was above the roofs.

On the eleventh floor of a building on Canal Street lived a woman named Aurelia Brand, who kept a jar of cloudy liquid on her windowsill. She offered him a cup of it that first afternoon. He did not drink it. He looked at the meter in her hall, and the needle was pinned exactly where it always was.

"You can write whatever you like," she said. "They'll believe you. They need you to."

That was the part that stayed with him. Not the lie, which was too big to hold in one hand, but the need. Every household paid its tithe to the Ministry in grey coupons, and the coupons bought the certificate that said the water had been measured and the city was orderly. The certificate hung in the lobby of every building. Without it, you could not get a ration card, a school place, a burial plot. The whole city stood on a number that nobody had read.

On the last day of the month Teodor walked his route in the rain. It was real rain, grey and cold and loud on the awnings, and it ran down the gutters in a way he had seen only in old films. People came out and stood under their doorways with their palms up. Nobody said anything. The rain went down the drains the Ministry had cleaned for the dry years, and drained away.

When he got back to the depot, Ilse had already entered his figures. He checked the screen. Every reading matched the morning before, to the hair. The tablet made its small contented sound.

He took the tablet, the lanyard and the route card, and he set them on her desk. Then he went out the side door, past the chain-link fence, and began to climb the hill toward the blue cistern. It was still raining. Behind him the city was filling, slowly and without permission, with water that nobody had certified.

He did know that. Everyone knew it, the way everyone knew the tap at the bottom of the stairwell was for show, and that the wide blue cistern on the hill, the one with the chain-link fence and the sign reading NO ENTRY BY ORDER, held the city's water and always had. He had never been up there. Nobody he knew had been up there. It was understood that the cistern was full, the way it was understood that the sky was above the roofs.

On the eleventh floor of a building on Canal Street lived a woman named Aurelia Brand, who kept a jar of cloudy liquid on her windowsill. She offered him a cup of it that first afternoon. He did not drink it. He looked at the meter in her hall, and the needle was pinned exactly where it always was.

"You can write whatever you like," she said. "They'll believe you. They need you to."

That was the part that stayed with him. Not the lie, which was too big to hold in one hand, but the need. Every household paid its tithe to the Ministry in grey coupons, and the coupons bought the certificate that said the water had been measured and the city was orderly. The certificate hung in the lobby of every building. Without it, you could not get a ration card, a school place, a burial plot. The whole city stood on a number that nobody had read.

On the last day of the month Teodor walked his route in the rain. It was real rain, grey and cold and loud on the awnings, and it ran down the gutters in a way he had seen only in old films. When he got back to the depot, Ilse had already entered his figures. He checked the screen. Every reading matched the morning before, to the hair. The tablet made its small contented sound.

He took the tablet, the lanyard and the route card, and he set them on her desk. Then he went out the side door, past the chain-link fence, and began to climb the hill toward the blue cistern. The meters on Carrow Street had been reading zero since the spring, so Imre went to them anyway, because the ledger still needed a number in the box.

He carried the tablet in one hand and a rag in the other. The rag was for the glass. Each cover had a film of dust that made the dials look like they were underwater, which was funny, since nothing on Carrow Street had been underwater in four years.

Number 14: zero. Number 16: zero. Number 18 was a cracked brass housing that the landlord had stopped fixing when the landlord stopped living there. Zero, obviously. He wrote it down.

The ledger was the city's real water. He had worked it out on the back of a ration slip one night: the reservoirs at Lower Sallow held enough for maybe nine weeks at current draw, and the Authority published eleven. The difference was not in the water. It was in the districts that had reported their usage as "estimated," which meant someone at a desk had typed a figure that felt reasonable. Those districts were the ones with the most people and the least say. Imre had seen the estimates climb, a hundred liters, then two hundred, the way a stack of plates gets taller when nobody is checking the bottom one.

Nobody asked him to find that out. Nobody asked him to say it. The job was to read the meters. Read them, enter them, and let the arithmetic happen somewhere up the hill.

He was at number 22 when the old woman came out of her doorway with a plastic jug. She did not say hello. She held the jug out, and he understood after a second that she wanted him to check it, to put the jug under the tap at the end of her standpipe and tell her how much was in it.

"There's nothing in the line," he said.

"I know that. Look anyway."

He looked. The jug stayed dry. Her standpipe dripped once, the sound loud in the quiet street, then stopped.

"My son said the Authority would send a tanker Thursday," she said. "It's Thursday."

"Tankers come when the route is cleared."

"Then clear the route."

He nodded because nodding was what he had. She went back inside with her jug. He wrote *22: zero, resident reports standpipe dry, tanker status unknown* in the notes field, which nobody read.

At the corner, a water cart the size of a bus idled with its engine ticking. Two men in grey coveralls were filling a bladder from a valve, and a third was standing by a chalkboard, copying figures from a sheet. The figures were the day's allocations. Imre did not need to read them. He knew the shape: the hill districts got their share first, then the government blocks, then the rest, divided in proportions printed in a tidy font that somebody had approved.

He could walk over and ask the man with the chalk whether the proportions were the same as the estimates. The man would say yes, probably, and maybe he would believe it.

Imre kept walking. He had reached the end of the street, and his tablet was nearly full. Eleven meters, zero reading on all of them. Zero is still a number, he thought. It has to be entered, same as anything else, and once it is entered it counts.

He pressed submit. The screen flickered its small green confirmation, and somewhere up the hill a figure he would never see moved a decimal point, and the city went on being precisely as dry as it had been that morning.

The Ledger of Vale Quarter

Dara Okonkwo read meters for the Civic Water Authority, which meant she read numbers that had stopped meaning anything. Every household in Vale Quarter got a ration card with a red bar across the top. Every card had been red since March.

Her route was 214 addresses in the grey blocks by the old rail yard. She carried a handheld terminal, a torch, and a clipboard her supervisor insisted on, because the terminal sometimes lost its signal under the overpass and the clipboard never did.

On the third Tuesday of October, the readings at number 9 Stellan Row came back wrong.

The terminal showed 3,000 litres consumed in the last cycle. The household was a widower, Mr. Teodor Vance, seventy-one years old, who lived alone with a cat and a cactus. The minimum ration for one person was 400 litres. The old man was not spending a fortune on baths. He was not, by any reading, using seven and a half times his allowance.

She knocked. He answered in a cardigan with the sleeves pushed up, and his kitchen smelled faintly of vinegar.

"Mr. Vance, I'm checking the meter."

"It's on the wall, love. Same place as always."

She looked at the meter. It was turning. Slowly, steadily, a small silver wheel that clicked over every time she blinked. Water was moving through his pipe at a pace no pipe in this city should have been able to sustain.

"Have you had any leaks? Any new appliances?"

"Only the tap, and it drips. Always has."

She crouched. Behind the meter cabinet, a thin brass line ran through the wall, the kind used for the old district mains. Vance's flat had been cut off from the city supply three months ago. She had the paperwork. She had signed it.

She stood up slowly.

"Mr. Vance, how long has it been dripping?"

He looked at the cactus on the windowsill. "Since they stopped the deliveries," he said. "I thought it was a fault. Then the rain came in, and I thought the pipe was catching it. But it stays full. Every morning there's a bucket's worth in the bath. I've been pouring it on Mrs. Ilenko's plants downstairs, because she has nothing left to pour."

Dara went back to the terminal. She scrolled through the sector records and found what she had been half-expecting since the summer: the household totals did not match the district total. Two hundred and fourteen households on her route had reported their usage, and the sum of their consumption came to 412,000 litres. The Authority's own intake from the reservoir at Hollin Ridge was recorded as 60,000. The difference was not missing. The difference was being logged as if it had been drawn, and then logged again, and again, in the sectors on the far side of the river, where nobody reads meters anymore.

She understood it then, the way you understand a sum after a long time staring at it. The city was not running out of water. Someone was booking it out, and the books were all that remained of the reservoir. The towers had been drinking the rain, and the paperwork was drinking the towers.

She photographed the terminal screen. Then she photographed the meter, turning. Then she took off her ration card and tore the red bar across the top, neatly, along the perforation.

"Mr. Vance," she said, "keep the bucket. Don't pour it on anything yet."

He nodded as if she had told him the weather. Outside, the first rain of the autumn had started on the rail yard, and for once, the gutters were full.

Dara wrote a single line on her clipboard, the one thing the terminal could not record: 9 Stellan Row, reading unverified, household claims nothing, water present.

Then she went on to number 11.
