Ines found the desk already set up for her, which she took as a good sign until she opened the drawer and found a binder labeled in marker: HANDOFF, DO NOT LOSE.

Dov from Facilities brought her a coffee she hadn't asked for. "Milk, no sugar. Mira said you'd want that, and Mira's usually right about people." He said it the way you'd mention the weather.

"Where is Mira?"

"Retired in March." He looked at the binder, then at the window. "She kept the north sensors calibrated by hand. Nobody else learned it. We're still working out what breaks next."

Ines opened the binder. The handwriting was small and slanted, and every page had the same entry at the top: the date, the reading, a single word. *Steady. Steady. Drift. Steady.* Pages of it. Years.

"What's the word for?" she asked.

Dov shrugged. "She didn't say. We figured it out eventually. It's the lighthouse on the point. The beam's been slipping a few degrees a year since the foundation settled. Nobody's noticed because ships don't look at it anymore. They look at the screens."

She turned pages until she found the most recent entry, dated the Friday before Mira left. *Drift,* it said. Then, underneath, smaller: *Tell the new one. She'll want to see it herself.*

The job listing said "Assistant Keeper, Coastal Fixtures." Nobody had told Mara what a coastal fixture was until she arrived at the grey office above the harbor and a man named Oswin handed her a pair of rubber boots two sizes too big.

"Low water is at 14:12," he said, not looking up from a ledger. "You'll walk the breakwater with me. Mind the green weed, it's slick."

She had imagined a desk. Instead she got a clipboard, a flask of tea that tasted of smoke, and a route marked in red ink along the rocks.

The breakwater was longer than it looked. Oswin walked it like a man reading a familiar sentence. At every iron post he stopped, pressed a palm to the rust, and wrote one word on his clipboard: "sound," or "tired," or once, "unhappy."

"Why does the post get a mood?" Mara asked.

"Because it has one." He nodded at a bolt she couldn't see from where she stood. "That one wants replacing by spring. Tell me if the paint peels off in a shape you recognize."

At half past two the water began to climb back over the stones, and the other two keepers came up the slipway with their boots full of sea. Nobody introduced her. They just nodded, the way people nod at weather.

Back in the office, Mara found her desk. Someone had left a jar of boiled sweets on it, labeled in careful capitals: FOR WHOEVER IS NEW.

She ate one. It tasted of salt and lemon.

Oswin wrote something in the ledger and turned it toward her. Under the day's date, in his small square hand, was a single word she did not yet understand, and a time: 14:12. It was the same as the tide had been, and it was the first thing anyone had written about her.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we start on the posts."

She pulled off the oversized boots and set them by the door, ready for the next low water.

The elevator in the Harnett Building had a button for every floor except thirteen, and on her first morning Marisol Okonkwo pressed the button for the ninth floor and waited.

The doors opened on the fourth. A man in a grey cardigan looked at her, looked at the panel, and stepped back out.

"Going up?" she said.

"Not in that one," he said, and the doors closed on him.

She had read the offer letter four times. It had said *Analyst, Records & Reconciliation, start Monday, 9:00*. It had not said anything about elevators.

The doors opened on seven. A woman with a lanyard full of keys got on, pressed nine, and then, without looking up from her phone, pressed the stop button between eight and nine and held it.

"Sorry," Marisol said. "Is something wrong?"

"Nothing's wrong. You're supposed to wait for the bell."

"What bell?"

The woman sighed and released the button. Somewhere in the walls, a faint chime, like a spoon on a glass, rang once. "There. Now you can go. You'll learn it. Everybody's first morning, somebody holds the car."

On the ninth floor, the reception desk was empty except for a plant and a laminated card that read *PLEASE SIGN IN — AND WAIT FOR THE BELL*. Marisol signed in. The next name on the sheet, two lines up, was her own handwriting from a visit she didn't remember making. Her name was already there, dated three weeks before she'd been hired.

She looked at it for a long time. Then she sat down in the chair across from the plant and waited, as instructed, for whatever bell came next.

**Tidepool**

The ocean is not far.
It is here, in a bowl of rock
the size of two hands,
doing its whole job
at a smaller wage.

A crab works the seam
like a man with a bill to pay.
Anemones open their pale machines.
The water sits, and sits,
and does not know it is a sample.

By afternoon the sun
has taken most of it.
What is left is salt,
a few stranded lives,
a shine that will not last the hour.

The child who found it
does not call it the sea.
She calls it hers,
and puts her finger in,
and the tide comes back
the way it always does —
not to save anything,
just to arrive.

**Breakwater, 3 A.M.**

Nobody clocks it in. It works the night
the way a nurse works nights —
quietly, on the hour, checking the ones
who cannot say what hurts.

It has moved the same stone forty years
and will not say so. It keeps
the small things that fall in: a glove,
a name half-said, the warm coin of a sun
it swallowed without meaning to.

Somewhere a boat worries its knot.
Somewhere the tide goes out like a breath
held a long time. The ocean
does not answer, and this is not
cruelty. It is only the sound
of something enormous
doing its job.

**The Woman Who Stopped Going Down**

She knows it the way you know a neighbor
through a wall: the cough, the chair pushed back,
the tap run late. It has been eleven years
since she stood on the sand.

It comes in anyway. Through the window seam,
through the letterbox, a cold breath
on the sill, and the salt sits down
in the curtains like a guest who won't leave.

At night it works on the cliff.
You can hear it filing, patient,
taking the headland down a grain at a time,
the way she takes her pills, one, then one.

She has heard it do things she won't say.
Once, in a storm, it got into the road
and left a boat there, upright,
as if it had walked up and set it down.

In the morning the gulls are loud about it.
She makes tea. She does not go to the window.
Some days she thinks the sound is her own blood,
and the ocean is just what blood sounds like

when there is a lot of it,
and a long way to go, and nothing
to break against, and it keeps going,
and it does not need her to look.

Somewhere off the pier a glove went in,
the left one, red, with the thumb already torn.
Nobody marked the spot. The tide came up
and took the rest of the afternoon with it.

The sea keeps what it's handed, badly, slowly.
A bottle cap. A child's shoe, one lace still tied.
A key to a house that someone sold in March.
It turns them over the way a clerk turns receipts.

I used to think it hid them out of spite.
Now I think it simply has no shelf for them,
so everything the coast gives up
goes down to the sand and stays,
one small weight among the other weights.

The glove will be somewhere past the reef by now,
its fingers folded like a hand that stopped waving.
I'm not asking for it back.
I only wanted someone to have seen it go.

Keeper's Log, Low Tide

Tuesday: one boot, left foot, laces knotted.
Wednesday: a bicycle bell, still ringing once when lifted.
Thursday: half a chart of the harbor, the channel marked in pencil.
Friday: a child's shoe, too small for anyone I know.
Saturday: a glass float, green as a bottle of cough syrup, unbroken.
Sunday: nothing. I wrote nothing. The wind was kind.

Monday: a wedding ring, cold, the inside engraved with a date.
I rang the bell at the station, the way I always do,
and sent word up the coast to the families who ask.
Most of them never come down. Most of them keep the list.

It is strange work, keeping what the water hands back.
I do not want the sea to stop giving.
I only want to know what it has been holding.

Her job was to answer the phone.

The dish was older than she was. Water enters. Water leaves. That is the entire job and we do not pretend otherwise.

Powder-coated steel, hand-washable, 24cm across. It will outlive the sink it drains into.

**Colander. For everything you want to keep, and nothing you don't.**

final: A century ago the god Veyra died, and the mountains that rose from her spine are the only thing keeping the sea from swallowing the lowlands. The town of Hallow's Reach was built on her shoulder blade. Its people are the ones who maintain the pilgrimage roads and the prayer shrines that keep the great corpse from rotting further. The novel's protagonist is a young stonemason's apprentice, and she is the first to notice that the body has begun to shift — not in the old, slow way of settling, but a deliberate, painful movement toward the sea. The empire's priests insist the mountain is a holy relic and the movement is a sign of favor. The guilds insist the surveys are wrong. The apprentice has been secretly keeping her own measurements because the town's official records have been falsified. As she investigates, she finds the migration is a resurrection: the god is not dead, only dreaming, and the dream is of a body that cannot be allowed to wake. The cost of stopping it is not a battle but a corruption of the land that the empire's economy depends on: the god's bones are the source of the metal that keeps the cities running. The apprentice must decide whether to let the god die, and the sea rise, or to wake her and end a world that already decided the corpse was more valuable than the god. It is an intimate, grounded story about a town that has been built on top of a lie, where the only thing that is real is the shifting of the ground beneath the people's feet.

final: A city called Rell sits on the only pass through the Grey Teeth, and it survives because the dead must be remembered accurately — the wrong version of a death lets something in through the gap. So Rell buys its safety the way it buys grain: with licensed mourning houses, paid by the week, whose job is not comfort but custody. The protagonist, Vess, is a junior archivist for the smallest house in the lower quarter, trained since childhood to sit with the dying and take down the exact shape of what they leave behind, down to the lies they told and the debts they hid. Then a magistrate's wife dies with two versions of her last hour already circulating, both false, both paid for, and Vess is ordered by her own employer to record a third. She begins to suspect her house has been selling the truth for years, and that the thing in the pass has been getting fed on purpose.

1. **A back-office for laundromat operators.** Laundromats run on coin, card readers, and one overworked owner, and no tool treats card fees, water, machine downtime and insurance as one ledger. The startup sells a single dashboard that flags the machine that costs more than it earns, priced per store rather than per machine.

2. **Shift differential and hazard tracking for night cleaning crews.** Custodial contractors lose money because nobody logs who was on which floor after midnight, so premiums go unpaid and disputes go nowhere. The product is a phone-based log that turns those hours into a clean invoice and a clean claim, sold to the contractor, not the building.

3. **A marketplace for selling a dead relative's small business.** When an owner dies, the family inherits a shop, a lease and no buyer list, and brokers want six figures for something worth a tenth of that. This is a low-fee listing and handoff service for the sellers who show up with a death certificate and a set of keys.

4. **Underwriting for water taxi and small ferry operators.** These are maritime businesses that get quoted like weekend boaters, and one bad hull claim can end a route that a town depends on. The startup bundles inspection, maintenance scheduling and coverage into one subscription priced off route hours.

5. **A co-op tool for commercial kitchen hood cleaning.** Hood crews work nights, under grease, and get paid by the job while the paperwork eats the margin. The product lets a crew own its scheduling, bidding and safety records together, so the operators keep the contracts instead of the franchise.

The city's guilds believe the bell still rings under the ice, and anyone who hears it will be called home by the dead. Ilde, who has never trusted anything that sings, takes the job for the money and for the one thing the guilds refuse to say aloud: the bell was cast from her own family's silver. They are queuing, patient and polite, below the surface, and some of them have been trying to surface for years.

**Name:** Oleander Vasquez-Imai, 58, retired court stenographer, currently employed as the night-shift cashier at a 24-hour laundromat in Tacoma.

**The obvious version:** a burnt-out detective with a dead partner and a bottle of whiskey. Set aside.

**The protagonist:** Oleander types everything people say, and she has done so for thirty-one years. She cannot stop. In a courtroom she produced transcripts so accurate that lawyers asked her to fix their grammar. Now she hears the laundromat's customers the same way: a woman who says "I'm fine" three times before she folds a single shirt, a man who asks the dryers, not the cashier, whether his son has called. She notices what people leave out, and she keeps a private record of it in shorthand on the back of the coin-exchange slips.

**The hook:** one night a customer she has never seen before drops a folded note on the counter with a dictated sentence she has typed a thousand times in another context, a court-reporter's habit of phrasing. She recognizes the rhythm before the words. Someone is speaking in the cadence of a deposition, and only she would catch it.

**Why she belongs here:** a stenographer's ear is the one tool that cannot be bribed, flattered or fooled by a confident voice, which is exactly what a mystery needs from its witness.

**Her flaw:** she trusts transcripts more than people. She will believe the record over a living friend, and the mystery turns on a line she typed wrong thirty years ago.

final:
**Nell Okonjo, professional witness.**

Nell testifies. That is the whole job. Attorneys hire her because she can sit in a courtroom for six hours and describe a parking lot the way a surveyor would: the light, the distances, the car that was idling. She has never been caught being wrong on the stand, and this is her entire reputation, and it is also the thing she has started to distrust.

She keeps a case file on herself. Every memory she has sold to a jury is logged in a binder by date, because testimony is a kind of forgetting: once you have said a thing under oath, in a clear voice, to twelve people, the saying replaces the seeing. Nell knows this the way a surgeon knows scar tissue. She has testified so often that some of her memories are now mostly the sound of her own voice saying them.

The mystery starts when she is hired for the other side.

A man is dead in a stairwell. Two witnesses saw different things, and both are certain, and one of them is lying, and Nell is asked to sit with each of them and quietly establish which. She does this by asking them to describe the stairwell again, then again a week later, then to draw it, then to describe it as if entering from the roof instead of the lobby. Certainty holds its shape. Lies drift. It is the closest thing she has to a gift.

Then the drawing comes back, and it is the stairwell from her own binder. The one she testified about nine years ago. The one with the water stain shaped like a bird. She has never told anyone about the bird.

So now she is a witness to something she cannot testify about without admitting she was wrong once, under oath, in a case that put a man in prison, and the man in the stairwell is that man's brother.

She does not solve it with a gun or a chase. She solves it the way she earns a living: she sits very still, and she listens to which details hold their shape, and she writes everything down, and she stops trusting the clearest voice in the room—which, for the first time in her life, is hers.

She has a bad knee from a fall in a courtroom she was not supposed to be in. She drinks tea, not whiskey. She is forty-three and has no idea whether she is a good person, only whether she is accurate, and she is beginning to suspect those are not the same question.

Every memory she has sold to a jury is logged in a binder by date, because testimony is a kind of forgetting: once you have said a thing under oath, in a clear voice, to twelve people, the saying replaces the seeing. Nell knows this the way a surgeon knows scar tissue. She has testified so often that some of her memories are now mostly the sound of her own voice saying them.

The mystery starts when she is hired for the other side.

A man is dead in a stairwell. Two witnesses saw different things, and both are certain, and one of them is lying, and Nell is asked to sit with each of them and quietly establish which. She does this by asking them to describe the stairwell again, then again a week later, then to draw it, then to describe it as if entering from the roof instead of the lobby. Certainty holds its shape. Lies drift. It is the closest thing she has to a gift.

Then the drawing comes back, and it is the stairwell from her own binder. The one she testified about nine years ago. The one with the water stain shaped like a bird. She has never told anyone about the bird.

So now she is a witness to something she cannot testify about without admitting she was wrong once, under oath, in a case that put a man in prison, and the man in the stairwell is that man's brother.

She does not solve it with a gun or a chase. She solves it the way she earns a living: she sits very still, and she listens to which details hold their shape, and she writes everything down, and she stops trusting the clearest voice in the room—which, for the first time in her life, is hers.

She has a bad knee from a fall in a courtroom she was not supposed to be in. She drinks tea, not whiskey. She is forty-three and has no idea whether she is a good person, only whether she is accurate, and she is beginning to suspect those are not the same question.
</final>

Protagonist: Odile Pankhurst-Mbeki, 71, a retired court stenographer in Accra who now transcribes the dying for a hospice that pays her in mangoes and grudging thanks.

She is not a detective. She writes down what people say in their last weeks, word for word, because the hospice requires it and because she has never trusted anyone's memory of anything. For thirty-one years at the Kumasi magistrate's court she typed every false oath and every true one at the same speed, and she learned that a lie leaves a rhythm: a pause before a name, a word repeated when it should not be, an adjective that arrives early. She still hears it. She cannot switch it off.

When a retired fishmonger named Kwabena Asante begins dictating a confession that contradicts the death certificate of his brother, Odile notices the rhythm is wrong in the opposite way. He is telling the truth, but he has rehearsed it, and the rehearsal has made the detail too tidy. She knows that grief does not come out in order. She starts asking the questions no one has asked, in the order a court clerk would ask them, because that is the only method she has ever had.

Her flaws are the engine. She is vain about her handwriting. She is rude to the hospice chaplain, whom she suspects of tidying up the dead. She will not drive, so she goes everywhere on the trotro routes she has memorized, and the mystery unfolds along those routes, passengers and conductors becoming the witnesses she interviews without meaning to. She keeps every transcript in a tin that once held Milo, and she reads them aloud at night to a dead husband who objected to her habit of being right.

The unusual thing is that her talent is not perception in the usual sense but attention to how words are assembled under pressure. She solves cases by listening to the scaffolding of speech, and the story can be told entirely through the transcripts, the margins she annotates, and the arguments she has with herself in the tin-lined kitchen. The reader learns to hear the lie as she does.

Dell Prine keeps a wall of keys behind her counter, and every one of them is a promise she wasn't supposed to keep.

Dell is a locksmith in a river town of nine thousand people, and she has worked every door in it at least once — rentals where the landlord changed the locks on tenants who hadn't moved out, bank boxes, the funeral home, the Methodist church, a gun safe whose owner forgot the combination and then forgot he'd called her. People hand you a key and then they hand you their house. She has a drawer of spares that were never picked up. She has never once used one. She could, and everyone in town half knows it, which is why she gets invited to things.

She's not a detective. She has no interest in the police, who once asked her to open a car and then asked her why she was so calm about what was in it. She is calm because a lock is a machine that tells you what happened to it: a scratched pin, a deadbolt thrown from the inside, a keyway that's been picked by someone who learned from a video and left their impatience behind. Dell reads doors the way other people read faces.

The mystery starts the way it always does, with a call that doesn't fit. A woman asks Dell to rekey her back door. Standard. But when Dell gets there, the door is already new — replaced, stained to match, hinges still tight — and the woman insists it's the same door she's had for twenty years. Dell doesn't argue. She takes the job, goes home, and opens her ledger, because she writes down every lock she's ever touched: make, wear, who paid. The ledger says she rekeyed that address eight years ago, and the door she rekeyed had a dent in the lower panel where a dog had worried at it. The new door has no dent. Somebody in this town replaced a door to erase what a door remembers.

That's the case: not who did it, but who has been quietly swapping the town's doors, one at a time, for years — and why Dell's own ledger is the only record that anything changed. She's not chasing a killer. She's chasing an erasure, and the only thing standing between the town and its own clean blank face is a woman with a drawer full of keys she has never used and a book of every door she's ever opened.

Her name is Odile Crane-Vautrin, and she is seventy-one, and she has not left the second floor of the Hollis Lane public library in nine years, because the librarians there have agreed to sort her overdue cards before anyone else touches them.

She is not a detective. She is the person who knows that the parish register of Wenlow was copied out in 1912 by a clerk with a rash on his left wrist, and that every birth recorded in the spring of 1913 has the same wrong date for the church bells. When the vicar's wife is found in the reed bed below the mill with her shoes tied together by their laces, the constable asks the village who was in the church that morning. Odile, who has never been asked anything by a constable, says the bells were off by a quarter-hour, and that this was a fact, not a rumour.

She solves the case the way a bookbinder repairs a spine: slowly, from the inside, by noticing what has been glued down wrong. The vicar's wife kept a ledger of which hymns the choir sang badly. Odile reads it as a timetable. The mill owner's son keeps a hive with a broken pane, and the bees are the only witnesses who never lie. Odile asks the library's oldest patron, a retired organist with a hearing aid he turns off when he disapproves, to play the bell pattern back to her from memory, and that pattern is the alibi.

She does not chase anyone. She waits in the reading room with a crossword she finishes in pen, and people come to her, because she has the one thing a village never thinks to hide from a woman in a cardigan: an accurate memory of what they said, and when.

The last scene is her returning a single overdue book, nine years late, with a fine she pays in old pennies. The librarian asks what it was about. Odile says it was about a bell that rang a quarter-hour early for thirty-one years, and that she now has to put it back on the shelf exactly where it was.

Picture a village where you have lived your whole life. You know the baker, the woman who mends shoes, the boy who is always running somewhere.

Now suppose something odd about this village: whenever two people have the same thing — the same song, the same letter from a cousin, the same photograph of a wedding — a copy of it sits in both their yards. Not the same object, a copy. If your neighbor learns a new recipe and writes it down, and later you ask her for it, she does not hand you hers. She keeps hers. You get your own.

You want something. You write on a slip of paper what it is, and you give the slip to a boy at your gate. He does not know where the thing lives. He only knows the next person to hand it to. That person hands it to the next, and so on. Every few steps someone says, "That one's in the yellow house past the bridge," or "Nobody here has that," and the slip either moves closer or comes back.

When it reaches the right yard, the copy is made. Then the new copy starts walking back the same way, or a different way — whichever is shorter that day — until it is in your hands. That is all that ever happens. A slip goes out. A copy comes back.

Here is the part worth holding on to. Nobody in this village is in charge of it. There is no mayor who decides what may be asked for, no office with a list of what exists, no center. If the bridge washes out, the slips simply go the long way round, and most people never notice. The village has no idea, at any moment, what is being asked or what is being sent. Each person only knows the few neighbors on either side, and the small job of passing things along.

That is why you can ask for something almost nobody has and still get it: someone, somewhere, has it in their yard, and there is a path of hands from there to yours.

And it is why a thing can be in a thousand yards at once and still be nowhere in particular. No single person kept it. Everyone did.

Picture a market town, big enough that you cannot see all of it from one spot. You live at one edge. Your cousin lives at the other. You want to tell her something — say, that the boat from upriver will arrive on the wrong day.

You don't know the roads. You don't know her house. You only know her name.

So you go to the market square and you tell a runner. Not one runner who carries the whole message to the end — that would be foolish, because the roads flood, or the runner forgets halfway, or gets stopped. Instead the square is full of runners going every which way, and your message gets broken into pieces, each piece small enough to be shouted, and each piece handed to a different runner heading in roughly the right direction.

None of them know the whole message. None of them need to. A runner only needs to know the next hand-off: who is standing at the next square, and which way to shout.

At every square, a runner arrives and shouts their piece to whoever is there. Someone writes nothing down — they just shout it on to runners heading further along. Piece by piece, by different routes, by different people, the whole thing arrives at your cousin's square. There it is reassembled, checked against how many pieces should have come, and read out to her. If a piece went missing, a runner at her square shouts back "send that again," and your square sends it again by another road.

The reason this works at all is that everyone agreed, long ago, on a few things: how to break a message into pieces, how to number the pieces, how to address them by name rather than by house, and how to shout "got it" back. Those agreements are the only thing held in common. Nobody owns the roads. Nobody owns the runners. Each square just keeps a list of which way to shout for which name, and that list gets passed around and corrected when roads close.

The internet is that, done by machines instead of people, fast enough that the shouting is invisible. Your message is the pieces. The runners are the wires and the air. The squares are the machines that pass things along. Your cousin's name is her address. And the old agreement about how to break, number, address and acknowledge — that is the part that makes a crowd of strangers behave like one town.

One thing worth knowing: the square near you, the one you always hand your message to first, is only a square. It is not the market. If it burns down, the town keeps talking, because there was never a center — only runners, and a habit of shouting.

Picture a town where every house has a mailbox, and nobody in it can read a map.

When you want a page from a shop across town, you don't drive there. You write the request on a card: "Please send me the Tuesday menu." You put the card in your mailbox with the address of the shop written on the front. The town's postal workers pick it up, and each one only knows the next stop. The clerk at the first sorting house glances at the address, passes it to a van, the van hands it to another van, and so on, until the card lands at the shop.

The shop writes the menu on a card of its own, and the same thing happens in reverse. The menu is not carried in one piece. It is cut into dozens of small slips, each numbered, each with the return address and the destination. The slips take different roads. Some go through the river tunnel, some over the hill, some in a truck that happened to be going your way. Some slips get lost and the shop sends them again. When they all arrive, your mailbox puts them back in order and you read the whole menu as if it had come in one envelope.

That is the internet. The houses are computers, the cards are requests, the slips are called packets, and the sorting houses are routers, which pass each packet onward without knowing or caring what is inside it. The addresses are numbers, like a house number on a street, and a directory service, something like a phone book, turns a name such as the shop's into the number the postal workers need.

Nobody runs the whole town. Thousands of separate postal networks agreed on the same rules for addresses and envelopes, and that agreement is what lets a card from your house reach a shop run by strangers on the other side of the world.

Think of the internet as a postal system for a city where every house has no street number, only a name, and every letter is cut into pieces before it leaves.

When you ask for a web page, your request is a letter that says, in effect, "send me the recipe for lentil soup from that kitchen over there." You don't know which road the letter will take. The post office in your neighborhood looks up the name in a directory, passes it to the next office, and so on, until it reaches the kitchen you asked for.

The letter itself is torn into small envelopes, each with a number on it and the return address. The envelopes may travel by different roads. One might go through a bridge that is busy today, another through a longer route that is clear. At the kitchen, a clerk lays the envelopes in order by their numbers, checks that none are missing, and asks for any that got lost. Then the kitchen sends the recipe back the same way, in pieces, and your own post office reassembles it on your side.

No single office knows the whole route, and no single road is essential. If one closes, the envelopes find another. That is why the system holds together even when parts of it fail.

The "names" you type, like a web address, are the directory entries. The clerks who look them up are computers that keep those listings. And the kitchens are other computers, holding the pages, waiting to answer whoever asks.

So when a page appears on your screen, it is the reassembled reply to a letter you sent a moment ago, carried by many hands you never see, along roads no one planned in full.

Imagine a town where every person knows only the neighbors next door. Nobody knows where anyone else lives, but everyone knows how to pass things along.

You want to send your friend across town a long letter. You don't hand it over whole. You tear it into little slips, numbered, so the pieces can be put back in order. Each slip gets written on the front with where it should go.

Now the slips are handed from neighbor to neighbor. Each person looks at the address and passes the slip toward it. If the usual road is blocked, they pass it down a different street. Slips may take different routes. Some might arrive before others, out of order, and that's fine, because the numbers tell your friend how to rebuild the letter.

Here is the part that makes this work: no single person needs the whole map. Each one only needs to know which neighbor is closer to the address. The town as a whole finds the way.

When your friend gets every slip, they lay them in order and read your letter, as if you had walked it over yourself. That is how the internet works. Your words, a photo, or a video are chopped into small numbered pieces, passed from machine to machine across cables and radio waves, each one choosing a path, and reassembled at the other end.

The sea has been coming ashore for longer than anything has been watching, and it has never once arrived. It reaches the same line, takes a little more sand, gives a little back, and turns around. Nobody calls that failure. Nobody stands on the cliff and tells the water to want it more.

You are allowed to work that way. To show up to the same ordinary day and move the same inch of ground. To measure yourself by whether you came back, not by how far up the beach you got.

Keep coming back. That is the whole of it, and it is enough to wear down stone.

Mona Pettigrew clears houses, and she is not sentimental about it, though she keeps a shoebox of things she is not supposed to keep: a bobbin of red thread used halfway, a dog's vaccination card, a dented measuring cup, a hospital bracelet cut open at the wrist. She works on a schedule set by the estate agents. She does not look for anything. She uses the word "reset." When she has finished, a house does not feel like a crime scene or a memory. It feels like a room with nothing to say yet.

The work has taught her one rule. People tell the truth in what they didn't finish. A person can say anything about themselves in a listing photo. But a man who leaves a half-glued chair in the basement, clamps still on the dowels, was interrupted mid-purpose. Someone planned to sit in that chair. Someone had one more sanding to do. Mona has never had to explain this to herself; she worked for nineteen years cleaning other people's houses before she cleaned the houses of people who had died, and both jobs taught her the same thing: the living leave themselves in corners.

---

The Sykes house, a two-story with a koi pond the partner wants filled in, looks fine. The widow says her husband, a retired actuary named Gordon, came home with a fever, went to bed, and stopped answering. The coroner agrees with the widow. Pneumonia on top of a compromised heart.

Mona doesn't argue with coroners, but the house is arguing with her.

The bedroom is orderly. Pristine. The side of the bed where Gordon slept has a pressed-flat pillow, and the bed is made tight enough to bounce a quarter. Mona has seen too many houses to believe in a man who makes his own bed on a fever night. She notices the good linen has been put on fresh, and whoever took the old linen didn't wash it; the bottom of the hamper smells of bleach.

In the den, the bookshelf has been sorted by size. In her experience, no one sorts a shelf by size unless they are clearing a space and don't want the gap to show. There's a gap, about the width of a boxed set of encyclopedias, on the third shelf, and a rectangle of unfaded wall paint where something hung. The fridge has one photograph left on it. Its magnet is still stuck, holding nothing.

Then the kitchen. A glass in the sink with a film at the bottom, bitter-smelling, and the dishwasher run so recently that the inside of the door is still beaded with water. The trash has been tied off and taken out. But under the sink, pushed back behind the recycling bin, there are two envelopes of Gordon's own prescription and a printed sheet folded in thirds: a hotel reservation, two nights, one guest, the weekend before he died. The name on it isn't Gordon's.

The actuary was not dying of pneumonia at home. On Thursday he was checking into a hotel alone under another name.

By now Mona has been in the house eleven hours and is getting paid to be blank. She wipes the counters. She throws out the prescriptions, which she does not need, and keeps the hotel sheet, which she also does not need, folded into the shoebox, because she knows the type of housewife who calls on a Thursday. She knows what the wife did when her husband's taxi left for the hotel. She cleaned. Anyone can tell you a frightened woman tidies.

But the house is not finished with its story yet.

The guest bathroom is spotless, except for one towel, folded over the rail the way good hotels fold towels, and a hair, long and grey-brown, in the drain. The widow has short grey hair. On the bedroom carpet, in the pile next to the laundry hamper, is a small triangular tear where a ring snagged and the thread got pulled up. Mona stays on her knees. She runs the back of her hand along the baseboard.

This is the part she loves and never tells anyone about, because you can't say it: the delight of a floor. A floor is honest. Doors slam, pillows lie, but a floor takes everything and keeps it.

She takes the hotel key card out of the driveway drain with a screwdriver or some tool; the widow's story has Gordon never leaving the house. The motel's name is not printed anywhere Mona can see, but she has seen the motel's key card before, in a shoebox of her own from a previous job, and she knows the printed room number 214 belongs to a chain that appears three times this side of the county line; but what she doesn't say is that all three are named after flowers. Only one, the Rose of Sharon on Route 6, sits a half-mile from the bus stop the widow takes to work. The wife could have visited. Or met him. Or slashed the tires.

Mona is not a detective. She can't send anyone to a hotel. But she takes the towels in.

In truth, what she does has a name she doesn't use: house reading. The court called her once. She handed over the shoebox. The investigator wrote her up as a witness with "an eye for domestic detail," which is a small thing to be, but it closed the case: the wife had been at the hotel, the husband had been somewhere else, and the man found at breakfast in his bed was a stranger's son with Gordon's coat. Nobody asked Mona to explain how. She doesn't.

You might not believe the koi pond has a purpose. She hates that she almost missed it. She feeds the koi because she doesn't want them to starve and because she doesn't like how they stare, and after she feeds them, they gather at the shallowest corner, all at once, the way fish go where something has been in the water. Mona drags a rake through reeds. She nearly turns her ankle on a submerged object.

It's a lockbox. It's rusted shut. Inside, in a zip bag, a debit card in Gordon's name; the key to the hotel room; and a typed note, two sentences, unsigned. The lockbox held the second key. There were two keys to that room. Gordon met someone in it.

By now Mona has been in the house nineteen hours. The widow is sitting on the porch. Mona has never told a client what she saw, because it is not her job. But this is a house that is telling her something, loudly and badly, in a dead man's voice, and she doesn't need to be a detective. She needs to be the person who knew the room was wrong before she went through the door. She puts down her rag, wipes her hands, and says to the widow, "You'll have to ask the other key."

The second key is not a suspect. It is a birth. It's Gordon, but not the Gordon the widow knew, not the actuary in the bathrobe; it's the other person he was, the one who checked into the Rose of Sharon for two nights and ate breakfast in the morning. Two nights is not a weekend. It's a life. It's whoever was in the room when the nurse left.

So the wife's question to the coroner, and the coroner's to the wife: whose bed was Gordon in?

The koi keep circling. Mona takes the shoebox with her and drives to Route 6, where the roses are dying and the desk clerk is a girl of about twenty with the hotel's name stitched on her blazer, and Mona says she is there to clear 214 and please not to call the front desk, she's not the guest. The girl says she's not sure. Mona says she's sure. And it is true that Mona Petitgrew has never been wrong about a house finished too fast, and she has been paid by every estate agent in two counties to straighten a room and say nothing, and at the end of it, she likes to sit in her car and know that a person was a place, and the place was a person, and it's her hands that keep them both from being erased.

Think of a very large village, much bigger than any village you have seen, spread across the whole world. Every house in it has a small box by the door, and every house has a number so it can be told apart from the others.

Suppose you want to send your neighbor a pair of gloves. You wrap them, and on the paper you write two things: the number of your neighbor's house, and the number of your own house, so they can send something back.

But you don't know where your neighbor lives. Nobody does. The village is too big.

So you hand the parcel to a boy named Tomas, who stands at the corner. Tomas doesn't know either. He knows only the houses on his own street and a few streets nearby. He looks at the number, decides the parcel is probably that way, and carries it to a woman two streets over. She knows her own corner of the village. She sends it on again. And again, and again — thirty people, maybe, each taking one step, each looking only at the number and their own small map. Nobody holds the whole way in their head. The parcel simply keeps moving, one hand to the next, until it arrives at a door with that number. The glove-maker in the next country, the grandmother three towns over, the office across the water: the same. A parcel, a number, and someone at the next corner who does not know the whole road but knows the next step.

Now here is the part that makes it worth the trouble. It isn't one parcel. It's millions at once, and each one arrives in less time than it takes you to blink. When you write to a friend far away, your message becomes one of those parcels. When you read a page, it's a parcel that came to you. When something goes missing, it's usually because one corner of the village forgot which way to point, not because the village disappeared.

The numbers on the doors aren't locked, though. Anyone standing at any corner can read the paper. So most people write in a private hand that only the person at the door can read, and the rest of the village just carries it along, blind to what's inside.

That's it. A village with numbered doors, and a great many people each knowing only the next few streets, passing things along until they're home.

Devin took the appliances. It was easier: the stand mixer, the toaster oven that always burned the right side, the matching things that would look fine in a truck bed and fine on a counter in another state.

I took the rest.

The cabinet above the stove went into grocery bags one shelf at a time. Cumin with a scoop fossilized in it. A jar of red powder with no label, terrible handwriting. Saffron in a little envelope, probably older than me. Devin carried the blender out and said, "You're keeping that?" He meant the mustard with maybe a teaspoon left. "I am."

The junk drawer was the worst and I took all of it. Birthday candles, nine of them, all the same number. A screwdriver that had never once been the right screwdriver. Rubber bands from asparagus. A battery taped to a toothpick that I didn't ask about.

Freezer: seven bags of soup, none labeled, all the same orange, all of them hers, all of them from after she stopped cooking for anyone but herself. I put them in a cooler.

Devin stood in the doorway with the keys. The room behind me looked like a room. He had taken everything that made it look like she was coming back. I held the bag.

"There's no system," he said.

"I know."

He carried the last thing out anyway. I stayed a minute longer, because the faucet dripped, and nobody had fixed it, and I wanted to remember exactly how it sounded.

Dana took the cast-iron pan first, the one with the crack filled in with what Mom called "patience," which was really just a glob of epoxy.

"You can have the colander," she said.

Tomas held it up. Full of holes, a dent in the rim where someone had dropped it on the tile. "Which of us she liked less?"

"Neither. It's the one she used for the greens."

He turned it over. Stuck to the bottom, a sticker from a grocery store that closed in 2009, the price half-scraped off. He picked at the corner with his thumbnail. It came away in one curl, sticky, and he laughed, a short hard sound.

They worked without talking for a while. The drawer of takeout menus, the rubber bands, the wooden spoon with the burnt handle that neither of them wanted and neither would throw away. Dana found the recipe box behind the flour. Index cards, most in her mother's slanted hand, some in her father's block capitals from before the divorce. She didn't read them. She set the box on the counter between them like something that could still go off.

"The good knife," Tomas said.

"You keep the good knife."

"You cooked more."

"You're the one who wanted to be the cook."

He stopped. Looked at her. Then he reached past the box, took the dish towel off the oven handle, folded it in half, and started wrapping the pan.

"Take the box," he said. "I'll take the pan. We'll fight about the knife at Thanksgiving."

Dana picked up the box. It was lighter than she expected.

The freezer bags did the talking first. Mama had written on every one in her own hand, blue Bic, the K's looped like earrings: KIDNEY. PEPPER SOUP BASE. GOAT. Ada read them out. Femi held the bags she handed him and didn't look down.

"You take the goat," she said. "You have the freezer."

"Freezer's in this kitchen."

"Your flat has a freezer. Mine has a shelf and a man who thinks jollof is a spice."

He laughed once, through his nose, the way he had at sixteen when she caught him smoking behind the water tank. Then he put the goat in her box anyway.

They worked the cupboards in silence: the mortar, the three wooden spoons, the good pot with the hairline crack nobody would fix. Mama's rice cooker weighed nothing without rice in it. Ada's box filled. Femi's box stayed flat, a punch bowl he'd never use, a tin of Ovaltine gone hard, a whisk.

At the door he stopped, hand on the jamb, and said the thing he'd come to say. "You can't read the rest of them."

"Which rest."

"Yesterday. There were two more she did after. I brought my phone in, I was going to — she was talking. I don't know what she said." He looked at the freezer like it had answered him in a language he'd left behind at seven. "You'll have to tell me what I'm eating."

Ada took the marker from her bag and wrote, on the first one, in her own looping hand: STEW. STEW. STEW.

They start with the knives, because nobody wants the knives.

"You take the good one," Dara says.

"You take the good one. I'll take the one with the wooden handle, the one Mum kept hiding behind the sugar."

"That's the one with the crack in it."

"That's the one with her thumb in it."

Dara turns the crack over with a fingernail and says nothing. Outside, a bin lorry grinds up the hill and stops at every house, the way it always did, and somebody on the next street is still practising the same four bars on a trumpet.

They divide the mugs by logic: anything with a chip goes to Dara, who collects chips the way other people collect postcards. The tin of buttons goes to nobody, then to both, then into a carrier bag marked MAYBE, which will be in the hall for a year.

The tea towels are a problem. There are nineteen. Tom holds up the one with the map of Corfu, faded to the colour of weak tea.

"Corfu was a disaster," he says.

"Corfu was lovely. You got sunburnt and blamed the sea."

"I got sunburnt because you wouldn't let me put the cream on."

"You were twelve. You'd have put it on the wrong bits."

He laughs for the first time since they arrived, a sudden bark that makes him look like their father. Dara sees it, and for a second neither of them moves.

Then the kettle, which is in the box marked KITCHEN, the one neither of them can bear to open and both of them packed. Tom plugs it in. It makes the same small click it always made before it boils.

"Keep the kettle," Dara says.

"You keep it."

"Tom."

"Fine. We'll have one cup each, and we'll argue about the milk."

It is the first thing either of them has decided all afternoon, and it's stupid, and they both know it's the right size for the job.

The multi-faith room at B gates is a beige box with six chairs and a rug nobody vacuums properly. Adele restocks the prayer books on Tuesdays. She's not religious; she works for the contractor that also does the moving walkways.

She knows which books get used. The Qur'ans stay sealed in their plastic. The Bibles get the wear, mostly the back pages where people have room to write. Lately people write in the front, on the title page, like they want to be first in the book.

This week: a phone number with no name. A grocery list. *Mom — I did try.* Someone had drawn a house with two chimneys, then crossed out one chimney, then crossed out the other.

The rug is the other record. Adele rolls it up Sunday nights and shakes it out over the service stairwell, and what comes off it is hair, mostly, and cracker crumbs, and once a set of house keys with the tag still on, HARLOW REALTY, 3B. She turned those in. Nobody claimed them. They went to the bin of unclaimed things in the basement, which is where the walkway parts go too when they fail.

She doesn't pray. She straightens the chairs. When someone comes in and sits and doesn't do anything, she straightens around them and leaves. You learn not to ask. The books tell her everything she needs. Last month a man wrote the same word down all four margins of a Bible, twenty-some times, small and neat, and the word was *reconsider*, and Adele wrote nothing back, because that isn't the job.

The room is between the baggage carousel and the prayer room and I have worked it eleven years and no one has ever asked me for directions to it.

Wednesday a cane with a wooden duck's head. Tuesday a coat, size forty-two, with a dry cleaner's ticket for a different coat. Monday: two phones, one passport, a brass urn, and the urn is what I want to tell you about, because we are not supposed to hold the urn. You hold the passport ninety days and then you are allowed to let it go. You hold the urn, I said to Petrov, and Petrov is my supervisor, you hold the urn and it means we are assuming the person who left it is not coming back, and coming back is this airport's entire job. Petrov said put it on the shelf, and I put it on the shelf, and twice a day since I pass the shelf.

The cane was claimed Thursday by a man who said his mother. He did not have a mother, he had a story, but the cane was his, I let him have it. The coat is still with us. The urn is still with us.

You would think I would be better at this. Eleven years of things people set down on a seat and walked away from, and I have never once called it lost. The belt, I call it, keeps going. That is the actual thing I look at all day, the belt, and how it will run whether or not anything is on it, and I think the airport is trying to tell us something, that's what I'd say if anyone asked, which they don't. Arrivals is the last place a person is still opened by a stranger. After that, everyone's just going home.

The urn has a small scratch on the base. I don't know what from. Petrov says it'll go to auction in the new year with the other unclaimed. I have a daughter flying in on the red-eye and I have not told her the room exists, and I don't intend to. I'll wait at the barrier with everyone else.

That is all I do. I take the tickets, I log the item, I put it on the shelf, I go home, I come back, and once a shift I stand in the doorway and listen to the departures board change like it's clearing its throat.

Mara took the colander first. She held it up to the window like it might tell her something.

"You can have the big pot," she said.

Tomas looked at the pot. It was the one that boiled over every Sunday. "I don't cook."

"Neither did she, really."

He opened the drawer by the sink. Foil, string, a roll of stamps from a decade ago. A rubber band the size of a bracelet. He put the rubber band on the counter, then picked it up again.

The oven clock still showed 4:12 and blinked when the power dipped. Neither of them had touched it.

Mara lifted the knives out of their block one by one and laid them on the table in a row, handles toward him. He didn't take them. She didn't put them back.

"The bread knife," she said.

"You keep the bread knife."

"I keep saying that."

The radio on the windowsill was tuned to the station she always had on. A man was reading the weather for a town neither of them had lived in. Tomas turned it off. The quiet sat between them on the table with the knives.

He reached for the chipped blue bowl, the one with the crack like a river on a map. Mara's hand moved toward it at the same time. They stopped, both of them, fingers an inch apart.

"You take it," she said.

"You take it."

Neither did. They left it in the middle of the table, the way she used to leave the salt.

Outside, a car door shut. Someone's dog barked twice and went quiet.

Tomas picked up the rubber band and slid it onto his wrist. Mara watched him do it and didn't say anything. Then she slid the bread knife into a dish towel, folded it twice, and set it by the door where they'd both see it on the way out.

They started with the fridge because it was the hardest.

Nadja held the crisper drawer, Yusuf held the shelf that slid in above it, and they worked outward: his the mustard, hers the olives, the jar of capers split by cap count. He read the dates off things and she decided. When they got to the door shelves it was nearly easy — he took hot sauce, she took jam. Neither wanted the pickles.

There was frost in the freezer, thick down the back wall, heavy as plaster. Yusuf said, half of that's mine. Nadja said then get a knife. They spent twenty minutes on the ice, not talking, breathing, until he had a bowlful and she had a bowlful and the wall behind showed the old blue.

After that it went fast and strange. He took the thermometer. She took the oven light. They argued, without heat, over which of them could honestly claim a drawer that had only ever held foil.

He said: I'll take the floor.

She looked down at the floor.

I mean I'll do the floor, he said. The mopping.

He wrote her name on a bag. She wrote his on a bag. In the last cabinet there was nothing but a single square of shelf paper gone brown at the curl, and neither of them would take it, and they left it there, and went down to the car with their bags.

The gate agent's name was Dolores and she had been paging the child for forty minutes, which meant the child was either hiding or gone, and the girl was neither. She was sitting under the row of seats by Gate B12, in the exact spot where she had been told to sit, with her backpack between her feet.

She had watched the page the whole time. Twice she stood up, and twice she sat back down, because the announcement never said her name. It said a name. It said *Amara Okonkwo, eight years old, traveling alone, please come to Gate B12.* Amara had checked on the way in: the boarding pass in the front pocket of the backpack said Okonkwo, Amara, and the birthday said she was nine as of three weeks ago in Lagos, and the passport in the other pocket agreed, and she had decided, somewhere around the second page, that the woman was probably looking for a different child and doing her best.

At the desk they were calling her mother, who was in a hotel in Houston. They were calling the unaccompanied-minor desk, which was calling the airline, which was calling back. Amara had a book and a bag of chin chin and the arm of the seat above her, which was warm from the lights, and the woman across the aisle had given her a look earlier like she was about to be helpful, so Amara had put the hood of her jacket up and become a kid with headphones, which is a kind of invisibility you learn early in airports.

The third time Dolores said *Amara Okonkwo* was the time the girl noticed the escalator had stopped running. It went still with its teeth showing. Everyone at the gate turned to look at the escalator, and then at the desk, and then at each other, and nobody looked down, where the person they were looking for was sitting exactly where she had been asked to be.

The lost-and-found at Terminal C is a room of shelves behind a door marked STAFF, and Donata has worked it for nineteen years, long enough to know which objects come back and which don't.

Umbrellas come back. Phone chargers come back within the hour, sometimes with an apology. Reading glasses come back if the person is over sixty and still in the building. Wedding rings almost never come back, because the people who lose them are already ashamed and don't want to say it aloud at a desk.

On Tuesday a man in a grey coat brought in a single brown leather glove and asked if anyone had turned in its pair. Donata checked the bins. Nothing. She told him the glove could stay with her for ninety days, the way the rules said, and he nodded as though she'd given him something.

"It was my father's," he said. "I didn't know it was missing until I was at the gate."

"They usually are," Donata said. "Missing until someone notices."

He wrote his number on the form in small square handwriting, then stood there a while longer than the form required.

She put the glove on the third shelf, between a child's rain boot and a box of loose keys. The shelf held the things people had lost on their way somewhere, and for ninety days, the glove would wait for the man to decide whether he was going back for it.

On Friday the bin in the corner, which she emptied every Saturday, held a second glove, brown, the mate of the first, wedged under a seat cushion in gate 14 where someone had been sitting with it all week. Donata turned the two gloves over. They were worn in the same places.

She did not call the number. She put both gloves on the shelf, side by side, and wrote on the tag in pencil: *Matched. Do not separate.*

Then she went back to the umbrellas.

The night after we moved to Marrow Bay, I noticed my shadow was late.

Not gone. Late. I'd walk into the kitchen and it would come in a second after me, like it had stopped to check something. My mum said I was tired from the drive. I stopped mentioning it.

It got worse. At the top of the stairs my shadow stayed at the bottom. In the hallway it lagged by the whole width of the door. I started watching it out of the corner of my eye, which is the worst way to watch anything, because that's when you see it move on its own.

Then one night I woke up and my shadow was sitting on the end of my bed.

The moon was up. It came through the window and laid a stripe across the floor, and my shadow sat in the stripe with its back to me, shoulders hunched, facing the wall.

I did not move. I have thought about that a lot since. I did not move, and I did not turn on the light, because some part of me already knew the light wouldn't help. A shadow needs a light. Whatever was sitting on my bed didn't.

It was crying. That's the part I still hear. Small, wet, hitching cries, the kind you make when you've been lost a long time and you're trying not to bother anyone.

So I did the thing you're not supposed to do.

"What's your name?" I whispered.

It stopped crying. It didn't turn around. It said a name I won't write here, and it was a kid's name, a normal one, and then it said, very quietly, "You're in my room."

I lay there a long time after it went.

In the morning there was nothing on my bed but the dent in the blanket, the shape of somebody small, sitting up, waiting.

My shadow was right behind me all day. On time. Not a second late. Like it had finally caught up, and now it wasn't going to let me out of its sight.

My sister taught me these rules the week we moved into the flats. She made me say them back to her. So I'm saying them to you. Say them back.

One. Don't take the stairs after the lights go off. Not because of anything on the stairs. Because of what counts you.

Two. If you hear a kid counting, stop walking. Counters count feet, and they only count up to the number of people on the landing before they start over. If they start over while you're still moving, they've counted you wrong. Stand still until they get to the top number and stop.

Three. Don't answer the door flat 8. Nobody lives in flat 8. If someone knocks from inside, it's just the pipes, and pipes can't hear you, so don't say anything.

Four. This is the important one. If it asks you a question, hold your breath while you answer. Not before. While. Like this—

My sister did it. She said, Are you cold, in a flat voice, the whole thing out with no air going in. She said that's how you get to keep the answer. If you breathe, the answer comes out of you and it belongs to them, and they'll ask again, and you'll be empty the second time. You can't hold your breath forever, she said. So answer fast.

I asked her who told her the rules.

She said the last girl did, when she was leaving.

Then she said it was nearly dark, and told me to go and get ready for bed, and I did, and I lay still and I listened.

Somewhere under the floor, someone was counting. She got to seven, which is the number of floors we have, and started over at one.

Outside my door, my sister stopped walking.

<final>My sister taught me these rules the week we moved into the flats. She made me say them back to her. So I'm saying them to you. Say them back.

One. Don't take the stairs after the lights go off. Not because of anything on the stairs. Because of what counts you.

Two. If you hear a kid counting, stop walking. Counters count feet, and they only count up to the number of people on the landing before they start over. If they start over while you're still moving, they've counted you wrong. Stand still until they get to the top number and stop.

Three. Don't answer the door flat 8. Nobody lives in flat 8. If someone knocks from inside, it's just the pipes, and pipes can't hear you, so don't say anything.

Four. This is the important one. If it asks you a question, hold your breath while you answer. Not before. While. Like this—

My sister did it. She said, Are you cold, in a flat voice, the whole thing out with no air going in. She said that's how you get to keep the answer. If you breathe, the answer comes out of you and it belongs to them, and they'll ask again, and you'll be empty the second time. You can't hold your breath forever, she said. So answer fast.

I asked her who told her the rules.

She said the last girl did, when she was leaving.

Then she said it was nearly dark, and told me to go and get ready for bed, and I did, and I lay still and I listened.

Somewhere under the floor, someone was counting. She got to seven, which is the number of floors we have, and started over at one.

Outside my door, my sister stopped walking.
</final>

My cousin Farah rides the 41 home from swimming because it's the only bus that stops near her flats. It's always nearly empty. The driver, Mr. Okonjo, knows her and waits if she runs.

One Thursday the bus went past her stop. She stood up and said, "Sir, that was mine."

"Nobody rang," he said.

He circled back. She got off, went home, and didn't think about it again until the next Thursday, when it happened again. And the Thursday after that. Always at the same corner, the one by the shuttered bakery with the peeling sign, he'd sail right past, then frown at the mirror and turn the bus around.

"It's that button," he told her the third time. "The one at the back. It rings on its own. I fix it. It comes back."

Farah sat at the back the next week. She wanted to hear it.

Nothing happened the whole ride. Then, right at the bakery corner, the button behind her chimed, one short ring. She turned.

The seat was empty. But the plastic was warm. Warm like somebody had been sitting there a long time, waiting for the right stop.

She didn't tell Mr. Okonjo. She just pressed the button herself, twice, so the bus would stop for whoever it was, and then she got off and walked home, and the night smelled like rain and diesel.

The next Thursday, the ring didn't come. The seat was cold. Farah rode to the bakery corner anyway, and when the doors opened, nobody got on.

But Mr. Okonjo sat very still for a second, both hands on the wheel, and said, quiet, like it was just to himself, "Alright. You're home."

Then he pulled the doors shut and drove on.

Ines had been in lost property for eleven years, long enough to know which things people came back for and which they only said they would.

The umbrellas came back. The phones came back, usually within an hour, the owners already shouting into the next thing. Reading glasses came back. A wedding ring in a paper cup, retrieved by a man who did not look at her and did not say thank you, only nodded at the counter as if she had handed him his own hand.

What nobody came back for was the small stuff. A single glove. A hair clip shaped like a swallow. A child's shoe with the laces still tied, which she kept on the second shelf because the first shelf was for things with a chance.

She logged each item in the ledger, with the date, the terminal, the gate if they knew it, and a short description. The descriptions were the part she liked. Blue cardigan, one button missing, smells of cigarettes and oranges. Passport, Hungarian, name half worn off the cover. Pocket notebook, last page written in pencil: call Dad back, tell him it was fine.

After thirty days the unclaimed things went to a van and then to a warehouse by the runway, where they were sold by weight or given to charities or thrown away, depending on the year's budget. Ines had never been to the warehouse. She had read the disposal forms, though, and she knew the ledger would outlast all of it, because the ledger was the only place anyone recorded what was left behind and why.

On Tuesday a woman came up to the counter with a canvas bag and said she had lost her suitcase on a flight from somewhere she did not name. She described it in detail. Green, a broken wheel, a name tag with a cartoon fox.

Ines checked the shelves. Nothing matched.

"It may still come," Ines said. "They often do."

The woman nodded and stood there a moment longer than necessary. Then she unzipped the canvas bag, took out a small red wallet, and set it on the counter.

"I found this on the floor by gate twelve," she said. "Would you put it in the book for me? I don't want to be the one who decided it was nothing."

Ines opened the ledger and wrote it down, and the woman watched her write, and neither of them said that the wallet looked as if someone had meant to come back for it.

**Gate Sweep**

Marisol worked the B concourse from eleven to five, after the last flight and before the first. She carried a grey cart, a long handle, a spiral notebook.

In the notebook she wrote what she found. Not the valuables, which went to Lost Property in a clear bin with a tag. The other things. A single black glove under row 14. A paperback with a boarding pass for a flight to Lisbon, folded as a bookmark at page 88. Three Chinese takeout chopsticks, still in their paper sleeve, lying parallel on the carpet as if someone had set them down to think.

She did not know why she wrote them down. She had started on her second week and kept going.

Tonight: a child's shoe, one, pink, velcro, under the third seat from the windows. A hotel key card on a hotel she had never heard of. Half a sandwich wrapped in foil, still cold. A printed photo of two men on a beach, one laughing so hard his eyes were shut.

She wrote: *Beach. Two men. One is laughing so hard he cannot see.*

Then she wrote the time, which was 2:14, which was when the gate's last boarding call had ended forty minutes before and nobody had gone home yet.

Near the window at the far end, a woman sat with a suitcase upright beside her, both hands on the handle. She had not moved in an hour. Marisol had seen her at the start of the shift, and again at midnight, and now.

Marisol pushed the cart toward her, slowly, the way you approach something that might fly.

"Is this yours?" she asked, and held up the photo.

The woman looked at it a long time. Then she took it, turned it over, and read the back, though there was nothing written there.

"No," she said. "That's his."

"I can put it in the bin."

"Don't." She tucked it into the front pocket of her coat. Her hand stayed there.

Marisol took the notebook out and turned to a clean page, then did not write anything. After a while she said, "I'll note it found. I won't put a name."

The woman nodded. Outside, a plane pushed back, its lights moving across the glass and across both of them, and then it was gone.

Every night, before she went to sleep, Maya counted the stairs.

There were fourteen. She counted them up from the hall, one hand on the rail, and every night there were fourteen.

On Tuesday there were fifteen.

She stopped on the top step and looked down. The new one was grey, a little bit dusty, the same colour as the old wood but somehow not the same. It did not creak when she stepped on it. It did not creak at all.

"Mum," she called. "There's an extra stair."

Her mum came out of the kitchen drying her hands. "There's no extra stair, love. Off to bed."

But that night, when Maya went up, she counted again. Fifteen.

On Wednesday there were sixteen.

On Thursday, when she came home from school, the stairs had gone on past the top landing and up into the ceiling, and nobody had noticed except her.

She sat at the bottom with her knees pulled up and thought about it for a long time. Then she stood up, went into the kitchen, and said quietly to the empty room, "Can you hear me?"

The fridge hummed. A tap dripped.

"I'll count them for you," said Maya. "If you want. Every night. That way you won't forget where you are."

That night she went up slowly, one step at a time, saying each number out loud. One. Two. Three. At seven she heard a little sigh from somewhere under the floorboards. At twelve the old house settled, the way a cat does when it finally lies down.

At fourteen, she stopped.

Only fourteen steps. No more, no less. In the morning, the grey stair was gone, and the wood was warm and plain, and the house felt like a house again.

Maya still counted the stairs every night before she went to bed. She did it because she liked it.

And sometimes, just as she reached the top, she could hear someone else counting along, very softly, a little bit behind her.

final: My grandmother sold hardware the way other people keep secrets: quietly, and only when asked. The store was where I was parked between school and supper, wedged behind the register with a book while she matched washers to bolts for strangers who called her Mrs. Kowalczyk like it was a job title. Now there are orange tags on everything, a color that means nothing in a hardware store, and my mother has a clipboard and a pen she keeps clicking. I am here to carry boxes. I am good at carrying boxes. Down the third aisle, where the paint used to be, the shelves are already bare and the wall shows a paler shape of itself, and I keep walking past it like it might still be a place I know.

The Sock Thief

Every Tuesday, one sock went missing.

Not from the washing machine. Not from under the bed. Just from the drawer, where Mira had folded them into pairs that morning.

"It's the ghost," said her little brother, Teo, with great seriousness.

"There's no ghost," said Mira.

But on Wednesday, another sock was gone. Then on Thursday, a red one with a yellow stripe. Mira kept a notebook, and she wrote each one down.

On Friday night she sat up in bed with her torch and waited.

The house creaked. The clock in the hall ticked. Then, very softly, the bedroom door opened by itself.

Something stood in the doorway. It was grey and thin, like a shadow that had been left out in the rain. It crept across the carpet on tiptoe.

Mira held her breath. The shadow bent over the open drawer. Its long fingers reached in and lifted out a sock, a small striped one, and held it up to the light.

"Hello," said Mira.

The shadow jumped. The sock fell to the floor.

"Oh, you can see me," it whispered. Its voice sounded like a page turning. "Nobody can see me anymore. Not since I lost my own socks, a hundred years ago."

"You lost them?"

"I lost them," said the ghost sadly. "And ever since, I've been looking for the other half of every pair. I cannot rest until every sock finds its partner."

Mira thought about this. Then she got out of bed and knelt by the drawer. "Which one are you missing?"

The ghost pointed a grey finger at the sock in her hand. "That one. It was mine, and its partner was left behind."

Mira looked at the striped sock, then at her own feet, where her left sock had a bit of hole in the heel.

"I think," she said slowly, "that if you give it back, you could pick up the rest."

So the ghost did. It held the striped sock to its chest, and for a moment it glowed a soft, silvery blue. Then it let out a sigh that sounded like a wind through leaves.

"Thank you," it said. "I can rest now."

It dissolved into the moonlight. The door clicked shut.

On Saturday morning, the drawer was full. Every sock was in its pair, and on top, folded very neatly, was one small striped sock with a note tucked inside:

*Keep the light on, please. The dark is lonely.*

Mira did. And she never lost another sock again.

final: The bin of loose screws had been mislabeled for as long as anyone could remember — MISC., in Marisol's father's block capitals, on a card gone the color of weak tea — and now, three days before the bank took the building, she and Denny were standing in front of it, arguing about whether it went in the lot for the auction or came home in the trunk of her car. Denny said their father would have wanted it sold. Marisol said their father would have wanted it sold to someone who'd know what it was. Neither of them said the thing underneath, which was that the bin weighed eleven pounds and could not be divided, and that after Saturday there would be no more Saturdays when they both had to be in the same room. Behind them, the register drawer sat open and empty on the counter, and the fluorescent light over aisle four, which had flickered for two years, flickered.

final: In the back of the store, under the register that no longer rang up anything, there was a shallow wooden drawer that Ray's mother had labeled KEYS UNKNOWN in pencil, and it had never once been emptied. Nobody remembered what was in it when the labels were first written. Now it held two hundred and some brass blanks, a clutch of rusted padlock keys still threaded on a loop of baling wire, a Schlage with a snapped bow, and a tiny flat one that might have opened a diary or a cash box or a shed in a town that had since moved away from its shed. Nobody at Hollow Lane Primary knew who checked the lost property box at night.

Mrs Dunning, the caretaker, said she never heard a thing. But every Monday morning the box in the corridor was a little tidier, and a single glove was always placed on top, very neatly, the fingers folded in.

Priya noticed first. She was the sort who noticed things, and she was the sort who brought a torch to school in her bag, just in case.

One Monday she stayed behind after the bell. She sat on the bench beside the box and waited. The clock above the door ticked. Somewhere a radiator knocked twice, then stopped.

At half past five, the corridor light flickered. Then, very slowly, the lid of the lost property box lifted by itself.

A girl's shape rose out of it, grey and thin as tracing paper. She wore a red cardigan with one button missing, and her face looked worried, the way people look when they have been searching for a long time.

"Sorry," said the girl. Her voice was soft as the hum of a fridge. "I'm looking for my blue hair ribbon. I had it in Year Three. I put it down, and I never came back for it."

Priya's heart thumped, but she kept her voice steady. "What does it look like?"

"Blue. With a white stripe. It smells of strawberries."

Priya rummaged through the box. Odd socks, a trombone mouthpiece, three water bottles, a single trainer. And there, folded small under a scarf, was a blue ribbon with a white stripe.

She held it up. The grey girl gasped and crept nearer, and Priya saw that the ribbon was faded, but it was still a little bit strawberry.

"Thank you," whispered the girl. She took the ribbon, and her grey outline seemed to brighten, just slightly, like a window catching the sun. "Now I can go home."

She stepped back into the box and was gone. The lid closed with a soft click.

On Monday morning, Mrs Dunning found a glove on top of the box, neatly folded.

Priya found a single strawberry sweet beside it.

She ate it, and went to class, and never told anyone, except you, now.

final: For thirty-eight years the Dimitrou family kept a shelf behind the counter for things that had been left. A cut-to-size brass hinge with the customer's name pencilled on its box. A hand-forged gate latch, a seized pump rebuild, a single drawer pull in a paper sleeve that said only "Mrs. Oduya, Tuesday." My father never threw any of it away. Customers who vanished came back years later, usually at the worst possible hour, asking whether we still had the part they'd ordered in 1989, and he would take the box down without looking at the label and hand it across the counter as though they had been gone an afternoon.
