1. **"Library After Dark"**: Keep the building open late one night a month with a teen-run café, a battle-of-the-bands in the reading room, and the stacks lit by string lights for anyone who wants to stay. Teens get a place to be that does not ask them to be quiet or to be anyone in particular.

2. **"Overdue, Forgiven"**: Announce a month when every fine is wiped and any teen can return a book they lost or never gave back, no questions asked. The message is that the library is a place you can walk back into, and the strongest hook is the story teens will pass along about the time they came back.

3. **"Read Me Your Worst Book"**: Invite teens to bring in a book they secretly hated and read a passage aloud to a room of strangers, with the audience voting on whether it deserves a second chance on the shelf. It turns reading into a shared, slightly ridiculous ritual that teens can join without having to admit they love books.

4. **"The Library Is Recording"**: Give teens a free booth, a microphone and an editor to make a podcast, audiobook sample or short documentary about their neighborhood, with the finished work archived in the library's catalog. Teens come for the making, and the library becomes the place where their work lives.

5. **"Borrow a Stranger"**: Set up a shelf where each book comes with a handwritten note from a local teen explaining why it changed their week, and anyone can check out the book and the note together. The teenagers become the library's most trusted recommendation system, and the visit happens because someone their age asked for it.

1. **The Library Is Where the Group Chat Goes Quiet.** Teens are tired of being watched on every screen they own, so this campaign sells the library as the one place where nobody is posting, scrolling or being tagged. Posters show empty study tables with the caption "No notifications. Just you and whatever you're avoiding."

2. **Overdue Fines, Reimagined as Tolls.** Each late fee is reframed as a small toll paid to enter a hidden world of books, games and quiet rooms, with teens invited to "earn passage" by visiting. A playful wayfinding map on the library's social feeds lets them unlock a new room with every visit.

3. **The Loudest Thing in Here Is You.** Teens are invited to record a 30-second audio note about any book, game or argument they're carrying, which the library then plays back in its reading rooms. The concept turns the usually silent building into a place where teen voices are literally heard.

4. **Ask the Librarian Something Embarrassing.** The campaign spotlights real questions teens are too awkward to ask elsewhere, such as how to write a cover letter, read a lease or research a rumor, and answers them in the library's voice. Each answer ends with an invitation to come in and get the full version.

5. **Borrow Something Impossible.** The library lends out things that aren't books, such as a tabletop game with a 40-page rulebook, a sewing machine, a telescope or a film camera, and the campaign shows teens checking them out like they would a rare sneaker drop. The message is that the library is the one place that has what the phone can't deliver.

1. **Night Baker.** You run a bakery that only exists between 2 and 5 a.m., and your customers are people who can't sleep; each order you fill tells you a little more about why they're up. The game is a real-time rhythm-and-memory loop where you learn regulars' orders by heart instead of reading a menu.

2. **Keeper.** There is no winning, only upkeep: you tend a lighthouse, a garden, and a dog, and the game ends when you decide to stop showing up. Sessions last as long as you want, and the only score is a log of the days you returned.

3. **Backroom.** You play the shopkeeper in someone else's epic — heroes come in to buy potions, dump loot, and argue about a quest you will never see. Your job is pricing, gossip, and deciding which hero to quietly sabotage.

4. **Two-Minute Kingdom.** Every time you open the app, your kingdom has advanced by however long you were gone, and it may have made bad decisions without you. You rule by reading the mess it left and choosing what to forgive.

5. **Signal.** You're a night-shift radio host whose only listeners are long-haul truckers; between songs, callers ask you to settle bets, and one of them is always lying. The core loop is picking which caller to believe using only their voice and the map.

1. **One-Handed Orchestra.** Every level is a piece of music where the notes fall on a track curved to fit a thumb's natural arc, so a commuter can play a whole song without repositioning their grip. Miss too many notes and the orchestra thins out instrument by instrument until you hear exactly what your thumb did wrong.

2. **Borrowed Ears.** You leave a voice message for a stranger, and a stranger leaves one for you; each message becomes the only clue to a small fictional mystery you solve together without ever seeing a name or a face. Real audio, no chat, no profiles — the game is what you choose to say into a phone in a quiet room.

3. **Last Bus Home.** You're the driver of the final route of the night, and every stop asks a small judgment call about who gets on. The route never changes; the passengers do, and so does the reason you keep the door open.

4. **Two-Minute Kingdom.** The whole kingdom exists only while your screen is on — the moment you pocket the phone it sleeps, crops unwatered, walls unfinished. You rule in the gaps between things, and the game's real skill is deciding what's worth waking it for.

5. **Heirloom.** You inherit a stranger's phone from a dead relative and have to decide which contacts to keep, which photos to delete, and which one message to finally send. Nothing is timed, nothing can be undone, and the ending is whichever small thing you couldn't bring yourself to erase.

1. **The Back Room Pass.** Teens get access to the parts of the building nobody tours — the microfilm machines, the local history room, the laminator, the dead CD-ROM databases — by completing a staff-set task in the public area. They end up knowing the library better than most adults, and the pass is the thing they bring friends back for.

2. **Ask a Teenager.** The library runs free drop-in help staffed by teens: unfreezing phones, digitizing a grandparent's photos, setting up a new device, filling out a form. Adults have to sit down across from a fourteen-year-old and ask, which flips who holds the expertise and gives teens a reason to be there that isn't studying.

3. **No Program Night.** One evening a week the meeting rooms are unlocked with nothing scheduled in them — no craft, no speaker, no sign-up — and staff only intervene if something breaks. It draws the teens who avoid anything that looks like a school event, and the empty rooms become theirs by habit.

4. **The Quiet Room's Secret.** A rotating display of strange true things from the collection — the 1911 map with a street that no longer exists, the microfilm of a since-closed newspaper, the donated diary with pages cut out — paired with a question only the archive can answer. Teens who crack one get their name on the shelf card, and the search keeps pulling them back into the building.

5. **Your Data Stays Here.** The library markets itself as the one place teens can use a computer, print something, or look something up without an account, a tracking banner, or a stranger's feed — and it posts that promise in the language teens actually use. It works because it's true and it's the thing no other free place in town can say.

Recommendation: **2. Ask a Teenager.** It's the only one where teens are the hosts rather than the guests, which changes how the visit feels and gives them a reason to return weekly instead of once.

1. **The Line Between Us.** You already talk to these people every day; you've just never watched them finish a sentence. Build the day around the half-finished thoughts — the Slack thread that got dropped, the "quick question" that turned into three weeks.

2. **Show Your Desk.** Half the company has never seen what the other half actually makes, only the version that arrives polished. Have each team walk the others through one real, unfinished thing, ugly draft included.

3. **The Fix List.** Every team carries a backlog of small, unglamorous things only insiders know are broken. Spend the day trading them across teams, because the person who can fix yours is usually sitting two tables away and has never heard of it.

1. **The Handoff**
Everyone spends one session teaching a skill they personally use to survive their job, and someone else has to practice it before lunch. The theme works because an offsite is the rare time peers can see the actual work behind each other's job titles.

2. **One Room, One Problem**
The company picks a real, unresolved problem it has been carrying all year and works it in mixed teams for a full day, with no slide decks allowed. A good offsite is remembered for what got decided, not for what got presented.

3. **The Annual Audit of Excuses**
Each team brings its most repeated reason for missing a goal, and the group separates the reasons that are true from the ones that are habit. It turns the usual trust exercise into something people can actually use on Monday.

4. **Second Week**
Plan the offsite as if the goal were to make the following week easier for everyone, and spend the sessions fixing the small systems that make work slow. The theme keeps the event from becoming a bubble that pops the moment people return to their desks.

5. **The Long Table**
Seat people by something other than their team, feed them well, and let the agenda be mostly conversation with a few firm anchors. For an annual gathering, the most valuable output is often who now knows whom.

Assumption: the offsite is for a general company, not a specific industry, so the themes stay broad enough to adapt.

1. **The Long Table.** Put the whole team around one table for three days and build every session around shared meals, so people who usually only meet on video get to know each other as neighbors. The agenda stays light, and the conversation runs as long as people want it to.

2. **Lost at Sea, Found in Town.** Send small groups out with a sealed map and one clue each, and have them rebuild the company's year from what they find along the way. Each team presents its own version at dinner, and the differences between the accounts become the basis for the next day's discussion.

3. **Repair Shop.** Bring in a carpenter, a bicycle mechanic and a potter for hands-on workshops, then ask everyone to fix something that has been broken at work for a long time. The session closes with a list of the real process problems the groups uncovered while mending their objects.

The offsite produces a shared document of the sentences people finished, which becomes the starting point for next year's planning.

5. **Night Shift.** Run the offsite so that the most important conversations happen after dark, in a small bar or a late walk, with the formal program limited to mornings. The aim is to give quieter team members the same access to honest talk that the louder ones already have during the day.

1. **The Long Table.** The offsite is built around shared meals, with each session starting where the last dinner ended, so the team's real conversations happen over food rather than in slide decks. It treats the company's history as something people cook together and argue about.

2. **Field Notes From the Other Side of the Desk.** Every team spends a day doing one another's jobs, from support staff shadowing engineers to finance joining sales calls, and then reports back on what surprised them. The goal is to replace assumptions about each other's work with first-hand knowledge.

3. **The Repair Shop.** Participants bring the broken process, the stalled project or the leaky tool they live with daily, and spend the offsite fixing one of them with whoever can help. Success is measured by what actually works on Monday.

4. **Bad Ideas Week.** Teams are asked to pitch the worst possible version of a product or policy, then find the one useful kernel hidden in it. The exercise lowers the stakes on speaking up and often surfaces the ideas people were afraid to propose seriously.

5. **Lighthouse, Not Map.** Rather than mapping next year's roadmap in detail, the offsite asks each group to name one thing they want the company to be known for in five years and to work backward from it. It gives people a shared direction without locking in a plan that will change within a quarter.

1. **The Long Table.** Every team sits around one shared table for three days, with no breakout rooms and no slides on the walls. The idea is that people who usually talk only through screens get to pass the salt and argue over the same map.

2. **Lost at Sea, Found on Land.** Teams are dropped into an unfamiliar town with a single brief, a camera-free phone and a budget for one shared meal. The exercise tests how people navigate uncertainty together, and the stories they bring back become the offsite's real record.

3. **Ferment.** Each team starts a small batch of something (bread, kimchi, cider) that must be tended across the whole offsite and tasted at the close. It is a quiet lesson in patience, shared responsibility and what grows when no one is in a hurry.

4. **The Repair Shop.** Teams spend a day fixing broken things for a local school or charity, bringing back bikes, radios and furniture that actually work. Helping strangers with real hands builds the kind of trust that carries straight back into the office.

5. **Night Shift.** The offsite runs on an inverted schedule, with the big conversations after dark and the quiet work done in the morning. Shifting the rhythm makes people notice how much of their usual collaboration depends on habit rather than choice.

**The Ledgerlands**

Nobody dies free. The dead leave debts, and the debts stay in the family, in the town, in the blood. Each village keeps a Ledger: a book of what the departed still owe, in coin, in labor, in years. Pay a share and the dead stay quiet. Skip it and they come to collect, walking in through the door they left by.

The living organize around this. **Reckoners** travel with locked boxes and settle accounts for the dead who had no heirs, taking a cut. **Quieters** are hired to sit with the recently departed through the first night, before the debt wakes up, and talk them down. **Heirs** are people who inherited a sum too large to clear and now work it off under contract, sometimes for the very ancestor who owes it.

Cities grow where old debts pile up. Vaulted, unlit, and organized by surname, with clerks who know which great-grandfather is still owed three hundred weights of salt and will not be reasonable about it.

Every player character starts with a number written next to their name. That is the campaign.

The sun over Vaunt is a cargo. It rides in iron pots on the backs of haulers, five hundred litres of morning per trip, and arrives where it's delivered.

Nobody has seen a sunrise in three generations. The Dawn Line runs from the Glassworks at the coast, where light is harvested off the water, up through eleven relay towns to the capital, which buys more of it than anywhere and so wakes first. Between the pots the land sits in ordinary night: crops in lampshade rows, children born squinting at noon-lanterns, dogs who never learn to sleep.

The Haulers' League owns the route and the clocks. They say the light belongs to whoever carries it. The Relay Towns say it belongs to whoever is standing there when it arrives. The capital says it belongs to whoever paid. So far this is settled by tolls, grudges, and the fact that spilled light does not go out — it pools. There are stretches of road where the ground still glows from a dropped pot in 40 A.C., and people farm there, and don't ask who dropped it.

You're a courier with a cracked pot, four days behind, and a town ahead that's been waiting in the dark long enough to notice.

The Salt Orchard of Quell

Quell is a country planted in the sea. Its farmers walk the tidal flats at low water and push seedlings of brine-rice into the mud, each one tied to a cord of kelp so the tide cannot carry it off. At high water the fields vanish, and the villages stand on stilts above the silver channels, where boats are the only roads.

Nobody here owns land. You own the rows you have replanted, and a family's standing is counted in ropes: the coils of kelp cord they can show at the spring tithe. A rope gone slack in the water brings shame and a visit from the Tallymen, who cut what they find and sell the salt.

The rice is sacred and also edible, which the priests are careful never to mention. Eating it is said to make you remember the sea, and so the old women chew it slowly at funerals.

Something beneath the flats has begun to sing at dusk, a low note that pulls the nets toward the deep channels. Fishers who follow it are never found. The Tallymen say it is a debt collector. The children say it wants to be planted.

Adventurers arrive by the sea road, carrying cords they did not earn.

The Leviathan has been dead for nine hundred years. Nobody agrees what killed it. Everyone lives inside it.

Its ribs arc over the Vault Cities like cathedral stone; its heart, the size of a lake, has not beaten since the Second Winter. Heat is the only currency that matters. Deep in the marrow galleries, the Last Warmed still work the old veins, coaxing one more degree from a body that is finally going cold. Closer to the skin, the Shiverfolk trade in rendered fat, bone-charcoal, the slow rot of the outer flesh. They are winning, in the sense that they are warm.

Adventurers come for the Gristle Maze—nerves still twitching after a millennium, where the humours of a god leak and pool. Alchemists pay well. So do the Worm Priests, who believe the body will rise if fed enough of the living, and the Cartomancers, who have mapped the colonnades and charge toll for the maps.

But the ribs are cracking. Frost is coming down from the skull. Whatever killed it is still out there, and it is patient.

**The Salt Cartographers of Quell**

Quell is a sea of dried brine, flat as a plate and bright enough to blind. The Thirsty Carders, a clan of tide-readers, walk its crust with sounding poles and chalk. Every dawn the pale floor gives up a thin new skin of salt overnight, and every dusk the crust cracks and sings, the sound carrying for miles over the flats.

Their maps are not drawn on paper. They are pressed into the salt itself, scored with bone rakes in patterns that vanish with the next storm. To lose a map is to lose a route to water, so the Carders memorize their charts through chanted tallies, each family hoarding a different verse.

Nobody lives on Quell for long. The brine pulls the moisture from the lungs and the sun pulls it from the skin. What lives there is trade. Salt is currency in the drowned port of Onder, but the Carders sell something stranger: directions. A buyer pays for a single verse, and the verse's owner must walk the buyer across the crust by memory. Bad verses lead people into the cracks, where the brine gleams like a mirror and something beneath it hums back.

The Carders say the old sea is still down there, waiting for someone to forget the way.

Halvenreach is a city of forty thousand people built on the back of a single turtle named Ossa, who sleeps beneath the harbor mud of the Greywash Sea. Nobody remembers laying the first stone. The oldest families say the foundations were poured onto her shell by her own keepers, who promised her a quiet century.

Ossa wakes once every nine years, on the tide-day, when the bay drains to a thread of silver. Then the city must move. Pulleys haul the market stalls onto the eastern cliffs, bells ring the children indoors, and the Tidewardens, a guild of salt-scarred widows, walk the spine of her shell chanting to keep her calm. Anyone who stays on her back when she turns is swallowed by the sea.

The canals are named for the people who fell through them. The bakery on Lantern Row still sells bread shaped like the sleeping turtle, and its owners will not say why it is never eaten.

Ossa's tide-day is eleven weeks away. The keepers' ledger has gone missing, and the Tidewardens have begun to argue over which of the old promises was the last one kept.

final: Halvern Quill never raises his voice, because he never has to: he buys the debts of the dead. Under imperial law a debt outlives its debtor by two generations, and Halvern has spent forty years acquiring those paper obligations at auction — a widow's rent arrears, a drowned ferryman's bond, the unpaid dowry of a girl three villages over — until half the province owes its labor to a man who has never once set foot in it. He travels with a satchel of receipts and a boy who reads them aloud, and when a family cannot pay he does not seize the farm or the livestock; he takes the name. The children are entered in his ledger under their parents' accounts, and from that day they work for him at whatever he assigns, in whatever town he chooses, for as long as the arithmetic demands. He is polite, punctual, genuinely sad about the whole arrangement, and keeps a small garden. There are no soldiers guarding him. There does not need to be. The province enforces its own law because it believes in it, and Halvern Quill is, by every measure the courts recognize, a patient and lawful man.

final: Serevine Hask was once the Crown's own surveyor of drowned villages, and she still carries the ledger in which she recorded every name the flood took, a list she has never stopped updating. She does not hate the kingdom; she believes it simply lacks a true count of what it has lost, and she is building one by her own methods: she sits at the bedside of the dying in the river towns and asks them, gently, what they were owed. Those who answer are rewarded with a debt paid in full, which is why the wardens who came to arrest her were all, one by one, found sleeping peacefully in their own beds with their accounts settled. Her cruelty is bookkeeping: each favor she grants is entered beside a claim she will one day call due, and she has never once been wrong about who would come to collect.

final: They call him the Toll-Keeper, and he is the reason the river has never once been forded in force. He is a small man in a wet coat, unfailingly polite, who steps out of the reeds at the sound of hooves and tells you the price: not coin, but what you will regret most in the coming year, named plainly, and collected at the day's end whether you cross or turn back. He does not enjoy it. He keeps a ledger of everyone he has charged and he knows, to the acre, how many children starve in the town that the toll's silver harvests feed — which is the point. The bridge is the only thing holding the northern passes open, and he cannot both build it and comfort every person it makes him charge. He has an old wound in his side that never closes, and he does not thank you for looking at it. He does not wish to be forgiven. He wishes somebody, once, would take the price out of his hands and not blink, and then do the arithmetic, and then decide the same thing he did, and leave.

**Marguerite "Gigi" Okonkwo-Ferrante, 61, the bridal shop's seamstress**

Gigi has been pinning hems for thirty-four years in a shop on a street that has changed its name twice. She keeps a tin of straight pins in her cardigan pocket and a running tally, on the back of an invoice pad, of every bride who has ever cried in her fitting room and then come back to thank her. The tally is at 211. She does not let the two leads forget that she is counting.

She does not believe in love, only in tailoring. "A man is a jacket," she tells the hero, who came in to buy a suit for his sister's wedding and stayed three hours. "He looks fine off the rack. Then you see what he actually needs." She has opinions about his shoulders that she shares loudly, in front of the customers.

When the heroine arrives in a panic, two weeks before her own wedding, with a dress that no longer fits because she stopped sleeping, Gigi does not say a single soft thing. She measures her, writes the numbers on her own forearm in marker, and says, "Eat the toast. I'll be here Thursday." Then she is on the phone with a supplier in Lisbon, arguing about lace, while the heroine sits frozen on the little velvet stool.

Gigi's rules, delivered as commands and never explained:
- Never sit on the bride's side of the dressing room curtain.
- Anyone who says "vintage" about a dress that is merely old gets a discount and a lecture.
- Her late husband Sal proposed to her by sending a button in the mail. She still has the button. She will not say which shirt it came from.

Her best scene: the hero's ex-fiancée walks into the shop to pick up an alteration, and Gigi, without looking up, pins the hem of a gown she has clearly been waiting thirty years to pin on someone. "Ah. The one who left. Stand still. You're getting old, your hips have moved. I'm not sorry, I'm measuring."

Gigi is funny because she is never trying to be. She is sure of everything, wrong about half of it, and entirely right about the thing that matters: that the dress has to fit the person, not the day.

**Marisol Okonkwo-Reyes, 61, the bridal shop's head seamstress**

Marisol has pinned more hems than anyone in the city and has never once been fooled by a nervous bride. She keeps a tomato-shaped pincushion that she calls "the Senator" and refuses to explain why. She eats a single pickled egg at 11:15 every morning and considers the rest of the world's breakfasts a personal failing.

She speaks four languages, uses all of them to insult people in the same sentence, and only switches to the warmest one when someone is about to cry. She has a rule: nobody is allowed to look in the three-way mirror until she says so, and she has been right every single time.

When the leading man, Theo, comes in to buy a suit for his sister's wedding and accidentally ends up in a tuxedo that belonged to a man who was jilted at the altar in 1989, Marisol takes one look at him, sighs, and says, "Stand still. You are going to be a disaster, and I am going to be paid for it." She ends up quietly rewriting the plot of his life through the tension of a single seam.

She has opinions about everyone's posture, a theory that all men are secretly afraid of hemlines, and a standing dinner invitation for any lonely person who wanders in looking for a bridesmaid's dress. She is the first person in the story to understand what the lead couple is actually fighting about, and the last person to tell them, because she is enjoying the show.

Her best scene: the leads finally confess their feelings to each other in the fitting room, and Marisol, from behind the curtain, says loudly, "Good. Now the trousers, please," and walks out without another word.

# Bogumiła "Bogs" Kaminski

**Who she is:** fifty-eight. Owner and resident manager of a six-unit building on the slightly wrong side of a good street. Her father bought it in 1981, worked doubles to hold it, and left it to her with a mortgage she pretends is paid off. She lives in 1A, next to the mailboxes, and knows the sound of every tenant's key in the lock. She wears cardigans over scrubs because they're comfortable and nobody's business, and she carries two things at all times: a ring of forty-one keys and a spiral notebook she calls "the ledger."

**The engine of her:** Bogs does not gossip. She *documents*. The ledger has columns. Move-in date, damage deposit, notable noises, who has a spare key, who has cried in the hallway. Not because she's cruel — because when she was nine her father was almost evicted by a landlord who "just didn't remember" their deal, and she has never once let a detail go missing since. She is not rooting for the couple. She is rooting for the truth, and it happens to be funnier and more romantic than anything the couple can come up with.

**How she steals scenes:**

- She turns her hearing aid off mid-sentence when someone starts lying to her, and turns it back on for the part where they admit the real thing. If you ask what she heard, she'll say, "I heard the important part. The middle bit I let you keep."
- She keeps a laminated list, taped inside the boiler-room door, of everyone who has ever been "just friends" in this building and how long it lasted. There are fourteen lines. Three are still going.
- She does not comfort. She provides *equipment*. When one of them shows up at her door crying, she hands over a bucket and a roll of paper towels and says, "The pipes above you make that face too, and I don't dry them off. Sit. You get eleven minutes, I'm timing it."
- She charges rent in a way that functions as a confession mechanism. Late rent: "Fine." Late rent with a story about the new person they're seeing: "$40 off, but I'm writing down what you said." She has never once collected on the notes. She has read them all twice.
- Her cat is named Dariusz. Dariusz belonged to a tenant in 3B who left in 2009 owing three months and a blender. She calls the cat Dariusz Junior to keep the debt visible. The cat hates everyone except the couple's most obvious obstacle, which everyone finds very funny and Bogs finds instructive.
- Her entrances: she never knocks if the door is unlocked. She'll be halfway through a sentence about the water bill before anyone in the room realizes she's there, and by the time they react, she's already said the one thing that makes the whole scene crack open.

**One true buried thing:** In 1994 she was going to move out, marry a man named Tadeusz, and run a bakery in Chicago. Her father got sick. She stayed. Tadeusz sends a card every Christmas; she keeps them in the ledger under a heading she labeled "Business." She has never explained it to anyone. It is dropped once, in one line, in the last third, and never mentioned again. It's why she notices when someone is about to let the good thing go — and why she does tell them, even knowing they'll be annoyed.

**Why she can't just be a plot device:** She has her own want, and it isn't helping. She wants to sell the building and move to Chicago before she's too old to enjoy it, and she can't, because every tenant she loses is a name she has to cross out. So she sabotages the sale without quite admitting it — finding a new leak, a bad inspection, a paperwork "problem." She's as stuck as the couple is. She just has better filing.

**The line that sets her:** *"I don't care who you end up with. I care who you're lying to, because I'm the one who has to repaint the walls after."*

**Her one physical tell:** she's always holding something practical — a lightbulb, a plunger, a wooden spoon — so that any conversation she interrupts looks like a small domestic emergency she intends to fix. She never fixes it. She leaves before she finishes the sentence, and you realize later she was right about all of it.

*Assumed a contemporary American setting with a walk-up building; swap the city and the 1981 backstory as needed.*

**Priya Vaidya, wedding videographer.**

She is not the DJ and not the florist. She is the person crouched at the edge of the dance floor with a stabilizer, filming the part everyone else will cut.

Priya has shot two hundred and eleven weddings. She has never been married, has never wanted to be married, and has opinions. She tracks couples with a private system she will not explain unless you ask, and then she will explain it in full: *First-Dance Criers* (do not trust, they cry at commercials too), *Speech Writers* (one of them wrote the other's toast — ask who), and *Second Weddings, Same Venue* (no comment, she says, and then comments for six minutes).

She arrives early to set up in the corner of the reception hall, the one with the dropped ceiling and the carpet that looks like it's been through things. She wears black. She eats from the kitchen, not the buffet, and she has a strong feeling about the difference.

What she does that steals the room is not a joke. It's that she says the quiet thing out loud, plainly, at the exact wrong moment — mid-aisle-walk, mid-toast, mid-cry — not cruel, just *unfiltered*: *"You two fight like you've been rehearsing,"* she says, adjusting the lens. Or, when the groom's mother asks if Priya is married: *"No. I've watched it."*

And she is right. Every time. Because she has watched two hundred and eleven versions and she remembers what happens after the cameras stop — not as gossip but as texture, the way she remembers which venues have good light and which ones don't.

She will show up in scenes exactly twice: once early, when the leads think this wedding is going to be about them, and once late, when Priya, without being asked, hands one of them a clip she shot three weddings ago — a bride who looked just like them — and says nothing. Then she goes back to the corner.

**Her own thing:** she is writing a book about all two hundred and eleven of them, and cannot get past the first page, because she keeps trying to find the pattern that explains the couples that make it, and every time she gets close, she throws the page out. Nobody in the movie knows this except us and, eventually, the one lead who finds the notebook in her equipment bag. She does not want advice about it. That's the whole thing.

Henri worked nights at the roller rink he was slowly losing. The owner had sold the building; the last session was in nineteen days and everyone kept saying it like a countdown. He taught seventeen-year-olds to skate because that was what he had, and because his knees could still do it if he didn't sit down in between.

He wasn't a speech man. He'd tighten a laces' knot with two fingers, turn your shoulders with one push of his palm, then send you back out to fall where everyone could see. When you asked how he learned, he'd tell you which cold morning, which bus, how much the skates cost in 1979 — never the lesson, only the receipt.

What he gave was attention that didn't flinch. He watched you the way you watch someone on the last good song, already knowing the floor won't be there next month.

Start young and the bread is on your side.

Mr. Okafor worked the ferry from Gallen Point and never once said anything nice to me. He taught me hitches instead. Round turn and two half hitches, which he tied with his thumb hooked through the rope, not looking. "Show me," he'd say, and I'd fumble until the line went slack and he'd pull it free and make me start over.

Somewhere around the third month he started talking while we worked. Not about his life. About the water: how a slack rope gives you away, how a boat that is pretending to be steady always leans to one side. Once, while I was coiling line on the stern, he said, "Your mother's better today?" I said yes. He didn't argue. He just kept coiling, and I understood he had heard the whole lie in one syllable.

I still tie the hitch the way he did, thumb first. Whenever someone tells me they're fine, I feel the rope go slack in my hands.

final: This is a brand for a hot sauce that is one farm's year, bottled. The company buys its peppers from a single plot, and the plot has opinions: too much rain and the Reapers go soft and sweet, a dry August and the same seed turns mean. So the identity starts in the field log, not the kitchen—every bottle carries the row it came from, the week it was picked, and a one-line weather report written by the person who grew it. No tasting-note poetry, no flame graphics, no mustaches; the visual language borrows from agricultural extension paperwork and handwritten harvest tags, the kind of thing clipped to a crate. The voice is a farmer telling you what happened that summer, plainly, including the summer nothing worked and the sauce came out wrong. Craft here means accountability to a place, not a small batch size: when Row Eleven fails, we say so on the label, and we sell the failure as what it is. The promise is not consistency. Slogan: Somebody's keeper, now yours.

Brand story:

Every chair in our shop has already been sat in, argued over, spilled on and slept on. We don't pretend otherwise. We think the marks are the point. A dent in a dresser is a record of a Tuesday that mattered to someone.

We started with a truck, a borrowed garage and a rule: if it still holds weight and still has a drawer that opens, it stays. We take it in from house clearances, estate sales and the back rooms of people who are moving on. We clean it, fix what needs fixing and leave the rest alone, because the history is part of what you're buying.

Most of what comes through our door costs less than a new flatpack. Some of it is older than the building it ends up in. All of it is looking for a new kitchen, a first flat, a spare room that needed something to sit on.

Bring the place you're setting up. We'll help you find the things that already seem to know where they belong.

**Slogan**

Nothing here is blank.

**Brand Story**

Most furniture arrives new, which means it arrives with nothing to say. Ours arrives with a life already on it. That's the whole inventory plan.

We buy from estates and moving trucks and people standing in their own kitchens at eleven at night saying I just need it out of here. What we get, we don't sand down to pretend it just left a factory. The dark ring on the maple table is 1970s coffee, near as the daughter remembers it. The one-inch pencil notch on the bookshelf's underside is her father's arithmetic, checked twice against a receipt he stapled to the back panel. The heavy oak dresser was drawn on in three languages, one of which the family no longer speaks.

There are three half-used tubes of paint taped to the underside of that dresser. On purpose. We left the owner's tape on because the paint came from the house and matched the wall in the back bedroom, and whoever buys the dresser might want to know the color. If they don't, it's still true underneath.

We clean what needs cleaning. Cracks get fixed. A drawer that fights its runner gets a new runner, and we tell you we did that. But a crack is information, and we've had people come in and go quiet in front of a table that had a whole family's childhood in the wood grain — they don't want a blank table. They want the one that did something.

Somebody's name is written on the underside of that shelf in pencil, with a phone number that's two digits short of any number used today. The timing's off, too. It's not a riddle we need solved. It's just part of the piece, the way a scar is part of the person.

So here's the policy. Every item in the shop has a past, and we say what we know of it, and keep quiet about what we don't. What we don't do is strip that past to make a sale. That would be easy. It would also make us a store that sells new furniture older.

Cookware and plants are at the back. Cash and card both work. The dark-ring table is in the front window, and it came out of a house near the park, and the coffee that made that ring was drunk there every morning for forty years.

The tomatoes are the problem. Everything else on the station runs itself. The air scrubbers hum along, the gyros hold, the solar arrays drink light and give it back. But the tomatoes need water every four days, and they need to be checked for the mites that came up with the last supply run, and if you don't tap the blossoms with a small brush the fruit won't set, because there are no bees out here, and there haven't been for a very long time.

When they told him the return window was closing, they asked what he wanted to bring down. He said the seeds. They thought he was being sentimental. He let them think that.

So he wakes at 06:40, which is not the real time of anything, just a number the clock was set to years ago, and he makes coffee that tastes like the bag it came in. Then he goes to the garden.

It's four racks in the forward module, lit pink, which makes his hands look like a photograph developed wrong. Twenty-two plants. He knows them the way you know stairs in your own house — not by thinking, by foot. The Roma on rack two, the one that leans, got that lean from a bag of soil he packed too loose three years back. He has never fixed the lean. It's the plant's personality. He would not trade it.

He talks to them, which he is aware is a thing to be aware of. But it's not the talking. It's that they answer. The leaves lift toward the light in the morning and drop by the sleep cycle. They drink what he gives and ask for more by drooping. When he waters them he feels the weight of the can drop, and that drop is a conversation, and he has decided that is enough.

The radio gets a ping every third day. A voice, sometimes, from the ground. He used to stand by it. Now he answers while he's working, hands in the soil, and the voice says things like *how are you holding up* and he says *fine* and he means it, mostly, because he has a job. That's the part people on the ground never get. They think being alone is the empty thing. It isn't. The empty thing is finishing a task. He repots a seedling, pats it in, and there is no one to hand it to and say *look at this one*. The job is perfect. There is no one the job is perfect *for*.

Last month a blossom opened on the brandywine, the first in a season, and he stood there with the little brush and did the work, moving pollen like a secret between the two flowers, and then he put his hand flat on the edge of the rack and left it there, and the pink light was on his hand, and he thought: this is the whole shape of it. A thing that grows and gets eaten and grows again, and the only witness is the man who kept it alive.

He writes the checklist every night. Water, check. Mites, clear. Brush the new blossoms. Log the yield, which he eats standing up out of the bowl with the light still pink on his face. Then he sleeps, and in the morning the leaves have lifted again, and he goes to them, because they have asked him to.

There's a window on the far side of the station and he doesn't look out of it much. Earth is down there, small and blue and busy. They're fine. They have bees.

The voices started at 0400, same as always. Mission Control, with the two-second delay, so you learned to talk into the gap.

"Morning, Anders. Sleep okay?"

He said he did. He always said he did.

The trick of it, he'd learned, was that a person on the ground thinks the loneliness is the dark. It isn't. The dark is a room. You get used to a room. The loneliness is the voices—how they come to you already finished, already polite, and how you answer into a silence you know is only there because of distance. He'd done the math on day one: 384,400 kilometers, 1.28 seconds each way. He'd made a little joke about it. Nobody laughed, then, and the delay ate it, and by the time the laugh would have arrived he was already a different man.

For eleven months he had run the same four conversations. He knew the shape of them the way you know a hallway in the dark.

*How's the garden?* They'd ask. The lettuce is bolting, he'd say. *Sounds like home.*

He had started to notice it in the way a man notices a leak: not at once, but by the stain.

On day 342 he asked a question that wasn't on the sheet—something small, about a bakery in Houston, whether it was still open—and the answer came back exactly as it had on day 9, word for word, the same pause before the same laugh.

He sat with that a long time. The capsule hummed. The lettuce, in its tray of damp foam, went on doing what lettuce does, which is nothing you can watch.

He could have called it in. That was the thing he kept turning over. He could have said, *the archive is stuck, you're sending me the same tape,* and they'd have fixed it, and a fresh voice would arrive in a day or two, tired and real and slightly annoyed, and he'd be lonely again in the ordinary way—the way you're lonely at a party, surrounded.

Instead he learned the loop the way a monk learns a psalm. He found where it stuttered. He found the half-second where the engineer's voice went flat and human, and he played that half-second until it was the truest thing he had.

The voices started at 0400, same as always.

"Morning, Anders. Sleep okay?"

He said he did.

And then, because it was his tape now, and nobody was listening, he told them the truth: that he'd slept badly, that he'd dreamed about the bakery, that the lettuce had finally died, that he was afraid, that he was not afraid, that he loved them, all of them, the whole finished chorus of them, and that he'd never tell a living soul.

Two seconds passed. The machine, faithful as weather, sent it back to Earth, where it would arrive in a room full of people who had already answered, long ago, and were now asleep.

The lag was four seconds on a good day, and Dana had learned to hear the gap the way you learn a stair in the dark. You speak, you wait, you hear the faint hiss of the other end deciding to answer.

Her name on the roster was Okafor, Lauren, Mission Support, Night Desk, Console Four. She had been at Console Four for nineteen months. Most nights the station called in for the scheduled items: the water loop, a pressure reading, a question about a torque wrench nobody could find. Then the call ended, the link went quiet, and the console showed the orbit line sliding across a map of nothing.

The astronaut's name was Ines Vella. She called at 02:40 station time on Tuesdays, which was not a scheduled slot, and she never said why.

"Console, Vella."

"Go ahead, Ines."

"The recycler's making the noise again."

"Which noise?"

"The one like someone clearing their throat before they say something bad."

Lauren wrote it down. Recycler, intermittent, throat-clearing. Under it she wrote, because she was supposed to, *crew reports normal ops.* Then she pressed the key. "Okay. I'll flag it to engineering. They'll look at the telemetry in the morning."

"Thanks." A pause, four seconds. "Tell them it's probably fine."

"I'll tell them it's probably fine."

The loop at Console Four had a hum that Lauren had stopped hearing months ago. She listened to it now. Somewhere up there, a machine was pushing water through its own body so that a woman could go on drinking it, and a man named Idris in a building forty miles from the launch pad had written the schedule for that machine, and no one would ever know his name on the station side.

She had worked out, somewhere around month eight, that the crew did not call to report faults. They called to hear a voice that was not in the tin can with them. The faults were the excuse. The excuse was excellent. Nobody on a shift argued with a throat-clearing recycler.

Lauren was not supposed to think of herself as company. Company was a word in the handbook, under things to avoid. But she kept the Tuesday slot free. She kept her coffee the same temperature. When the station had a bad week, a stuck valve, a crew member with a cold, she put a small mark next to the timestamp, and on the next call, when the link came up, she said the one thing the handbook allowed: "Good to hear you, Ines."

At 03:05 Ines said, "Okay. That's it from me."

"Copy. Console Four, off."

"Four, off."

The link dropped. The map showed the station sliding behind the night side of the planet. Lauren wrote the closing time, then, in the margin where nobody audited, the words *recycler, probably fine.*

She finished the coffee. Outside the window of the desk there was a parking lot and a single lit sign for a 24-hour pharmacy. Someone would be a long way from home tonight, and the phone would be answered.

Mira came in at seven because she wanted the room before anyone else, and the room had already been got. There was a mug on the desk, white with a hairline crack down one side, and a cardigan over the back of the chair, and the monitor turned a few degrees toward where someone shorter would sit. The drawer held a hairbrush, a packet of those ginger sweets, a phone charger wound with a rubber band. She put the mug in the cupboard above the sink, where mugs went, and the cardigan over the back of the chair, which is where it stayed.

By nine the desk was hers. Priya from accounts came by with a laptop and said, "You'll want to sit with your back to the window, the glare's brutal after lunch," which was the kind of thing you'd only know if you'd sat there. Mira said she liked the glare. It was a small, ugly thing to say and she heard herself say it.

The work was fine. The work was more than fine. Two years of spreadsheets that had been maintained by someone careful, tabs labeled with a system that made sense the moment you looked at it, the formulas clean, everything in its column. She changed the date range on the summary sheet and the numbers came back to her like a dog that knew its name.

At lunch she sat with them. They asked where she'd come from and she told them, and then Dale said, "So you're filling Rosa's seat," and the table did a small thing with its faces.

"Rosa's on leave," Priya said.

"Rosa's on leave," Dale agreed, and ate.

Mira looked it up on the shared drive that afternoon, because the spreadsheet had a name on it in the properties, and the name was there and then not there. The file history showed edits going back a long way and then stopping, six weeks ago, in the middle of a Tuesday. She opened the tab she was told to open and closed the properties panel and typed in the first figure.

At five she put the cardigan in her bag. She didn't know why she did it. It smelled of the ginger sweets and of something older, and on the walk to the station she thought she'd give it to a charity shop on the high street, and then she thought she wouldn't, and she carried it home.

The next morning the mug was back on the desk. Not the same mug, a new one, clean, no crack, and beside it a small card, and the card said *Welcome, Mira*, in handwriting she didn't recognize, and she stood there for a while with her coat still on, understanding that the room had been tidied, and that she was the tidying.

She worked until six. When Priya left she said goodnight, and Mira said goodnight, and kept going, and the glare came in off the window the way Priya said it would, and Mira turned the monitor a few degrees toward where someone shorter would sit, and kept typing, and got it done.

The check-in form had nine fields. Name, shift, vitals, and then a line marked "Crew Morale (self-report, 1–5)," which Dana Oyelaran had been filling in with a 3 for seven months.

Mireille Duval had been on the station for two hundred and eleven days. She was the only one aboard now, the other three having gone home on the last crew rotation, and the new crew was not due for another five weeks. Her reports came down every morning at 0600 Houston time. Dana read them over coffee before the shift handover, the way you might read a neighbor's letters if you were the only one on the block who could.

They were not long. Mireille reported the reactor temperature, the water recovery numbers, a leak in the aft cooling loop she had patched with tape and a prayer. Then, under Crew Morale, she typed things like *3, but the tomatoes are doing well* or *2, the radio cut out during the Pacific pass and I spent the whole orbit hearing nothing but my own breathing.*

Dana was supposed to log the number and forward the rest to the medical officer. She did log the number. She also started writing back in the free-text box, which nobody read but the system kept.

*The tomatoes are a good sign,* she wrote on day forty-four. *Tell me which ones.*

The reply came the next morning, shorter than usual. *The small red ones, the cherry kind. The big yellow one is sulking. I think it wants more light and I can't give it more light.*

After that the free-text box filled up. Mireille described the window at dawn, a seam of blue along the edge of the world, and how she had stopped being able to tell which of the three clouds belonged to which continent. Dana told her about the weather in the parking lot where she left her car, and about her daughter's science fair volcano, which had erupted on the judge's shoes. She did not think of it as a conversation. It was closer to passing a lantern down a dark corridor, one hand to the next.

In month six, the morale number stopped being a 3. Dana noticed before the medical officer did. Mireille wrote *4* on a Tuesday and then, in the box, *don't put that in the summary, they'll think I'm getting soft.*

Dana put it in the summary. She told them it was accurate.

On the last day of the gap, before the new crew's launch window, Mireille's report arrived at 0553, early.

*Crew Morale: 3,* it said. *I'm going to be honest with you. It's going to be strange, having people on the ship again. The ground sent a memo in week nine. It said the crew would stop referring to the hydroponic trays by names, because names caused confusion during reconciliation and because, the memo said, "plants are not crew."

Ilse read it twice in the galley, under the hum of the scrubber fan, then folded it into a square and clipped it to the wall beside the schedule.

Tray four was called Dolores. Tray five was called Mr. Osei, after the man who taught her to splice cable at seventeen, though she had never told the ground that. Tray six had no name yet. It was the one that had come up crooked, its first leaves folded like hands.

She did not name them out loud. Out loud, the others would have heard, and Teodor would have gently asked if she was sleeping. She named them in the log instead, in the margin of the nutrient readings, where the ground's software read only numbers.

*D: pH 6.1, flowering early. Dolores is showing off.*
*Osei: root mass up 4%. Needs a word.*
*Tray six: still no name. Crooked. Good.*

The ground team had started to notice. Their replies came back at 0200 station time, always courteous.

*Please clarify the reference "showing off."*
*Please confirm the designation for tray six.*

She answered every one. *Tray six is unnamed.* *Dolores is the tomato, in case of confusion.* She did not add that confusion was the only thing she ever got from them that wasn't a timestamp.

Teodor found her at the window in the evening. He did not look at the Earth. He looked at the trays through the hatch glass, where the grow lights made everything a faint, unreal purple.

"You talk to them," he said.

"I log them."

"You log them like people." He smiled, not unkindly. "I used to do it with the bread, on my first rotation. Stupid. The bread didn't complain about the rations."

"Did you stop?"

"When the bread went moldy," he said. "Then I named the mold."

She laughed, and it surprised her, the sound of it, short and cracked, in a room built for fourteen hours of quiet and eight of shift overlap.

That night she checked the record. Her logged names went back to week two. Every one was in the margin. None had been flagged. Someone on the ground had read them, or had at least let them through, and she decided that counted for something.

In week ten the tomato on tray four split its first fruit, a small red thing slightly out of true. Ilse cut it open with the galley knife and ate half at the window, the juice warm and sour from the lamps. She did not log it. She wanted, for once, to keep one thing that no one would make her report.

Then she wrote in the margin anyway, because she was who she was.

*Dolores: first fruit. Ate half. Left half for Osei.*

The next morning the half was gone from the cutting board. Nobody said anything. The memo stayed clipped to the wall, and beside it, in Teodor's cramped capitals, someone had written a new line on a strip of tape:

*TRAY SIX: CALL IT WHAT YOU LIKE.*

She didn't answer it. She just watered the crooked one first.

The checklist is taped inside the airlock door, where he passes it twice a day.

*Filters: changed.* He changes them Tuesdays and Fridays. He does not know it is Tuesday. He knows it is the day after the day he changed them last, and that has been enough for eleven years.

*Water: recycled.* It tastes like water. Sometimes it tastes like the inside of a coin, and he drinks it anyway.

*Position: holding.*

He has a name. Nobody uses it. He says it out loud some mornings to keep the shape of it, the way you'd turn a key in a lock that hasn't been used.

The station is a ring, four hundred meters around, and he walks it. Not for exercise. For the sound. His boots on the grating make a note, and the note comes back off the far wall a half-second later, and for that half-second there are two of him.

The garden is the warm end. Sixty trays under pink light, radishes and dwarf wheat and one tomato plant that has never once fruited and that he will not pull. He talks to the wheat because it's polite about it. He does not talk to the tomato.

He has a system for the windows. Six of them, evenly spaced, and he only lets himself use one per day, and never the same one twice in a row. It's not a rule anyone gave him. It's just that if he used them all, he'd run out.

Mostly he doesn't look out at all. There's nothing out there that changes. But there's a scratch on window three, a short pale line like a hair, and he likes it because it's the only thing in the sky that was made by someone who isn't there anymore.

He keeps the radio on. Not the receiver — the receiver is a green light and a hiss and he has learned not to sit with it. The other one. The internal loop, the one that carries his own voice back to him from the far end of the ring, delayed and thin.

*Check the filters,* he says, and a half-second later, from four hundred meters away, somebody says *check the filters.*

He is aware of how this sounds. He's aware. It's just that a man can be aware of a thing and still stand in the corridor at the end of the day, waiting for the echo, and when it comes, feel his shoulders come down.

The anniversary is the same day every year and he marks it with a small thing: he takes the good cup. The one with the chip in the rim. He makes the coffee too strong and drinks it at window one, and he doesn't look out, he just holds the cup, and the heat comes through the ceramic into both hands.

He doesn't think about the launch. He doesn't think about the field, or the wet grass, or the woman who was crying and laughing at the same time and kept saying *don't look back, don't look back* — because he looked back. He turned at the top of the ramp and looked back, and the last thing he saw of the ground was her hand up, not waving exactly, just up.

He doesn't think about that. He thinks about the cup. He thinks about the heat in both hands.

There was a time he wrote things down. Forty notebooks, filled, stacked in the sleep bay like a wall. He stopped because he read one back and it was all weather and filters and the sound of his own voice, and he understood that he was writing to someone, and there wasn't anyone, and a letter with no one to send it to is just a man talking to paper.

He still writes the date on the wall by the airlock, in pencil, small. Nobody asked him to. He does it because the pencil is the only thing on this station that gets used up.

Tonight the loop is running. He's in the warm end with the wheat, and he says something small, something he wouldn't say if he thought anyone could hear it — he says *it's alright,* not to the wheat, just to the air, just generally, the way you'd say it to a dog.

And a half-second later, from four hundred meters away, somebody says *it's alright.*

He stands there in the pink light a while longer. Then he goes and checks the filters.

Delia had been at the cannery eleven years, which meant she knew the sound the line made when it was about to jam, and she knew that the new girl would not know it, and she knew she would be the one to say something.

The new girl arrived at 6:40, ten minutes early, which Delia noted. Early was either eager or afraid and both were a kind of noise. She had a lunch bag shaped like a small house and she set it on the counter next to the sink like she'd been told to, and she had not been told to.

"You can put that in the fridge," Delia said. "It'll get warm out here."

"Oh — thank you." The girl picked it up again. She looked around for the fridge like it might be behind something.

"Under the microwave."

She found it. She came back and stood with her hands at her sides, and Delia could see her trying to figure out where a person was supposed to stand, and there was no answer to that, so Delia didn't give her one.

The line started at seven. Delia showed her the gloves, the two sizes, which one for what, and the girl nodded at everything. Nodding was cheap. Delia had trained six people in eleven years and four of them had nodded like that and two of those were gone by the third week.

"You'll feel it here first," Delia said, tapping her own forearm. "The vibration. You get used to it in a day or two and then you can't feel it anymore, which is worse."

The girl laughed. Delia hadn't meant it as a joke.

By nine the supervisor, Ruel, came through with his clipboard and stopped behind them and watched for a while, and Delia kept working, and the girl kept working, slower, and Ruel wrote something down. He did that. He wrote down things that didn't need writing down. Delia had asked him once what he did with the notes and he'd said filing, and she'd let it go.

When he left, the girl said, quietly, "Is he—"

"He's fine."

"He seemed—"

"He's fine," Delia said.

The girl went back to work. Her hands were good. That was the thing Delia noticed and didn't want to notice. The girl's hands were good. She had the grip already, the right amount of pressure, not too much, and you couldn't teach that, not really, you could only wait for someone to find it or not. Delia had found it in her fourth month. This one had it at nine-forty on her first morning.

At the break Delia sat outside on the loading dock because she always did, and the girl came out too, uncertain, and sat on the edge with her feet hanging and ate half a sandwich out of the house-shaped bag. The air smelled like brine and diesel. Neither of them said anything for a while, which Delia respected.

"They said you've been here the longest," the girl said finally.

"Not the longest. Marta's got two years on me. She's on nights."

"Oh."

Delia ate her apple. The girl watched the trucks come in and out of the yard like she'd never seen a truck before, which she probably had, but she watched them anyway, and Delia remembered watching them like that. Eleven years ago she'd sat on this same dock and watched the same trucks and thought about how she'd only be here a year, maybe two, just until something else.

"You'll want to keep your hands warm tonight," Delia said. "They'll ache. First week they ache."

"Okay."

"It's not an injury. It's just the—"

"The vibration," the girl said. "Yeah."

Delia finished her apple and threw the core in the barrel and stood up and went back in, and the girl followed, and the line was running again, and Delia took her position and the girl took hers, one station down, where Delia could see her out of the corner of her eye without turning her head.

At the end of the shift Ruel came by with his clipboard and said the girl had done well and the girl said thank you and Ruel left and the girl stood there a second like she was waiting for something else to happen.

"You can go," Delia said.

The girl got her bag out of the fridge and put on her coat and said, "See you tomorrow," and Delia said, "Yeah," and the girl went out through the door and it swung shut and Delia stood in the noise of the stopped line, which was its own kind of quiet, and looked at the empty station one down, where the gloves were hung up neat on the hook, both pairs, the right way, and Delia turned off the lights over that section and went to get her own coat.

The ocean keeps a record of its own—
a hardbound ledger in cold water, spine
relaxed where shallow shelves go soft.

It writes in salt, and where the salt will not
hold, it writes in pressure. Every wreck
below a hundred metres is a clause.
It files the driftwood alphabetically
along the length of continents, and keeps
a tide as a mistake it will revise.

Ask it nothing. It is not the sort

Nothing here is blue. That word is ours,
ours and the brochure's. What the water keeps
is a ledger in a language of pressure:
salt thickening, cold going down like a stone,
the long gray note the shipping lanes sing
that no one on deck can hear.

It has been keeping this longer than we have kept anything.
It does not keep it for us. It files
the whale's low complaint beside the split hull,
the anchor's drag, the one gull going under,
and the sound of a telephone dropped in a bathtub —
all of it the same size down there,
all of it fine.

Somewhere under everything, in the dark
where no light has ever bent, a shrimp
turns toward a smell of decay
and goes on about its life.

The sea gives back what it no longer wants:
a shoe with no one in it,
a bottle with a note gone to pulp,
a child's plastic spade, still bright.

It doesn't mean to. It turns them over,
the way you turn a coat for the lining,
and sets them down in the wrack line
where the gulls stand on one leg and wait.

Every morning the beach is a little emptier
and a little more full of other people's losses.
The tide is not sorry.
It is only tidying.

The printer room smelled of warm ink and cold paper, and nobody had told Mara about the second key.

Her manager, a tired man named Osei, had shown her the press in ten minutes and then left her with a clipboard. "Proof every sheet against the tables," he said. "Check the high water. Check the low water. If the two don't match the moon, don't ship it." Then he was gone to a meeting about a broken van.

So she proofed. The tables for the harbor came in batches of thirty-one days, four tides a day, each time in a column so narrow the digits seemed to lean on one another. She ran her finger down the figures and matched them against the almanac taped to the wall, its corners gone soft.

On the third sheet she found a low tide an hour early. Her stomach dropped. She checked the almanac again. Then the cleaner, a woman in a grey cardigan who had been mopping the corridor since she arrived, leaned into the doorway and pointed at the calendar.

"Clocks went back last night," the cleaner said. "Your table's still on the old time for the first week. Somebody always forgets."

Mara looked at the sheet. The number was right for the sea and wrong for the clock. She marked it, found the setting in the press menu, and changed it. The next sheet came off clean.

"Thank you," she said.

"Don't thank me. Thank the boat that doesn't hit the rocks." The cleaner went back to her mop.

At lunch, Mara ate a sandwich on the loading step and read the notice board. A printed card was pinned under a rusted staple: *Every table is checked twice. Once by the machine. Once by a person who has stood on the quay.* It was signed with initials she didn't know.

She went back in and did the afternoon run. Thirty-one days, four tides each. She did not hurry. She stood, when she could, on the quay side of the window and watched the actual water come in over the stone steps, and when the number on the sheet matched what the water was doing, she initialed the corner the way the card said.

By five the stack was done. Osei came back, looked at the clipboard, and said only, "You found the clock thing."

"Yes."

"Good." He tucked the stack under his arm. "Nobody tells you that one. It's in the cupboard, on the back of the door."

She went to look. It was there, faded, in pencil: *Clocks. First week. Check.*

Outside, the tide was turning. Mara walked to the bus with the almanac's dates still in her head, and for the first time all day she was not afraid of getting something wrong.

Below the last lamp at the harbor wall
the tide leaves its inventory:
one orange float, split along the seam,
a rope gone soft as bread,
a boot with no partner who was ever found.

My father read the water like a ledger.
Forty years of numbers on the back of his hand,
the cold that comes up through the hull in February,
the names of boats still out there,
the sound they made going quiet.

Nobody maps the deep as they map the coast.
Most of it stays a guess.
He told me that and turned the radio down.

In the morning I walk the line where the wet sand darkens
and pick up what the sea is done with.
I keep the float. I keep the rope.
I leave the boot where it is,
in case someone comes back for it.

Marisol had been told the new scheduling system was "intuitive," which in the logistics office at Harmon Freight meant someone had stopped answering questions about it.

Her first morning, Dale Ostrander, twenty-two years on the dispatch desk, stood behind her chair with his coffee held in both hands like he was warming them, though it was June.

"The routing module," he said. "It changed last night. Somebody pushed it at two a.m."

"Okay," Marisol said.

She opened it. The screen had the same grey columns it had yesterday, but the trucks were listed by driver ID now instead of depot, and the depot codes had shifted by a letter. Dale watched her read it the way you'd watch a dog decide whether to bite.

"You're not going to be able to do this," he said. He said it kindly. "Nobody could, the first time."

"What did the old code do with the Tuesday loads?"

"Stacked them. Everything Tuesday stacks."

"Then Tuesday's wrong now, because you've got it split by driver."

Dale didn't answer. She clicked through the column headers one at a time, a little slowly, and found that the new version read the service windows from a field nobody had filled in. She filled them. Two hundred and six rows. The screen went quiet in the way it does when the numbers settle.

"Huh," said Dale.

By ten she had cut the Tuesday stack from nineteen trucks to eleven. By eleven the dispatcher on the north lane was asking who the new girl was, and Dale said, "Marisol, she started today," in a voice that made it sound like a complaint he was still deciding whether to file.

At lunch he sat across from her in the break room and unwrapped a sandwich with great care.

"My wife keeps asking how the job is," he said. "I tell her it's the same job. I've been doing the same job for twenty-two years."

"It's not the same," Marisol said. "The depots moved."

"Yeah." He chewed for a while. "Yeah, I know."

In the afternoon he brought her a laminated card with the old depot codes on it, and under them, in his square handwriting, the new ones, with a line through each old letter. He set it on her keyboard without saying anything. She didn't need it. She kept it anyway.

At five the office emptied. Dale stopped at her desk with his jacket over one arm.

"Same time tomorrow?" he asked.

"Same time."

He nodded and went down the hall toward the elevator, and she heard him stop, and then she heard him say something to no one, a short laugh, the kind that means a thing has finally gone right.

She turned back to the screen. Tomorrow's loads were already coming in, three hundred and forty of them, every one with a window nobody had typed yet.

The new woman came in through the loading dock at 7:52, which nobody did. I know because I was the one watching the camera feed, and the feed showed her standing at the wrong door with a lanyard in one hand and a paper coffee cup balanced on the other forearm, reading a sign she had clearly been told about and did not believe.

I buzzed her in. She said her name was Odile Crane, which I wrote on the sheet, and that she was starting today in Facilities, which I also wrote, though nobody has been in Facilities since the spring the boiler went. I didn't say that. You don't tell people on the first morning what the building is like. They find out or they don't.

She asked where the elevator was. I said it was past the freight lift, and it was, and she took the stairs anyway because she said she wanted to see the floors. Four flights. I counted her breathing on the monitor. By the second landing she had stopped reading the signs and started reading the walls, the old tiling, the brass plates for companies that folded before she was born. She touched one of them on the way past, the way you'd touch a horse.

At the top she came out into the corridor with the broken window and the lamp that hums in the key, and she stood there for longer than a person would stand if she was only lost. Then she asked me, over the intercom, whether the pigeons still got into the vent over the third-floor stairs. I said they did. She said good. She said she'd have to deal with that eventually, but not today.

Her desk was the one by the dead radiator. Nobody had sat there in years, but somebody had cleaned it, which I had not known until she took her coat off and I saw the dust-free outline where a telephone used to be. She put the coffee down exactly on that outline. She got out a pencil, a little steel ruler, and a notebook with the cover taped on. She opened it to a page already half full of drawings of valves, and she bent over it like someone finishing a sentence.

At ten the head of the department came up, a man named Hollis who has not been up here since his retirement party was supposed to happen. He stood in the doorway and asked whether she'd found the key for the cabinet. She said it was in the drawer, under the manual, where the last person had left it. He looked surprised. She said she had assumed.

The machine in the basement has not run since before I started this shift, which is eleven years. It is the old pressure unit that the building was built around, a dark green thing with a dial like a pale moon. Hollis told her it was not to be touched. She asked when someone had last oiled the bearings. He didn't answer, and she said she'd need to see the logs, and he said there were no logs, and she said she would start them.

By lunch I was watching her walk the length of the corridor with her ruler held out in front of her, measuring something I could not see, stopping at the window and writing a number down. At one point she looked straight up at the camera in the ceiling by the stairs, the one that has been pointed at the wall for two years, and she nodded, as if it had told her something she'd half expected.

At six the building emptied. I heard the lock on the loading dock go, and the sound of her footsteps going down all four flights, unhurried, one hand on the rail. On the monitor, the desk by the dead radiator was dark except for the lamp she had left on. The notebook was still open. Someone had drawn a small green circle on the page, and beside it, in pencil, she had written the word *tomorrow*.

I didn't turn the lamp off. I'm not sure why. Somebody should check on it.

Lifeguard's Count, Tuesday

Eleven in the water by two.
Nine by three. One boy,
blue trunks, went out past the buoy
and came back waving a shell
as if the sea had owed him that.

Four more by four, all of them
the age that thinks it's immortal.
The tide tables say high at six.
I write it down. I always write it down.

Nobody in the water is counting.
That's the job. Someone has to.
One of them is a woman
who floats on her back
and watches the gulls not sink.

By five the flags are folded.
Nineteen names in the book,
none of them drowned, all of them
walking up the beach in the same direction,
salt-stiff, not looking back.

Tomorrow I'll start at zero.
The water won't remember.
I'll remember for it.

1. **Night-shift nurse meal planning:** Most meal-kit and grocery apps assume a daytime household, yet night-shift nurses cook at odd hours and often eat from vending machines. A simple service that plans and portions cook-ahead meals around 12-hour rotating schedules would fill a real gap in their week.

2. **Bilingual small-claims paperwork help:** Tenants and small-business owners in immigrant communities often lose small disputes because court forms and procedures are only available in English. A low-cost tool that walks users through filing in their own language, with local court rules built in, would make that process workable for them.

3. **Repair-first appliance subscriptions for renters:** Renters pay for broken appliances they do not own and often wait weeks for landlords to fix them. A subscription that bundles fast, vetted repairs for fridges, washers and water heaters, paid monthly and billed to the renter's own account, would give tenants control over a problem no current service solves.

4. **Dialysis-day transport coordination:** Patients on dialysis need rides three times a week at fixed times, but ride-hailing apps and paratransit schedules often fail them. A dedicated scheduler that matches recurring trips with reliable volunteer and contracted drivers, and syncs with clinic calendars, would reduce missed sessions.

5. **Seasonal farmworker payroll and housing records:** Seasonal farmworkers often move between employers and states, leaving gaps in pay records and housing documentation that affect their benefits and tax filings. A portable, offline-capable record app that growers and workers can both verify would give workers proof of their work history and cut disputes for employers.

1. A scheduling and logistics layer for rural volunteer fire departments, who coordinate by group text and shared paper calendars. The gap is not software — it's that no vendor treats a 40-person volunteer roster as a real org chart, so the tool has to model rank, certification and truck-availability, not just "who's free Tuesday."

2. A payroll and compliance tool for households that employ a nanny, elder-care aide or housekeeper directly, where the "employer" is a family with no HR and no idea they're on the hook for unemployment insurance. The underserved part isn't the worker — it's the family, who quit doing this after the first confusing tax form.

3. Onboarding and certification software for short-line freight railroads, which are exempt from much of what the big carriers have to do and so have no product built for them. The pain is a compliance officer who is also the dispatcher.

The underserved market is the installer, not the utility — the installer has no legal way to take back what it sold.

5. A bookkeeping tool for tiny, cash-heavy vendors at farmers' markets and pop-up stalls, where the entire record is a shoebox. The gap isn't accounting — it's that these vendors are already paying for card readers and a phone, so anything requiring a laptop is dead on arrival.
