1. Payroll rail for seasonal crop crews. Farms hire and release dozens of workers in waves, and every one of them gets paid in cash or a handshake, which is why farm labor is where wage theft and bookkeeping collapse happen. A phone-based system that logs hours by photo of the field ticket and pays out same-day to a prepaid card would sell to the grower as compliance insurance, not charity.

2. Tool library for tradespeople who work out of a hatchback. An electrician needs a $900 thermal camera twice a month and a $400 conduit bender once a quarter; buying both is how a good tradesperson stays broke. A membership depot with same-day pickup, keyed to a job address instead of a home address, turns idle capital into a subscription the trade already understands.

3. After-hours pharmacy courier for night-shift nurses. The people who dispense medication all day are the ones least able to reach a pharmacy during open hours, and their scripts run out at 3 a.m. like everyone else's. A locker-and-rider network that holds refills for pickup at hospital exits, priced per delivery, serves a workforce with money, no time, and a schedule nobody builds for.

4. Death-cleanup booking for renters and small landlords. When a tenant dies alone, the family gets a hazmat bill and the landlord gets a vacancy nobody will touch; both are quoted by the job with no upfront price. A fixed-price dispatch service with vetted crews and photo-verified completion would take the worst week of someone's life and turn it into a line item.

5. Repair brokerage for farm and construction equipment in the off-season. A combine that breaks in October gets fixed in a day; the same combine in February sits for six weeks because every mechanic is booked for harvest. A marketplace that sells winter slots at a discount and routes them to shops with idle bays would fill the calendar both sides can't fill alone.

final: Every spell in the empire is a loan. The mages' guild is a bank, and it lends at interest — a fireball is a small sum, a resurrection is a mortgage on your remaining years, and the interest is paid in luck, in health, in the slow theft of the things you love, collected by men and women who arrive at your door with a ledger and a smile and a very good memory. Sera Vane is a collector, eleven years in the field, and she is very good at her job: she has taken a farmer's rain, a widow's eyesight, a child's name. Then she is sent to close an account that should not exist — a debt so old and so large that the guild itself has been quietly paying it down for two hundred years, and the borrower is not a person but the empire's dead god, who is not dead, only very deep in arrears. Sera has one week to collect or the guild forecloses, and the only thing standing between her and the end of the world is a ledger she can't read and a borrower who has been waiting a long time for someone to knock.

final: For nine hundred years the world has been saved, and that is the problem. The prophecy was fulfilled cleanly a millennium ago — the dragon died, the sundered land stitched itself whole, the songs were written — and every generation since has lived inside the resulting peace like furniture in a finished house. Then a junior auditor at the Bureau of the Fulfillment is assigned a routine fine-print review of the miracle's original terms and finds the accounting doesn't close: the days run three minutes short, every church wall in the realm faces the same direction regardless of how it was built, and no one alive can name the year the saving actually happened. The Bureau exists to make sure the prophecy stays true. Its newest employee is starting to suspect it was never finished — that something has spent nine centuries quietly holding the story up, and that the people who keep the record are the ones who'd have to let it fall.

Le Guin and Terry Pratchett who want the stakes of a sword-and-sorcery quest told in the language of arithmetic, with the cost of every decision on the page.

Most people meet the dead at the funeral. Nell Ibarra meets them three weeks later, in the room they died in, after the police have taken the body and the tape and left the smell.

She runs a biohazard cleanup crew out of a storage unit off the highway. Three vans, two employees, a license the state took eighteen months to grant. When a landlord calls the county, the county calls Nell. She walks into what's left: the stain bled down through the subfloor, the flies in their last week, the pill organizer with Tuesday still in it. Her job is to make the room smell like nothing. She is very good at her job.

The trouble is what she knows before she starts. Nell can read a room the way a coroner reads a liver. A man who died alone with a cross-stitch hoop on the chair and no thread in the house did not die the way the report says. A house with forty-one jars of saved rainwater and one empty shelf at eye level has a person missing from it. She can't testify to any of this. What she does is a trade, not evidence, and the smell of it doesn't hold up in court.

So she keeps a notebook. Not the deaths — the cleaning. Mileage, chemical lots, hours. And in the margins, in her square landlord's handwriting, what didn't fit: the second toothbrush dry as a bone, the dog bowl scrubbed clean when the dog died in March, the receipt for two coffees.

She is not brave. She has walked out of rooms that would have gotten her killed and reported the rooms that wouldn't. She has a bad back, a mother in Tucson who thinks she is a maid, and a rule she has never broken: she does not open the mail. The mail is not hers. She will stand over a dead stranger's kitchen table with a respirator on and a HEPA filter screaming and not touch a single envelope. It is the only line she has, and she holds it like a railing.

That's how she catches the third one. Not by solving it — by being sent back. Same address, different tenant, fourteen months apart, and the second room smelled of the first. Not decomposition. Something under it. A soap. Not the soap in either house. She remembered it the way you remember a song from a car in 2009.

She sat in her van with the engine off and the notebook open and did the thing she has never done. She read a name off a piece of mail she'd already broken her rule to look at. Then she called the number on the card of the one detective who had ever bothered to learn her name.

She still cleans. The vans still run. She has not been asked to testify, and she would say no. The room tells her what happened, and then she takes it apart until the room says nothing, and both of those are the job.

**Dunmore Okafor-Hale, 52, municipal pest-control officer for the east districts**

Dunmore has spent eleven years counting pigeons for the city. Not culling them, mostly. Counting them, tagging the ones that nest in the clock tower of St Agnes, logging which roofs have been fouled and which have been quietly cleared by someone who doesn't want a complaint filed. The job means he is up before the bakeries and on rooftops, stairwells and loading bays that no detective ever walks through. People stop noticing him the way they stop noticing weather.

He has a bad left knee, a flask of stewed tea that tastes of the flask, and a habit of speaking to the birds by name. The names are not cute. They are the names of the people who used to feed them: Mrs Ferriter, a retired seamstress; a dock foreman called Pell; a boy whose name he never learned, only his coat.

**Dolores Imhof, 58, restorative cosmetician at Halvorsen & Daughters Funeral Home**

Dolores has spent twenty-six years giving the dead the faces their families asked for. She knows that a bruise under foundation shows as a faint green at the edge, that a cut hidden with wax has a particular sheen, and that a family who insists on "something natural" is usually hiding a thing they are ashamed of. She has never been a detective. She has only ever been the last person in a room who sees a body before the world does.

She keeps a ledger of what she was asked to cover and what she actually found. She does not share it. Her colleagues think she is fussy; the coroner's office thinks she is an excellent witness who never offers an opinion.

Her method is patient and slightly unpleasant. She talks to the dead while she works, out loud, and she has learned that the living grow careless in the hour between death and the viewing, when they come in to choose lipstick shades and say things they would never say upstairs in the parlor. She listens to who asks for what, which shade they reject, who arrives early and sits with the body alone.

She is widowed, dry, and unimpressed by authority. She cannot drive well and will not learn. Her one real vanity is her hands, which she moisturizes every night.

**Hook:** A wealthy widow asks Dolores to make her husband look "rested, like a man who died in his sleep." Dolores lifts the collar of his shirt and finds a bruise in the shape of a cufflink, pressed in hard. The widow has already signed the death certificate. Dolores has been paid, and she is not sure she wants to be right.

**Dorothea "Dot" Vance, 58, mortuary cosmetologist, Harrow & Sons Funeral Home**

Dot has done up nine hundred and twelve faces in twenty-six years, and she can tell you which of them were lying to the coroner. Not lying out loud. Lying in the skin: the faint crescent under a left eye where someone's knuckle went in, the blue ghost along a wrist that a sleeve was meant to hide, the yellowing of a bruise she recognizes from the way it sits when it was given a week before the death, not an hour. She keeps a ledger of these in a green notebook, and nobody has ever asked to read it.

Her method is patience and a small, cold kit: a chalk-white base, a sable brush, a jar of concealer the colour of old piano keys. She covers what the family should not have to see. Dot's rule, which she has never once broken, is that she only conceals what is not part of the story.

When the body of Ray Okafor comes in on a Tuesday, the sheriff's report says "fall, stairwell, accidental." His widow asks for an open casket. The deputy wants it closed by Friday. Dot lifts the collar of his shirt with two gloved fingers and finds four small, perfectly spaced marks on the left side of his neck, healed at the edges, dated in her head to about ten days back.

Four marks, spaced the width of a human hand. Someone held him there before he ever reached the stairs.

She has a choice, and she knows it. She can cover the marks, as she has covered a hundred things she was paid to cover. Or she can take the green notebook out of the drawer, write a single line, and carry it across town to the one detective in the county who has ever returned her calls.

Dot picks up the sable brush. Then she puts it down, and reaches for her coat.

Wren Fowler empties houses for the county. When someone dies without family in the district, the sheriff's office calls her, she walks through with a clipboard, and she decides what was a life and what was trash.

It takes two days, usually. Day one is the obvious things — the furniture, the dishes, the clothes that still hold a shape. Day two is the part nobody wants. The medicine cabinet. The freezer. The boxes under the bed that were taped shut twice. Wren photographs everything before she touches it, then bags the keeping and hauls the rest. She has a nose for which sock drawer was opened in a panic, which coffee table had something taken off it in a hurry, which bill was paid the week someone stopped being able to pay anything.

She is not a detective. She has said this to the sheriff twice, both times holding a bag of somebody's teeth.

The thing about Wren is that she has never met a person she's emptied. She knows them the way you know a song's last chord — the residue, the shape of where the sound was. She knows Ed Pardo had a girlfriend he never mentioned, because there's a woman's hairbrush in a drawer of men's undershirts and no dish in the apartment that could hold two people's dinner. She knows the young man on Delaney Street was left-handed and stopped sleeping, because his lamp was dragged to the other side of the bed and his sheets have the scuff of someone who got up at the same hour every night to stand at a window. She knows these things because they are the only things left, and she has learned to read them like a page someone tore out.

When the sheriff brings her a case that isn't hers — a woman missing, not dead, no house to clear — Wren says no. Then she goes home and stands in her own kitchen, and looks at it the way she looks at everyone else's, and can't find anything in it that would tell a stranger she was ever happy. She calls the sheriff back the next morning.

She moves through the case the way she moves through a house: slowly, in the wrong order, opening the cabinets last. She does not interview people. She looks at their kitchens while they talk. She asks what someone threw away in the last month, and watches their hands when they answer.

Her method is a method of absence. She solves cases backward, from what is missing, and the only reason she is good at it is that she has spent nine years believing that the missing thing is the truest thing about a life — which is either wisdom or a wound, and Wren has stopped trying to sort out which.

Think of a city so large that no one has ever seen all of it, and where nothing is ever delivered whole.

You want to tell your sister, who lives across the city, something long — the story of your week. In this city you do not write it down and mail it. You cut the story into small pieces, each piece short enough to shout across one alley to a neighbor. Then you stand at your window and shout the first piece to whoever is nearest.

That neighbor does not deliver it. He shouts it to the next person he can see. That person shouts it onward. Piece by piece, alley by alley, your story hops across the city toward your sister's building. Each piece may take a different route. Some go over rooftops, some through courtyards, some get shouted ten times before they get anywhere.

And here is the strange part: nobody carries your words for you. At every window, the person who hears a piece says it again from memory, word for word, and only then passes it on. If a piece is dropped — the neighbor was asleep, the window was shut — the person waiting further along notices a piece is missing and asks for it again. It comes by another alley. Nothing is lost as long as someone, somewhere, still has a copy.

Your sister's building has a doorman whose whole job is to stand there and gather pieces all day. When every piece of your story has finally arrived, in whatever order it happened to come, he lays them out together and hands your sister the whole week. It reads exactly as you said it.

That is how anything reaches anyone here, every time, thousands of times a second, all over a city nobody can see the edges of. The mail is never sent. It is remembered, piece by piece, from window to window, until it is complete.

Imagine a city where every house has a number, and the postal service delivers letters by passing them from one post office to the next until they arrive.

You want to read a page from a faraway friend's house. You write a request on a slip of paper: "Please send me the letter at house 4821." You hand it to your local post office. The clerk does not know where house 4821 is. He only knows which post office is closer to it, so he passes your slip to the next office in that direction. That office does the same. The slip hops from office to office, each one choosing the next best route, until it reaches the office that serves house 4821.

Then the reply travels the other way. The friend's copy of the letter is cut into small pages, each stamped with a number so they can be put back in order. The pages do not have to travel together or by the same road. One might go through five offices, another through seven. If a road is blocked, the offices reroute the pages around it. At your door, the pages are put back in sequence and you read the whole letter.

In this city, the houses are computers and phones, the numbers are addresses, the post offices are the routers that pass information along, and the pages are the small pieces data is broken into. Your web browser is the clerk who writes the request, and a website is simply a letter kept at a particular house, ready to be asked for.

The internet is the whole network of post offices working together, agreed on one set of rules for addressing, passing and reassembling, so that any house in the city can write to any other.

Nobody in the town can walk to every other house, so when you want something from across town, you write a letter with the address on it and hand it to the postal clerk at the corner. The clerk doesn't know the whole town, only which neighbor to pass the letter to. That neighbor passes it on, and on, until it reaches the right house.

The letter doesn't travel whole. Before it leaves, it's cut into small numbered slips, each with the address and its place in the order. The slips can take different roads, arrive out of sequence, and wait at different corners. At the destination, the receiver lays them in order and reads the message. If a slip goes missing, the receiver asks for it again.

The tide gauge reader

Nobody thanks me for the numbers.
I walk the pier at six, unlock the hut,
and write what the water did all night
while everyone was sleeping on the hill.

It goes down. It comes back up.
That is the whole plot and it never ends,
which is why the sea is not a story.
A story ends. It has a reason.

I keep it in a book: the height,
the hour, the weather if it mattered.
Sometimes a storm will pull the line
so far up the page I have to start a new one.

People come here to feel small.
I come here to make it small enough to hold —
one more line, one more morning,
the enormous thing written down at last.

My first day, Marguerite walked me around the floor and told me which chair was mine.

It was the one by the window. The seat was still warm from the last person, she said, and laughed, and then didn't, and then said it wasn't warm, that was a joke. It was a joke. The cushion had a dip in it the size of a person.

The job was putting numbers in a system. Nine to five, one hour, and the numbers came in by email and you put them in the system and the system made them into other numbers and those went out. Marguerite trained me for three hours. She was patient, and she was watching me the whole time like I was a scale she was weighing something on.

Think of the internet as a postal service for messages that never sit still.

Say you want a recipe your aunt wrote. You don't walk to her house and ask. You write down a request: "Please send me the lasagna recipe." You put the note in an envelope and write where it is going on the outside. The postal service doesn't know what is inside, and it doesn't need to. It only needs the address.

The envelope doesn't travel whole. Your aunt's answer is too long for one envelope, so it is cut into dozens of small numbered pages. Each page gets its own envelope, its own address, and its own number. The pages travel by different routes. Some go through a sorting office in one city, some through another. The sorting offices are the routers, and each one reads the address and passes the envelope to the next office closer to its destination.

Pages can arrive out of order, or a few can get lost. That is fine. Your mailbox keeps the numbers, notices what is missing, and asks for those pages again. When everything is present, it puts them back in order, and the full recipe appears as if it had come in one piece.

The addresses work like this. Every device on the network has a number, a bit like a house number, so the postal system knows where to deliver. A separate directory, a bit like a phone book, turns a name you can remember, such as a website's name, into the number the post office needs. You type the name, the directory provides the number, and the pages set off.

Finally, there are the rules everyone agrees to follow: how to write an address, how to number the pages, how to say "this page did not arrive, please resend." Because the whole world uses the same rules, a letter written in one country can be delivered in another without anyone translating it.

So when you open a web page, you are sending a request by mail, and the answer comes back cut into pages that are sorted and reassembled on your side.

A protagonist for a mystery should be someone the crime cannot help but reveal itself to. Most detectives look for the secret. This one has already been told it, and cannot make anyone believe her.

**Wren Achterberg, sixty-one, professional house-sitter.** Twelve years in other people's homes, usually while they're away for a season or a death in the family. She keeps their plants alive, takes in the mail, learns the way a house sounds when it is empty, the way it sounds when it is not.

She is compulsive about the truth. She cannot lie, cannot shade, cannot even let a kind lie stand — and she can hear one. Not metaphorically. A lie lands in her like a dropped plate: the pitch of a voice goes flat, breath shortens, a sentence gets a hair too smooth. It is not mind-reading, it is closer to perfect pitch, and it is useless as evidence, inadmissible as testimony, and it has cost her every job where tact mattered.

**The case:** She is sitting a house on the coast for a family who will not be back. On the fourth night, the mail brings a letter addressed to the owner in the owner's own handwriting, dated three days after the owner died. Wren hears the neighbor's story about the death and the story is wrong — not the facts, the *sound*. So she begins, in the way she knows, with the only two tools she has: a key ring to a house that is not hers, and the ability to hear what every person in this town is trying not to say.

**What makes her strange on the page:** she is a guest everywhere and a citizen nowhere. She is invited into people's most private rooms and is never asked to stay. She can solve the murder and will never be believed, because her gift cannot be shown, only suffered. The mystery is not whether she's right. It is what she does when being right is not enough — and what a person who cannot lie does with a town that has been lying to itself for forty years.

**Her flaw, and the reason she keeps taking the jobs:** she cannot forgive a lie, including her own. She left a husband twenty years ago over one he told, and she has never once admitted that she could have stayed and heard him out. Every empty house she keeps is a version of the house she walked out of.

Imagine a town where nobody ever locks a door, because nothing can be stolen — anything you take, you've only copied. The original stays on the shelf where you found it.

You want a recipe from the woman on Elm Street. You don't drive over. You write on a slip of paper: "Elm Street, the house with the blue door, the recipe card in the kitchen." You hand it to your neighbor. He doesn't know her either — but he knows someone who knows someone, and each person passes the slip along until it lands in the right kitchen. She copies the recipe, and the copy comes back the same way, hand to hand, into yours.

That is the whole thing. That's the internet.

final:
Picture a village of a few hundred houses. Every house has, bolted to its front wall, a huge board. Every board is the same board: it's the entire village's shared knowledge — everyone's letters, recipes, photos, gossip, weather.

Here's the strange part. No one owns the board. There's no central copy in a town hall, no master shelf. Each house's board is its own copy, and when you write something new on yours, the village's other boards gradually fill it in too. Slowly, by different routes, they all catch up with each other. So when you "look something up," you aren't reaching into a distant building. You're walking out your front door and reading your own wall, which happens to know what everyone else wrote.

Nothing travels whole. If you want to send a long letter, you tear it into a hundred scraps, number them, and hand each scrap to a different neighbor. Each neighbor passes it to another, choosing their own way through the village. The scraps take wildly different paths; some are lost, some arrive twice, and the scrap gets handed on again—no one in the middle reads the whole letter or knows what it says. At the far wall, the scraps are laid out by their numbers and pieced back into your letter. If a piece never shows up, the sender just makes another copy and throws it into the crowd again.

That's why it's hard to knock down. There's no single door, no single building, no single shelf. You'd have to silence every wall in the village at once, and every wall is holding everyone's work for everyone else.

And that's the last strange thing: the village's whole memory lives in the walls of ordinary houses, kept in trust for neighbors nobody has met.
